World.title: Officials report 43% drop in Guanajuato homicides: Friday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

📉 Guanajuato homicides down 43% this year : At Friday’s mañanera in Irapuato, National Public Security System chief Marcela Figueroa reported an average of 3.2 homicides per day in Guanajuato in August, 75% lower than in February 2025, the state’s most violent month under Sheinbaum. The daily average for the first eight months of 2026 was 4, a 43% year-over-year decline. This year is on track to be the state’s least violent since 2017.

: At Friday’s mañanera in Irapuato, National Public Security System chief Marcela Figueroa reported an average of 3.2 homicides per day in Guanajuato in August, 75% lower than in February 2025, the state’s most violent month under Sheinbaum. The daily average for the first eight months of 2026 was 4, a 43% year-over-year decline. This year is on track to be the state’s least violent since 2017. 🚔 10,699 arrests in Guanajuato since October 2024 : Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said 172 of the people detained through Aug. 31 were “priority targets.” In the same period, authorities also seized more than 6 tonnes of drugs and over 2,000 firearms, and dismantled two methamphetamine labs.

: Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said 172 of the people detained through Aug. 31 were “priority targets.” In the same period, authorities also seized more than 6 tonnes of drugs and over 2,000 firearms, and dismantled two methamphetamine labs. ⚖️ Suspect arrested in murder of Spanish student : García Harfuch confirmed that a man known as “El Trompas,” identified as Francisco Javier Meléndez, was detained Thursday in Cuautla, Morelos, in connection with the murder of Claudia Tacoronte Aguilera, a 21-year-old Spanish exchange student.

: García Harfuch confirmed that a man known as “El Trompas,” identified as Francisco Javier Meléndez, was detained Thursday in Cuautla, Morelos, in connection with the murder of Claudia Tacoronte Aguilera, a 21-year-old Spanish exchange student. 📞 Sheinbaum says her call with Trump was “very good”: Sheinbaum said she spoke to the U.S. president about trade issues on Wednesday. She said differences have not yet been resolved, but that good progress is being made.

Why today’s mañanera matters

President Claudia Sheinbaum held her Friday morning press conference in Irapuato, a city in Guanajuato, a state that in recent years has been Mexico’s most violent in terms of total homicides.

At the mañanera, federal security officials took the opportunity to outline the progress that has been made in combating violence in the state. Much of the violence in Guanajuato is related to organized crime, and, in particular, a long-running turf war between the Jalisco New Generation Cartel and the Santa Rosa de Lima Cartel.

Also of note at today’s mañanera was Security Minister Omar García Harfuch’s confirmation that a man known as “El Trompas” was detained in connection with the murder in Cuautla, Morelos, of Claudia Tacoronte Aguilera, a 21-year-old Spanish woman who was studying at the Autonomous University of the State of Morelos on an exchange program.

In addition, Sheinbaum spoke briefly about her trade-focused call on Wednesday with U.S. President Donald Trump. The call came less than two weeks after Trump asserted that Mexico has “nothing” the United States needs — apart from “hot tamales” and “tomatoes” — and therefore the U.S. could cease trading with its southern neighbor. In reality, Mexico supplies a wide range of goods to the U.S., and the economies of the two countries are highly integrated.

Homicides down 43% in Guanajuato this year

National Public Security System chief Marcela Figueroa reported that there was an average of 3.2 homicides per day in Guanajuato in August. Figueroa highlighted that the daily average in August was 75% lower than that in February 2025, the most violent month in Guanajuato since Sheinbaum took office in October 2024.

She reported that there was an average of 4 homicides per day in Guanajuato in the first eight months of 2026, a reduction of 43% compared to 2025. Data presented by Figueroa showed that 2026 is on track to be the least violent year in Guanajuato since 2017.

More than 10,000 arrests in Guanajuato since Sheinbaum took office

García Harfuch reported that more than 10,600 people were arrested in Guanajuato between Oct. 1, 2024 — the date Sheinbaum was sworn in as president — and Aug. 31, 2026.

Of the 10,699 people detained in the state in the period, 172 were “priority targets,” García Harfuch said.

He also reported that over 6 tonnes of drugs and more than 2,000 firearms were seized in Guanajuato between October 2024 and August 2026. In addition, two methamphetamine laboratories were dismantled, García Harfuch said.

Suspect arrested in Morelos femicide case

García Harfuch reported that federal and state security forces detained Francisco Javier “N” on Thursday in connection with the murder of Tacoronte. The suspect has been identified as Francisco Javier Meléndez in media reports. He was detained in Cuautla, a city around 40 kilometers southeast of Cuernavaca, the capital of Morelos.

García Harfuch first reported the arrest in a social media post on Thursday evening.

On Friday morning, he said that “preventing femicides and addressing violence against women” is a “priority” of the federal government.

En #Morelos, autoridades federales y estatales detienen a un hombre por el feminicidio de una joven de nacionalidad española. https://t.co/mLtMcbL8ch pic.twitter.com/jyLFGK6NtE — Secretaría de Seguridad y Protección Ciudadana (@SSPCMexico) September 18, 2026

Sheinbaum discloses ‘very good’ call with Trump

Sheinbaum told reporters that she spoke to Trump on Wednesday.

“It was a scheduled call,” she said, adding that she often speaks to the U.S. president without publicly announcing their discussions.

“Why? Because we’re making progress on trade issues,” Sheinbaum said.

She said that differences over trade have not yet been resolved, but stressed that good progress is being made.

Reuters reported on Sept. 11 that “Mexico and the United States are racing to reach a bilateral trade deal before the U.S. midterm elections,” which will take place on Nov. 3. As part of a bilateral deal, Mexico is seeking the reduction — or ideally the elimination — of U.S. tariffs on Mexican steel, aluminum and vehicles.

On July 1, the United States announced that it had declined to renew the USMCA in its “current form,” although the three-way pact remains in effect.

Sheinbaum said her call with Trump was “very good.”

“… The Foreign Affairs Minister Roberto Velasco and Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard were with me in the conversation,” she added.

By Mexico News Daily chief staff writer Peter Davies (peter.davies@mexiconewsdaily.com)

World.title: A mountain, a legend and a dream: Chavela Vargas’ Tepoztlán home
World.content:
The story goes that when Chavela Vargas, the iconic singer of Mexican ranchera music, visited Tepoztlán in the state of Morelos, she was captivated by the mountain known as Chalchitépetl. She was amazed by its beauty, but more importantly, Vargas was struck by the fact that she had dreamed of that exact formation many times, despite never having seen it before. After seeing the mountain, she decided to make the town her home.

“She came, knocked on the door, and asked what she had to do to live here, and that is how she ended up staying,” said Gerardo Ramírez, the manager of Casa Chavela.

How Chavela chose her home

Vargas, who was Costa Rican by birth and famous for her declaration, “We Mexicans are born wherever the hell we want,” arrived in Mexico at age 17 and began her career singing in cantinas. She was later discovered and mentored by the iconic Mexican singer José Alfredo Jiménez. Vargas was a close friend — and perhaps more — to figures like Frida Kahlo, Diego Rivera, Joaquín Sabina and Federico García Lorca, and she became a major icon for the LGBTQ+ movement.

Vargas arrived in Tepoztlán in 2007, by which time she was already a legend whose career was celebrated throughout Latin America and Europe. The house she chose was located on the Tepoztlán-Cuernavaca Federal Highway and belonged to Emma Teresa Ortiz, known as “Monina.” At the time, the property was called Quinta Monina. There were once two other houses on the property, which were also inhabited by artists, including the famous actress María Eugenia Llamas.

When Vargas arrived at Quinta Monina, she requested changes to the house that reflected her strong personality and creativity. Today, the building has become a landmark of Mexican architectural design.

An architectural gem

The initial design of Casa Chavela was straightforward, with a large hallway connecting the kitchen, living room, dining room and two bedrooms, as well as a terrace. This was later transformed at Vargas’ request. Today, the house is a blend of volcanic rock — typical of Tepoztlán construction — and large windows with orange ironwork that bathe the interior in light, reminiscent of functionalist architecture.

“The reason all the ironwork is this orange color is that, when Chavela moved into this house, she asked for the terrace to be enclosed with glass, which has become a distinctive feature of the house,” Ramírez explained.

In 2020, the Romero family — comprising architects, designers and engineers — purchased the property and remodeled it using local materials, inspired by Vargas’ original ideas.

They replaced the tiles, added two rooms and expanded the orange ironwork windows to the bedrooms and dining room, giving the house openness and light. In terms of decoration, the home features ocote pine crafts from the nearby town of Ocotitlán, and Vargas’ iconic jorongos (traditional Mexican woolen garments) hang on the walls. Her famous equipal — a handcrafted, pre-Hispanic-style armchair — lined in bright colors, can also be admired.

A place for art, inspiration and creativity

The surrounding gardens contain more than 60 trees that the owners have added in recent years, while preserving the original vegetation. A Y-shaped pool and numerous totems made from traditional clay from Amayuca, Morelos, add to the house’s unique atmosphere.

A podium in the shape of a kiosk crowns the garden and is used for ceremonies such as weddings. Furthermore, as the land slopes down, an area of old stables appears; these now serve as rooms for artists in residence.

Further down is a huge open living room that serves as a cultural space for concerts, meetings and exhibitions. While Casa Chavela welcomes guests through Airbnb and by renting out rooms like a hotel, it also has a social purpose: It offers free lodging to artists in residence.

Since 2022, five artists have completed residencies of between two and three weeks, donating their work to the house collection. Many of these pieces were inspired by Vargas, though the work can cover any topic.

Vargas spent her final years in this house, from 2007 to 2012. During this time, she found peace and formed a profound relationship with the mountain of her dreams, Chalchitépetl. After a complicated and magnificent life, she found a place of contemplation here, as well as the strength to overcome her struggles. Casa Chavela is undoubtedly imbued with the personal magic and spirit of her personality.

Ana Paula de la Torre is a Mexican journalist and collaborator for various outlets, including Milenio, Animal Político, Vice, Newsweek en Español, Televisa and Mexico News Daily.

World.title: Which neighborhoods in Mexico City have the highest seismic risk?
World.content:
First of all, there is no such thing as Earthquake Month in Mexico City or anywhere in Mexico. One could argue every day is Earthquake Day because of the country’s high seismic activity. Still, residents carry the heavy grief of the coincidences of Sept. 19, the date on which — in completely different years and decades — devastating earthquakes caused the capital to succumb to panic and ruin.

Although scientists know it is practically impossible to predict these seismic events, residents cannot shake the thought that an earthquake might hit Mexico City on Sept. 19.

Beyond the dark humor, the reality is that because Mexico City sits on ancient lakebeds, some areas of the capital are at greater risk during an earthquake.

Colonia Cuauhtémoc

The Cuauhtémoc borough is among the areas most prone to earthquake damage in Mexico City. The neighborhood of the same name, in the heart of the borough, suffered severe damage after the earthquakes of 2017 and 2022. Bordered by Paseo de la Reforma, Juárez and the Historic Center, Colonia Cuauhtémoc remains a hybrid between the business world of tall corporate buildings and residential life.

Besides having some of the tallest buildings in the city, the neighborhood suffers the consequences of poor urban planning. Because it sits primarily in Zone III (Lake Zone) of the city’s seismic microzonation, an area characterized by deep, highly compressible lacustrine clay deposits, it experiences significant wave amplification and has suffered severe damage during historical earthquakes.

Colonia Centro

The Historic Center has layers upon layers of Mexico City’s architectural and archaeological history, sitting directly atop the ruins of Tenochtitlán. For this reason, it is also one of the neighborhoods most affected by strong earthquakes.

Despite being one of the areas with the greatest archaeological and historical wealth in the country, the buildings and temples — some more than 500 years old — bear the scars of earthquakes. A striking example is the Church of Loreto, which tilts noticeably because of seismic tremors.

Colonias Roma Norte and Sur

The streets of Mexico City are known for chaos, and in the Roma Norte and Roma Sur neighborhoods, some of that chaos is visible in the cracks in the pavement. The streets are broken by tree roots pushing through the asphalt, but more often by the shockwaves from major earthquakes.

Efforts by the Cuauhtémoc borough cannot fully patch the scars of past quakes. Among the trendy bars and local cafes lies a stark reminder that this is one of the areas most affected by seismic activity in central Mexico.

Colonia Condesa

The ever-iconic Colonia Condesa, besides being a favorite spot for Sunday strolls, is also sadly one of the areas most affected by earthquakes. The neighborhood rests firmly within Zone III (Lake Zone), which, as noted, is predominantly composed of thick, highly soft clay deposits that dramatically amplify seismic vibrations during major quakes.

For this reason, several older and poorly retrofitted structures collapsed during major events like the 2017 earthquake. Furthermore, due to corruption and a perceived disregard for the safety guidelines required by Mexico City, many fear similar outcomes in the event of future strong earthquakes, as reported by the newspaper Excélsior.

Colonia Juárez

Colonia Juárez does not wait until June to celebrate Pride; popular nightlife venues in the area operate year-round. Despite the area’s lively atmosphere, it is also one of the neighborhoods where earthquakes are felt most intensely.

During low-intensity tremors, business owners and residents often evacuate into the streets even before the seismic alert sounds — a sign of how accustomed locals are to the ground shaking.

Andrea Fischer contributes to the features desk at Mexico News Daily. She has edited and written for National Geographic en Español and Muy Interesante México, and continues to be an advocate for anything that screams science. Or yoga. Or both.

World.title: A dog dressed as a taco stand wins Morelia’s pre-Grito Patriotic Pup Contest
World.content:
Pet owners and dog lovers in Michoacán’s state capital kicked off Independence Day festivities early last Sunday, taking part in a Most Patriotic Pup contest.

Morelia’s popular bakery and pastry shop Melón o Sandía sponsored the first-ever “Concurso de Perritos Patrióticos” (Patriotic Puppy Contest) at the city’s Parque Canino 1 on the grounds of the Convention Center in the southern part of the capital.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by MELÓN O SANDÍA (@melonosandia.morelia)

Around 40 dogs participated in the contest, which attracted over 100 onlookers who acted as the voting audience. No entry fee was needed, though owners were required to register their dogs in advance via an online sign-up form.

Dogs of all shapes and sizes showed up in patriotic outfits, ranging from tiny mariachi suits to rebozos and tricolor ribbons, while others were decorated with popular Mexican dishes. A few even were adorned with a food stand theme.

Melón o Sandía hosted the event and offered gift vouchers for the winners, while PetFood Morelia and Maka Recetas — a Mexican pet food company — also supplied prizes for winners and participants.

The top three “best-dressed” dogs won gift vouchers for Melón o Sandía, ranging from 500 pesos (US $29) to 1,000 pesos (US $58) to 1,500 pesos (US $87), and each of the three winners received prize packages from PetFood Morelia worth 1,300 pesos (US $75).

A dog named Maple, who sported an outfit designed to look like a complete taquitos al pastor “Alemán” food stand (a play on words linking the popular “tacos in the style of a shepherd” with the familiar dog breed), was declared “The Most Patriotic Dog.”

Also on offer at Maple’s food stand were “Guaguacoa” (a pun on the sound of a dog bark and barbacoa) and “Suaperro” (a portmanteau between “suadero” — a thin, fatty cut of beef — and the Spanish word for dog).

Second place went to Bebukis, who was adorned with a food tray featuring elotes y lomitos (corn kernels and pork loin) and a tiny cowboy hat, while the third-place prize was awarded to a little pup named Avenita, who carried a bowl of red pozole almost twice its size on its back.

With reports from Mi Morelia and Melón o Sandía

World.title: Fire damages 108 stalls in Acapulco’s Central Market
World.content:
A fire broke out at Acapulco’s Central Market early Wednesday, damaging more than 100 stalls. No serious injuries or fatalities were reported.

The blaze began before 6 a.m. and quickly spread to engulf scores of stalls in the footwear and flowers sections of the market, the largest in Acapulco.

Some 100 firefighters brought the fire under control on Wednesday, but continued working on Thursday to “cool down” three spots from which smoke was still emanating, according to the Acapulco-based newspaper El Sur.

The cause of the blaze hasn’t been officially determined, but a short circuit in the market’s electrical system has been identified as a possible trigger. Raúl Noyola Rocha, Acapulco’s civil protection chief, said Thursday that an investigation by the Guerrero Attorney General’s Office would take up to a week to yield results.

The Acapulco municipal government on Wednesday reported a preliminary toll of 90 stalls damaged — 75 in the market’s footwear section and 15 in the flowers section.

However, Acapulco Mayor Leticia Lozano said Thursday that a total of 108 stalls were in fact damaged.

El Sol de Acapulco reported that cleanup work, including the removal of rubble, was taking place at the market on Thursday. Mexican soldiers and affected shopkeepers were assisting the efforts.

El Sol de Acapulco reported that there was still smoke in the market on Thursday and that “new outbreaks of flames” were occurring. The newspaper also reported the presence of “burnt metallic structures” and “goods reduced to ashes.”

Affected stallholders are set to receive an initial economic support payment from the municipal government on Friday. The government didn’t specify how much each stallholder will get.

Local authorities are also planning to adapt part of the market to accommodate up to 110 temporary stalls while the footwear and flower sections are rebuilt. El Sol de Acapulco reported that a total of 12 fires have now occurred at the Acapulco Central Market, which was built in 1969. A massive blaze in 2023 destroyed around 570 stalls.

With reports from El Sol de Acapulco and El Sur

World.title: Ghana National Cathedral Board Dissolved, Site Due Back by 31 October
World.content:
GHANA · POLITICS

Key Facts — What happened Mahama dissolved the Board of Trustees of the National Cathedral of Ghana Project on 18 September 2026.

— Who signed Mahama Ayariga, Minister for Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs, signed the letter.

— The deadline Trustees must work with the project consultant and hand over the site by 31 October 2026.

— The reason given The letter says the handover will allow government to determine the future of the project.

— The catch The forensic audit of roughly US$90 million in spending is with the Attorney General and not yet public.

— What comes next A Christian Council of Ghana committee has one month to propose funding and location options.

A week after saying churches, not taxpayers, should pay for the cathedral, the president has removed its trustees and asked for the site back.

The Anglican Holy Trinity Cathedral, Accra’s oldest church; the unfinished National Cathedral project is a separate site (Photo: Williams Penuku, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

President John Dramani Mahama has dissolved the Ghana National Cathedral board with immediate effect. A letter dated 18 September 2026 orders the trustees to hand the project site to a government ministry by 31 October.

What the letter to the Ghana National Cathedral board says

The letter says the president “has directed the dissolution of the Board of Trustees” with immediate effect. Minister Mahama Ayariga signed it on 18 September 2026.

The trustees must liaise with the project consultant and formally hand over the site to his ministry. The deadline is 31 October 2026.

The letter says the handover is needed “to allow government to determine the future of the project”. It does not say what that future will be.

Copies went to the Secretary to the President, the Chief of Staff and the head of the National Cathedral Secretariat. No other instructions were made public.

The board was chaired by Apostle Prof Opoku Onyinah. The minister thanked members “for your commitment to promoting the Christian faith in the country”.

A follow-up to last week’s funding row

The move comes days after Mahama spoke about the cathedral during a citizens’ engagement tour of the Upper West Region. There he said public money should not fund the project.

He called the cathedral a personal pledge to God by former President Nana Akufo-Addo, not national policy. He suggested Christians could each give 1,000 cedis (about US$87 at 18 September 2026 rates).

Mahama also questioned the location. The site sits among government buildings in Accra, and judges’ homes and diplomatic buildings were pulled down to clear it.

The dissolution turns that position into an administrative step. The state is now taking direct control of the site while the churches consider whether they can pay.

How the case built up since 2024

In November 2024, Ghana’s Commission on Human Rights and Administrative Justice (CHRAJ) reported on the project. It recommended a forensic audit and possible prosecution of the Board of Trustees over procurement breaches.

CHRAJ found that a US$312 million construction contract with Ribade Company Limited went against mandatory provisions of Ghana’s Public Procurement Act. It urged further investigation of the trustees.

On 18 July 2025, the presidency said the National Cathedral Secretariat was dissolved with effect from 1 May 2025. It also said legal processes had begun to disband the board.

The presidency also asked the Auditor-General to carry out a full forensic audit. It told the Attorney General to take legal steps to end the project contract.

The presidency also asked the Auditor-General to carry out a full forensic audit. The 18 September 2026 letter now completes the break with the old board.

The 18 September 2026 letter now completes the break with the old board. It comes nearly two years after the CHRAJ report.

The US$90 million question

Mahama said this month that the forensic audit is finished and with the Attorney General. He said it looks at how about US$90 million was spent.

He promised to give a copy to the Christian Council of Ghana so it can review the spending. The report itself has not been published.

The US$90 million figure is the president’s own estimate. No detailed, published breakdown of the project’s total cost has been released.

What the churches are doing

On 11 September 2026, Christian Council chairman Rev Enoch Nii Narh Thompson announced a technical committee on the cathedral. It will study funding, location and other practical questions.

The committee has one month to finish its work. Its findings are due to go to Minister Ayariga and then to the president for a decision.

That timetable runs close to the 31 October handover date. Both processes could shape what happens to the site next.

Why this matters to expats and investors

For foreign residents and investors in Ghana, the case shows how a new government can unwind a predecessor’s flagship project. Contracts tied to such projects can be reviewed, paused or ended.

Firms and suppliers linked to the cathedral should watch the Attorney General’s next steps and the handover. The site sits in central Accra, among government buildings, so its future also affects the capital’s layout.

More broadly, the government is signalling spending discipline after Ghana’s recent debt crisis. It wants private or faith-based money, not the budget, to carry projects like this.

What is still not known

The government has not said whether the cathedral will be finished, redesigned, moved or abandoned. The trustees have not publicly responded to the letter.

It is also not known whether the Attorney General will bring charges, or when the forensic audit will be released.

Nor is it clear who will pay to secure the partly built site after 31 October. The church committee’s report and the handover are the next milestones to watch.

Frequently Asked Questions

Frequently Asked Questions

Who dissolved the Ghana National Cathedral board?

President John Dramani Mahama ordered it on 18 September 2026. Minister Mahama Ayariga signed the letter.

When must the trustees hand over the site?

By 31 October 2026, to the Ministry of Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs, working with the project consultant.

Will the National Cathedral still be built?

That is not decided. The government says the handover will let it determine the project’s future, and the Christian Council is studying funding options.

Sources: Ministry of Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs letter, 18 September 2026; Presidency of Ghana statement, 18 July 2025; Christian Council of Ghana; MyJoyOnline; Citi Newsroom; Graphic Online.

World.title: Nigeria’s Nasarawa Mining Ban Bars Under-18s From Sites
World.content:
NIGERIA · MINING

Key Facts — What happened Nasarawa State in Nigeria banned children below 18 from mining sites and set up an enforcement team.

— Who announced it Margaret Elayo, the state commissioner responsible for environment and mining, spoke at a press conference in Lafia.

— Where it applies The directive covers all 13 local government areas, with special concern for Wamba, Nasarawa-Eggon and Kokona.

— Which roles Children may not work at sites as labourers, errand runners or food vendors.

— The catch No arrests or prosecutions under the new directive had been reported by the announcement day.

— Why now It followed the deaths of dozens of suspected illegal miners in custody in neighbouring Niger State.

A Nigerian state in the lithium belt says children must stay away from mining work, and it has set up a team to check.

A truck passes the welcome arch on a road in Nasarawa State, a centre of tin, lithium and other mining in central Nigeria (Photo: Kambai Akau, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

The Nasarawa mining ban, announced on Friday 18 September 2026, keeps every child below 18 off the state’s mining sites. Commissioner Margaret Elayo said violating companies, site operators and parents will be arrested and prosecuted.

What the Nasarawa mining ban actually says

Elayo announced the directive at a press conference in Lafia, the state capital. She said no child below 18 may be found at any mining site in Nasarawa State.

The rule names three roles: labourer, errand runner and food vendor. It applies across all 13 local government areas of the state.

She said any company, site operator or parent who breaks the rule will be arrested and prosecuted. The legal basis she cited is the Child Rights Law and the mining regulations.

The government also created a special monitoring and enforcement team. Its job is to tackle illegal mining and child labour in mining communities.

The team will visit mining sites to check compliance. It can also arrest people or firms mining without the required licences.

The state says it will work with security agencies, traditional rulers and community leaders. It is also working with the federal mining ministry to organise small-scale miners into cooperatives.

Why the state acted this week

Elayo said the ministry had received videos showing minors mining around Wamba Local Government Area. She also named Nasarawa-Eggon and Kokona as areas of concern.

Days earlier, suspected illegal miners died in the custody of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) in Niger State. Reports put the toll at between 33 and 37.

The federal interior minister suspended the Niger State NSCDC commander and ordered an investigation. Elayo offered condolences and said illegal mining is unacceptable whoever does it.

She also said some mining companies hold only exploration permits but still dig on a large scale. She urged residents to report illegal mining.

The Nasarawa mining ban is therefore about more than child labour. It is also part of a push to bring unlicensed digging under state control.

Nasarawa’s place in Nigeria’s lithium plans

Nasarawa sits at the centre of Nigeria’s lithium ambitions. Lithium is a key metal in batteries for electric cars and power storage.

On 3 July 2026, a lithium processing plant was commissioned at Endo in Nasarawa. The federal information ministry says it can process 6,000 tonnes a day.

The plant belongs to Diamond New Energy, a Chinese firm working with Chinese partners Jiuling and Canmax. The ministry put the investment at about US$250 million.

President Bola Tinubu said the plant showed Nigeria was ready to move from raw mineral extraction to local processing. Minister of Solid Minerals Development Dele Alake said new mining licences now need a local processing plan.

What it means for expats and investors

For investors with exposure to Nigerian lithium, the directive adds a compliance question. Processors and their buyers may need to show that ore was not dug by children.

Many international battery and car makers audit their mineral supply chains for child labour. A clear state ban gives those checks a local rule to point to.

The Nasarawa mining ban could also shape how lenders and partners judge local risk. Firms that already keep children off their sites face little extra cost.

Licensed operators could gain from a cleaner field if enforcement is fair. Informal diggers and their families are likely to feel the change first.

For expats living near mining areas, the change may be visible on the ground. Families that relied on children’s earnings at sites may lose that income.

What is still not known

The state has not published the size, budget or reporting line of the enforcement team. It is also not clear how often the team will visit sites.

No figures have been given for how many children work at Nasarawa’s mining sites. The number of licensed and unlicensed sites is also not stated.

It is not yet known how the rule will be applied to children who live in villages beside mining sites. Officials have not explained what help, if any, families will receive.

Many small sites are scattered and informal, which makes checks difficult. If enforcement is uneven, child labour could move out of sight rather than stop.

A wider push across Nigeria’s mining states

The directive fits a wider tightening of mining oversight in Nigeria. The deaths in Niger State have put safety and custody conditions under national attention.

Nasarawa’s plan to organise small-scale miners into cooperatives points the same way. Registered groups are easier to inspect, train and tax than scattered diggers.

Other mining states are likely to watch whether Nasarawa’s team produces cases in court. The first prosecutions would show how far the directive reaches in practice.

Frequently Asked Questions

Frequently Asked Questions

Who announced the Nasarawa mining ban?

Margaret Elayo, the state commissioner responsible for environment and mining, announced it in Lafia on Friday 18 September 2026.

Does the ban cover children selling food at mining sites?

Yes. The commissioner said no child below 18 may be at a site as a labourer, errand runner or food vendor.

Have there been arrests under the new rule?

None had been reported by the announcement day. A new monitoring and enforcement team has powers to visit sites and make arrests.

Sources: Nasarawa State Ministry of Environment press conference, 18 September 2026; Federal Ministry of Information and National Orientation; P.M. News; Daily Times Nigeria; The Eagle Online.

World.title: Minna Custody Deaths: Tinubu Seeks Prosecution if Officials Are Culpable
World.content:
NIGERIA · POLITICS

Key Facts — What happened Niger State officials say 37 suspected illegal miners died in paramilitary custody in Minna.

— The president’s order Tinubu wants a full, transparent probe and prosecution of any official found culpable.

— Who is suspended The Niger State commandant of the civil defence corps, pending investigation.

— Who is investigating The police, the corps itself, the security service and a state committee of inquiry.

— The catch The cause of death has not been established, and the victims have already been buried.

— What comes next Findings from the inquiries, and whether any criminal charges follow.

Nigeria’s president says any official found responsible for the deaths of 37 detained suspected miners in Niger State must be arrested and prosecuted.

The city gate in Minna, capital of Nigeria’s Niger State (Photo: F5pillar, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

President Bola Tinubu on Friday, 18 September 2026, ordered a full investigation into the Minna custody deaths of suspected illegal miners. He said any official found responsible must be arrested and prosecuted.

What President Tinubu ordered

The statement came from the State House in Abuja and was signed by presidential adviser Bayo Onanuga. It said the life of every Nigerian matters.

If an official is found to have contributed, that officer “must be arrested and prosecuted in accordance with the law”, he said. “There must be accountability,” he added.

He added that suspension of officers “is only an administrative step”. It must not replace a proper finding on criminal responsibility, he said.

Tinubu asked investigators to examine the arrests, the detainees’ condition, the detention conditions and the number of people held. The medical care given and the events before the deaths are also covered.

He told the Ministry of Interior and the corps leadership to cooperate fully. “The sanctity of human life is non-negotiable,” he said.

What happened in Minna

The Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) is an armed agency under the interior ministry. It protects infrastructure and acts against crimes such as illegal mining.

The corps arrested dozens of suspected illegal miners on 15 and 16 September 2026. The operations took place at mining sites around the M.I. Wushishi/Lukoto area of Minna, the Niger State capital.

The corps said some detainees were found dead in the early hours of Thursday, 17 September. It first pointed to a suspected disease outbreak.

It later said the cause of death had not been established and would be set by medical examination. The bodies were taken to the General Hospital, Minna.

Niger State Governor Mohammed Umaru Bago confirmed that 37 people died. He said many were children aged 14 to 18, according to Reuters.

“There are issues of illegal mining, and it is taking a toll on our children,” Bago said.

Suspension and several investigations

Interior Minister Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo ordered the immediate suspension of the Niger State commandant, Suberu Siyaka Aniviye. The suspension lasts until a full investigation is complete.

The corps set up its own investigative team, led by its deputy commandant-general for intelligence and investigation. The state police commissioner, Adamu Elleman, also ordered a police investigation.

Bago set up a state committee of inquiry chaired by Deputy Governor Yakubu Garba. He said the Department of State Services and the police had formed their own panels.

The governor said forensic checks and autopsies would be carried out. He also declared three days of mourning and ordered illegal mining around the M.I. Wushishi site to stop.

Protests and a curfew

Residents protested in Minna on Thursday night and on Friday. Reuters witnesses said security forces fired live rounds, and one witness reported seeing one dead person.

The state government imposed a 24-hour curfew in Minna from after Friday prayers, until further notice. Reuters said order had been restored before the curfew began.

Bago also cancelled a campaign rally of the governing All Progressives Congress (APC) planned for Saturday in Minna.

What rights groups are asking for

Amnesty International called for a prompt, independent and transparent investigation. It said anyone found responsible should face justice, not only internal or administrative sanctions.

Some relatives told reporters that people arrested included farmers and minors. These claims have not been independently confirmed.

The mother of one detainee told Reuters she had found her son in a cramped cell before learning he had died. The corps did not respond to Reuters’ requests for comment.

Why the Minna custody deaths matter to expats and investors

For foreign residents and investors, the case shows how Nigeria handles alleged abuse inside its security agencies. The answer affects how people judge legal and governance risk.

Nigeria has tried for years to curb unlicensed mining at thousands of informal sites. Authorities say it damages the environment and costs government revenue.

Companies with mining interests in north-central Nigeria may see tighter enforcement and closer scrutiny of how it is carried out. Local tension can also delay site visits and community talks.

For anyone living in or travelling to Minna, the practical point is simple. Follow the curfew and official advice until authorities lift it.

What is not known

The cause of death has not been established. The victims were buried late on Thursday under Islamic tradition, and it is not yet clear how forensic checks will proceed.

It is not known when any of the inquiries will report. It is also unclear whether the several investigations will share findings or run separately.

No official has been charged so far. The presidency has not set a deadline for the investigation.

The next steps will depend on what the inquiries find and how quickly they share their results.

Frequently Asked Questions

Frequently Asked Questions

What did President Tinubu order after the Minna custody deaths?

He ordered a full and transparent investigation. He said any official found to have contributed to the deaths must be arrested and prosecuted.

How many people died?

Niger State Governor Mohammed Umaru Bago confirmed 37 deaths. The cause has not yet been established.

Who has been suspended?

Suberu Siyaka Aniviye, the corps’ commandant in Niger State, was suspended by Interior Minister Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo pending investigation.

Sources: State House, Abuja statement by Bayo Onanuga, 18 September 2026; Ministry of Interior; Niger State Government; Nigeria Police Force, Niger State Command; Amnesty International; Reuters; Premium Times; TVC News; The ICIR.

World.title: South Africa’s Mozambique Anti-Dumping Duties Hit Steel Pipes and Tiles
World.content:
SOUTH AFRICA · TRADE

Key Facts — What happened South Africa’s trade regulator found preliminary dumping of Mozambican steel pipes and ceramic tiles.

— Steel pipes A provisional charge of 28.86% applies to large welded pipes from Mozambique until 18 December 2026.

— Ceramic tiles Mozambican tiles face a provisional charge of 132.65% until 9 January 2027.

— Who asked Pipe maker Hall Longmore and tile makers Ceramic Industries and Sinotile lodged the complaints.

— The catch These charges are temporary, and final decisions on both cases are still pending.

— What comes next The regulator must issue final findings before the provisional periods run out.

Two South African trade probes now put temporary charges on large steel pipes and ceramic tiles made in Mozambique.

The Maputo–Katembe bridge under construction in Maputo, Mozambique (Photo: Jcornelius, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

South Africa’s Mozambique anti-dumping duties now cover two industrial goods: large welded steel pipes and ceramic tiles. Both charges are provisional while South Africa’s trade regulator finishes its investigations.

How the steel pipe probe began

The International Trade Administration Commission (ITAC) opened the pipe case through Notice 3568 in the Government Gazette on 24 October 2025. It covers welded steel pipes wider than 406.4 millimetres, under tariff subheading 7305.19.

The complaint came from Hall Longmore, a South African pipe maker. The company said cheap imports from Mozambique were hurting producers in the Southern African Customs Union (SACU).

SACU groups South Africa, Botswana, Lesotho, Namibia and Eswatini. ITAC handles trade remedy cases for the whole bloc.

The initiation notice put the alleged dumping margin for Mozambique at 261.24%. That figure was based on the complaint’s price data, not on checked company records.

The applicant pointed to price undercutting, lower sales, weaker profits and lost market share. ITAC examined dumping from 1 April 2024 to 31 March 2025, and injury from 1 April 2022.

What ITAC found on Mozambique anti-dumping duties for pipes

After checking the books of exporter ETG Steel Solutions Limitada, ITAC calculated a much smaller margin of 28.86%. The same rate applies to all other Mozambican pipe exporters.

ITAC’s Report 779 says pipe imports from Mozambique rose from about 1.48 million kilograms in 2023 to 12.24 million kilograms in 2025. By 2025, Mozambique supplied 98% of these pipe imports into SACU.

The regulator made a preliminary finding of dumping and of material injury to local industry. It asked the South African Revenue Service (SARS) to collect provisional payments for six months.

According to Freight News, SARS published the measure in June 2026 and it runs until 18 December 2026. The Mozambican exporters had objected to the case and questioned whether it should have started at all.

The ceramic tile case

A second probe covers ceramic and porcelain wall and floor tiles from India, Mozambique, Zambia and Zimbabwe. ITAC opened it on 21 November 2025 through Notice 3639 in the Government Gazette.

The complaint came from Ceramic Industries and Rayal Industrial, which trades as Sinotile. Together they make more than 80% of the tiles produced in SACU.

ITAC said 54 foreign firms responded to its questionnaires, including one from Mozambique. Imports from the four countries rose 114% between 2023 and 2025, to about 31.6 million square metres.

In its preliminary Report 782, ITAC set a provisional charge of 132.65% on tiles from Mozambique. The rates are 95.87% for India, 132.82% for Zambia and 231.62% for Zimbabwe.

The charges apply from 10 July 2026 until 9 January 2027. ITAC also noted that many Mozambican tiles had earlier been cleared under a different tariff code.

What provisional charges mean

A provisional payment is a temporary security that importers pay while an investigation continues. If final findings confirm dumping, it can be turned into a definitive duty.

If ITAC does not confirm dumping, the payments can be refunded. That is why importers are watching the final reports closely.

Provisional payments are charged on top of normal customs duties. They are calculated as a share of the import value.

Why this matters for expats and investors in Africa

For investors in Mozambique’s factories, South Africa is the nearest large market. Mozambique anti-dumping duties of this size can make exports to SACU much harder to sell.

For builders and project owners in South Africa, the charges can raise the cost of imported pipes and tiles. Large pipes are used in water, gas and mining projects.

Importers who signed supply contracts before June may face costs they did not plan for. Checking contract terms on duties is a sensible first step.

Expats renovating homes or running construction firms may notice higher tile prices if importers pass on the charges. Local makers, in turn, may gain market share.

The cases also show that trade friction can arise between close neighbours, not only with Asian suppliers. Firms that source across Southern African borders should check ITAC notices regularly.

What is not yet known

ITAC has not yet published final determinations in either Mozambican case. The final margins could differ from the provisional ones.

It is also unclear how much Mozambican shipments have fallen since the charges started. No trade data covering that period has been published yet.

It is also not known whether Mozambique’s government will respond formally. No official reaction from Maputo has been confirmed.

What to watch next

The pipe measure expires on 18 December 2026, so a final pipe decision is due before then. The tile decision is due before 9 January 2027.

Final rulings, if any, will appear in the Government Gazette and in SARS tariff amendments. Until then, the Mozambique anti-dumping duties stay provisional.

The bottom line

South Africa has moved from probing Mozambican imports to charging them, at least for now. Both cases remain open and could still change.

The coming weeks should bring clearer answers for traders on both sides of the border.

Frequently Asked Questions

Frequently Asked Questions

Which Mozambican goods face South African anti-dumping charges?

Large welded steel pipes under tariff subheading 7305.19, and ceramic and porcelain wall and floor tiles. Both charges are provisional.

Why is the pipe duty lower than the 261.24% in the gazette notice?

The 261.24% figure came from the complaint at the start. After checking exporter data, ITAC calculated 28.86%.

Are the Mozambique anti-dumping duties final?

No. They are temporary payments while ITAC completes its investigations, and final decisions are still pending.

Sources: International Trade Administration Commission of South Africa, Government Gazette Notice 3568 of 24 October 2025 and Reports 779 and 782; South African Revenue Service; Freight News; IOL Business Report.

World.title: Santam Curt Meyer Appointment Signals South African Insurer’s Push Abroad
World.content:
SOUTH AFRICA · BUSINESS

Key Facts — What happened Santam named Curt Meyer Executive Head of Pan-Africa and International on 14 September 2026.

— Where The role covers selected African markets plus the Middle East, India and South-East Asia.

— The numbers Business outside South Africa made up 23% of Santam’s premiums in the first half of 2026.

— The target Santam wants international operations to reach 30% of gross written premium by 2030.

— The catch Santam has not named new countries, deals, budgets or a timeline tied to the role.

— What comes next Santam’s full-year 2026 results should show whether the international share keeps rising.

A new Pan-Africa and international post at Santam’s specialist unit shows where the Cape Town insurer wants its next growth to come from.

Cape Town city centre and harbour in the morning, seen from the Table Mountain cableway base station (Photo: Daniel Case, CC BY-SA 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

South African insurer Santam has created a new executive role to grow its business abroad and named Curt Meyer to lead it. The Santam Curt Meyer appointment was announced by the company on Monday, 14 September 2026.

What Santam announced

Meyer becomes Executive Head of Pan-Africa and International within Santam Specialist Solutions (SSS). SSS is the group’s business unit for specialist and complex risks.

Santam called it a dedicated new executive role for international growth. Its focus is selected Pan-African and international markets, including the Middle East, India and South-East Asia.

Santam describes itself as South Africa’s largest general insurer. It is listed on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange (JSE), and financial services group Sanlam is its majority shareholder.

Who Curt Meyer is

Santam says Meyer has more than two decades of experience in the insurance industry. He was once chief executive of Mirabilis Engineering Insurance Specialists, Santam’s construction and engineering division.

Most recently he headed corporate property, construction and engineering, and marine insurance within SSS. He holds a BA in law and an MBA from Milpark Business School.

Gareth Beaver, chief executive of SSS, praised Meyer’s record. “Curt brings extensive leadership experience, strong technical expertise and deep commercial insight within the specialist insurance sector,” he said.

Beaver called the appointment “an important milestone” in Santam’s effort to broaden its reach. He said Santam wants to enhance the value it delivers outside South Africa.

What the Santam Curt Meyer appointment is meant to do

Meyer said the new job lets him focus fully on three areas. These are Santam’s GIFT City office in India, its collaboration through Sanlam Allianz, and other international opportunities.

“We are building a scalable platform for growth,” he said. He added that Santam wants a stronger presence in priority markets and to support partners with specialist risk cover.

GIFT City, or Gujarat International Finance Tec-City, is India’s international financial hub. Santam received a reinsurance branch licence there in January 2026 from India’s International Financial Services Centres Authority.

Santam said it was the first insurer based in a BRICS country to set up in GIFT City. BRICS is the bloc of emerging economies that includes Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa.

Sanlam Allianz is a joint venture between Sanlam and the German insurer Allianz. It launched in 2023 and offers insurance and financial services in 27 African countries outside South Africa.

Why Santam is looking beyond South Africa

International growth is a key pillar of Santam’s FutureFit 2030 strategy. The company wants international operations to contribute 30% of gross written premium by 2030.

In the six months to 30 June 2026, premiums written outside South Africa made up 23% of the total. A year earlier, that share was 20%.

That foreign business grew 25% to R5.3 billion (US$326 million), at 18 September 2026 rates. Santam’s conventional gross written premium rose 10% over the same period.

The half-year also showed the risk of depending on one home market. Catastrophe and other large losses, driven mainly by severe South African weather, reached R1.5 billion (US$92 million) after reinsurance.

Even so, Santam raised its interim dividend by 10.2% to 650 cents (about US$0.40) a share. Headline earnings per share rose 7% to 2,006 cents (about US$1.23).

Santam also started writing business through its own Lloyd’s of London syndicate, Syndicate 1918, on 1 January 2026. The group says it is the only African-headquartered participant at Lloyd’s.

Why this matters to expats and investors

For investors in JSE-listed financial shares, the new role shows where Santam hopes future growth will come from. Income from several regions can soften a bad year at home, such as heavy weather losses.

For companies and expats running projects in Africa, India or the Middle East, another specialist insurer adds choice. That matters most for engineering, construction, property and marine risks.

Brokers placing large cross-border risks also gain one senior contact at Santam. Whether that brings better prices or terms will depend on each local market.

What Santam has not said

Santam has not named any new countries it plans to enter because of the new role. It has not published a budget, hiring plan or timeline for the function.

It is also unclear how the role will share work with the GIFT City office, the Lloyd’s syndicate and Sanlam Allianz. Insurance is licensed country by country, so each new market needs local approval.

Foreign income also carries currency risk. Premiums earned in other currencies can lose or gain value when converted back into rand.

What to watch next

The clearest test will be Santam’s results for the full 2026 financial year. Investors will look at whether the international share rises above 23%.

Any new licences, partnerships or offices in the target regions would show the plan moving forward. For now, Santam is building steadily from the foreign base it already has.

Frequently Asked Questions

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Curt Meyer?

He is Santam’s new Executive Head of Pan-Africa and International. He previously led Mirabilis Engineering Insurance Specialists and Santam’s corporate property, engineering and marine business.

Which markets will he focus on?

Selected African markets, plus the Middle East, India and South-East Asia. Santam has not named specific new countries.

How big is Santam’s international business?

It made up 23% of gross written premium in the first half of 2026. Santam is aiming for 30% by 2030.

Sources: Santam Group media release, 14 September 2026; Santam interim results for the six months to 30 June 2026; Santam GIFT City licence release, 19 February 2026; Allianz; Bizcommunity; Insurance Business.

World.title: Niger Nationality Decree Strips Five Exiles, Including Ex-Prime Minister
World.content:
NIGER · POLITICS

Key Facts — What happened Niger’s head of state signed a decree on 17 September 2026 affecting five people.

— Who is named The five include Ouhoumoudou Mahamadou, prime minister under deposed President Mohamed Bazoum.

— The accusations The decree cites spreading disruptive information, intelligence with foreign powers and undermining state security.

— The catch The loss is provisional and becomes final only after a prison sentence of at least five years.

— How big The state news agency says 25 people have lost nationality provisionally since October 2024.

— What is unclear It is not known whether any of the five will challenge the decree.

The loss of citizenship is provisional for now, and all five people named live outside Niger.

Niamey, the capital of Niger, at night (Photo: Roland, CC BY-SA 2.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

General Abdourahamane Tiani, Niger’s head of state, signed a Niger nationality decree on Thursday, 17 September 2026. It provisionally removes Nigerien nationality from five people, the state news agency reported.

What the decree says

Niger’s state news agency, known by its French initials ANP, reported the decree late on 17 September 2026. It calls Tiani “President of the Republic, Head of State” and “General of Army”.

The five people named are Amadou dit Ange Barou Chekaraou, Ouhoumoudou Mahamadou, Oumarou Moussa Ibrahim, Ousmane Abdoul Moumouni and Boubacar Seyni Souley. The agency also listed their dates and places of birth.

According to the decree, they face accusations of spreading data likely to disturb public order and of intelligence with foreign powers. It also cites defamation by electronic means.

Other listed accusations include taking part in an effort to demoralise the army and the nation, and undermining state security. The decree also mentions activities likely to disturb peace and public safety.

These are accusations in a government decree, not court verdicts. No trial has yet tested them in public.

Provisional, not yet final

The measure is provisional. Several outlets, including allAfrica and Ouestaf, say it becomes final only after a prison sentence of at least five years.

Until then, the five remain in a kind of legal limbo. They have lost their Nigerien nationality for now, but the decision can still change.

The decree itself, as summarised by ANP, does not set out that rule. It comes from the 2024 legal framework, as described in those reports.

The legal basis for the Niger nationality decree

The Niger nationality decree applies article 9 of ordinance 2024-43 of 27 August 2024. That text was later changed by ordinance 2024-46 of 7 October 2024.

The ordinance created a national file of people and groups linked to terrorism. It also covers other offences against the nation’s core interests or public safety.

Being placed in that file opened the way to the loss of nationality. According to ANP, this latest decree brings the total to 25 people since October 2024.

Who the five are

Ouhoumoudou Mahamadou was prime minister under President Mohamed Bazoum. The army removed Bazoum from power in a coup on 26 July 2023.

Ouestaf, a regional news site, describes Amadou dit Ange Barou Chekaraou as a former deputy chief of staff to Bazoum. It calls Ousmane Abdoul Moumouni a former presidential adviser.

The same outlet describes Oumarou Moussa Ibrahim as a close associate of Bazoum. It says Boubacar Seyni Souley is an activist based in the United States.

Ouestaf and allAfrica both report that the five live outside Niger. One outlet, Bsean Media TV, reports that Mahamadou has lived in Europe since the coup.

A wider pattern

Human Rights Watch, an international rights group, addressed this practice in a July 2026 report. It said the authorities had temporarily stripped at least 18 exiled opposition figures of citizenship since late 2024.

The group said this was based on the 2024 order that created the terrorism database. It described the practice as part of an effort to suppress criticism beyond Niger’s borders.

In June 2026, the group also reported the case of Mariama Djibrine. She leads a coalition of diaspora opposition groups from Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso.

The September decree adds five more names to that list. It suggests the practice has continued since the July report.

Why it matters to expats and investors

For people living in or invested in West Africa, the main issue is legal predictability. Here, a major legal status changed by decree before any court ruling.

Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso are all led by military governments. People doing business there often depend on local partners, some with political ties.

The Niger nationality decree fits a wider approach in which disagreement is treated as a security matter. That approach can shape how officials, banks and regulators treat people seen as critics.

A partner who loses nationality may face problems with identity papers, bank accounts or property. That can affect contracts and joint projects too.

Investors do not need to take a political side to follow this. They should watch whether courts or decrees decide important questions of legal status.

What is not known

It is not known whether any of the five will challenge the decree, or in which court. None of them had publicly responded by 18 September 2026.

It is also not clear whether any trial is planned. That matters, because only a court sentence can make the loss final.

It is also unclear whether family members of the five face any direct effects. The published decree only names the five individuals.

What to watch next

The next steps will show whether courts take up these cases. Any ruling would help explain how the 2024 ordinances work in practice.

For now, the five keep their provisional status, and the legal process is likely to move slowly.

Frequently Asked Questions

Frequently Asked Questions

Who lost Nigerien nationality in September 2026?

Five people named in a 17 September 2026 decree, including former prime minister Ouhoumoudou Mahamadou.

Is the loss of nationality permanent?

No. It is provisional and, as reported, becomes final only after a prison sentence of at least five years.

How many people have been affected so far?

The state news agency says 25 people have lost nationality provisionally since October 2024.

Sources: Agence Nigérienne de Presse (ANP), 17 September 2026; allAfrica; Ouestaf; Wakat Séra; Human Rights Watch, July 2026.

World.title: UN Mission Seeks Libya Executions Halt in the Country’s East
World.content:
LIBYA · HUMAN RIGHTS

Key Facts — What happened UNSMIL said on 16 September 2026 that more than 30 people had been executed in eastern Libya.

— When it began The eastern forces’ military prosecutor announced ten executions on 23 August 2026, according to Amnesty International.

— Who carried them out Amnesty said the Libyan Arab Armed Forces, led by Khalifa Haftar, carried out the executions.

— How many at risk Amnesty said at least 50 more men under sentence of death face imminent execution.

— The catch UNSMIL asked for the sentences to be suspended, but its statement sets out no way to enforce this.

— What comes next UNSMIL wants the cases reviewed in line with fair-trial standards and Libya’s legal obligations.

More than 30 people have been executed in eastern Libya since late August — the first known executions in Libya since 2010, according to Amnesty International.

The former Italian-era cathedral in Benghazi, the main city of eastern Libya, pictured in 2007 (Photo: Siculo73, CC BY-SA 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

The United Nations Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL) called for a Libya executions halt on Wednesday, 16 September 2026. It said more than 30 people had been put to death in eastern Libya in recent weeks.

What the UN mission said

UNSMIL said it had engaged political and technical authorities after it received the first reports of executions. It urged them to suspend the death sentences pending a credible review of the cases.

The mission said the executions went ahead despite its efforts. It said the resumption raised serious human-rights concerns.

UNSMIL said any review should meet fair-trial standards and Libya’s obligations under national and international law. It also recognised that the authorities have a duty to prosecute terrorism and that victims have a right to justice.

The mission said the resumption undermines public trust in Libyan institutions. It said this comes at a key time for national reconciliation and the rule of law.

What Amnesty International reported

Amnesty International published its findings on 11 September 2026. It said at least 30 people had been executed since 23 August 2026.

The rights group said at least 50 men under sentence of death in eastern Libya were at imminent risk. It called on the authorities to halt all executions immediately.

Amnesty said the convictions came from secretive trials before military courts. It described the trials as grossly unfair and said many defendants reported being tortured into confessions.

Amnesty called the Libyan Arab Armed Forces (LAAF) the de facto authorities in eastern Libya. The LAAF is commanded by Khalifa Haftar.

How the executions began

According to Amnesty, the LAAF’s military prosecutor announced on 23 August 2026 that ten people had been executed. The men had been convicted of joining terrorist groups and of murder.

Amnesty said these were the first executions in Libya since 2010. The UN Human Rights Office said on 26 August 2026 that they ended a de facto moratorium of about 15 years.

The High Council of State, an advisory body based in Tripoli, raised concerns on 24 August 2026. It asked for the names of those executed and details of the courts and trials involved.

The council also urged a pause in further executions until all legal procedures had been fully respected.

Why the Libya executions halt call matters now

Libya has been divided since 2014 between a government in Tripoli and rival institutions in the east. The east is under the control of Haftar’s forces.

Military courts in the east work outside the Tripoli-based justice system. That makes it hard for outside bodies to check how cases are handled.

The UN call is a public diplomatic step, not a legal order. UNSMIL’s statement does not set out any way to enforce its request.

No formal response from the eastern authorities to the UN call has been reported. They have not publicly said whether they will pause further executions.

What it means for expats and investors

For foreign companies and investors with links to eastern Libya, the executions add a human-rights question to any business decision. Firms working on energy, services or construction projects there may face closer questions from partners.

Banks, insurers and funds often review human-rights records before agreeing to finance projects. A continuing rise in executions could make these reviews slower and more detailed.

Foreign governments that deal with eastern institutions may also face questions at home. This can affect the pace of official visits, trade missions and support programmes.

For expats living in Libya or nearby countries, daily life is not directly affected by these rulings. However, it is worth following official travel advice and any updates from embassies.

What is not yet known

It is not known whether the eastern authorities will stop further executions. The full number of people sentenced to death by the military courts is also unclear.

The High Council of State asked for the names of those executed, and it is unclear whether they have been published. It is also not known whether any review has been scheduled.

UNSMIL has not said whether the authorities replied to its request. No timeline for a response has been given.

The longer view

Libya kept the death penalty in its laws but had not carried out any known executions for about 15 years. That long pause is why rights groups describe the recent executions as a turning point.

The recent executions change that pattern in the east. Rights groups and UN bodies are now asking for the sentences to be suspended and reviewed.

The coming weeks should show whether the executions pause while those reviews are considered.

Frequently Asked Questions

Frequently Asked Questions

How many people were executed in eastern Libya?

UNSMIL said more than 30 people were executed in recent weeks. Amnesty International said at least 30 people had been executed since 23 August 2026.

Who runs the military courts that issued the sentences?

Amnesty International said the courts operate under the Libyan Arab Armed Forces (LAAF), led by Khalifa Haftar. Amnesty calls the LAAF the de facto authorities in eastern Libya.

How many more people are at risk?

Amnesty International said at least 50 men under sentence of death in eastern Libya were at imminent risk. UNSMIL has asked for their sentences to be suspended and reviewed.

Sources: United Nations Support Mission in Libya statement, 16 September 2026; Amnesty International, 11 September 2026; UN Human Rights Office; High Council of State; The Libya Observer; The North Africa Post; The New Arab.

World.title: Equity Group DRC Insurance Push: Two New Firms Await Congo Licences
World.content:
DR CONGO · BUSINESS

Key Facts — What happened Equity Group shareholders approved two new insurance companies in DR Congo on 24 June 2026.

— How big The life insurer gets US$12 million in capital and the general insurer US$13.37 million.

— Who runs it Both will sit under Equity Group Insurance Holdings Limited, the group’s insurance holding company.

— Also in Kenya Shareholders also backed a Kenyan microinsurance company with KSh192 million (US$1.5 million) in capital.

— The catch Everything depends on regulators, and no Equity insurer appears yet on DR Congo’s official insurer list.

— Why Congo Equity BCDC, the group’s Congolese bank, raised first-half 2026 profit after tax by 30%.

Kenya’s Equity Group wants to sell insurance in DR Congo, where its bank already earns strongly. Shareholders agreed in June, but the regulator must still say yes.

Boulevard du 30 Juin in central Kinshasa, capital of the Democratic Republic of Congo (Photo: MONUSCO/Myriam Asmani, CC BY-SA 2.0 via Wikimedia Commons)
