The Equity Group DRC insurance plan is two new companies: a life insurer and a general insurer. Shareholders of the Kenyan lender approved both on Wednesday 24 June 2026, subject to regulatory approval.

What Equity Group shareholders approved

Equity Group Holdings is one of East Africa’s largest banking groups, based in Nairobi. It held its 22nd annual general meeting online on 24 June 2026.

Shareholders approved every resolution on the table, according to the company’s statement. These included three new insurance companies, all conditional on regulatory approval.

Two are in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). A life insurer will have US$12 million in capital, and a general insurer US$13.37 million.

That is US$25.37 million in total for Congo. The third company is a microinsurance business in Kenya, with KSh192 million (US$1.5 million) at 18 September 2026 rates.

Microinsurance means small, low-cost policies for people on modest incomes. The Kenyan company would be the group’s first dedicated microinsurance business, according to The Kenyan Wallstreet.

All three will be held through Equity Group Insurance Holdings Limited. Shareholders also authorised the board to set up and run the new companies.

What the bosses said

Managing director and chief executive James Mwangi linked the vote to the group’s wider strategy. “The approvals to expand our insurance footprint strengthen our ability to offer more holistic financial services,” he said.

Chairman Isaac Macharia said “the approvals received today reflect our shareholders’ confidence in Equity’s strategy and oversight.” Neither gave a launch date.

Why the Equity Group DRC insurance move makes sense

Equity already sells insurance in Kenya through life, general and health companies. In the first half of 2026, that insurance business grew gross written premiums by 24% to KSh6.4 billion (US$49 million).

Its profit before tax rose 34% to KSh1.25 billion (US$9.7 million), the group said on 19 August 2026. Gross written premiums are the total insurance sales before claims and costs.

Equity has been in DR Congo since 2015, when it bought a majority of ProCredit Bank. It later merged that bank with Banque Commerciale du Congo to form Equity BCDC.

In the first half of 2026, Equity BCDC raised profit after tax by 30% to KSh11.8 billion (US$91 million). Selling insurance to its existing customers is a natural next step.

Dividend and other decisions

The same meeting approved a dividend of KSh21.7 billion (US$168 million) for 2025. That is KSh5.75 (about US$0.04) per share, up 35.5% on the previous year’s payout.

Shareholders re-elected four directors, including Macharia. They also appointed Eliane Ubalijoro to the board, subject to regulatory approval.

Congo is where Equity is hiring

Equity’s total staff rose to 14,265 in June 2026, from 13,855 in March. The DRC unit showed the largest growth in employee numbers, Kenya’s Business Daily reported.

That hiring fits a group putting more people and capital into Congo. The new insurers would add a further business line there.

Most profit still comes from Kenya

The group’s subsidiaries outside Kenya now hold 54% of its loans and 51% of its deposits. But they deliver only 42% of banking profit, the group says.

They also bring in 47% of banking revenue and hold 52% of banking assets. In other words, more than half of the group’s banking balance sheet now sits outside Kenya.

Equity Bank Kenya still earned KSh25.7 billion (US$198 million) after tax in the first half. That is more than twice Equity BCDC’s result, according to the outlet Bankable.

The Rio Times described this gap on 22 August 2026: most lending has left Kenya, but most profit has not. Insurance in Congo is one way to earn more from the same customers.

Why this matters to expats and investors

For expats and firms working in DR Congo, a new insurer tied to a large bank could mean more choice. Life and general cover could be sold at the same branches where people already bank.

The regulator, the Insurance Regulation and Control Authority (ARCA), lists ten licensed insurers online. None carries the Equity name, so the market remains small.

For people who already bank with Equity BCDC, nothing changes today. Accounts, loans and fees are not affected by the insurance vote.

For shareholders in Nairobi or abroad, the capital involved is modest. Group profit after tax was KSh45.5 billion (US$351 million) in the first half of 2026 alone.

What is not known yet

Equity has not said when it will apply for, or expect, DRC licences. Its 19 August 2026 half-year results did not mention the Congo insurance plan.

There are also no published names, managers, products or price plans for the two companies. The timing depends on ARCA and other regulators.

The next clear signal will be a licence from ARCA or a launch announcement from Equity.

Frequently Asked Questions

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Equity Group shareholders approve for DR Congo?

Two new companies: a life insurer with US$12 million in capital and a general insurer with US$13.37 million. Both need regulatory approval first.

Are the new insurers already operating?

No. ARCA’s online list of licensed insurers does not include any Equity company, and no launch date has been announced.

Why does Equity Group want insurance in Congo?

Its Congolese bank, Equity BCDC, is growing fast. Insurance lets the group sell more services to the same customers, as it already does in Kenya.

Sources: Equity Group Holdings AGM statement, 24 June 2026, and half-year results, 19 August 2026; Insurance Regulation and Control Authority (ARCA) of DR Congo; TV47; The Kenyan Wallstreet; Business Daily; Bankable.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Juan Santamaría Airport Keeps Highest Passenger Experience Accreditation
World.content:
Costa Rica’s Juan Santamaría International Airport has renewed the highest level of an international passenger experience accreditation, placing the country’s main airport among just 12 worldwide holding the distinction in 2026. The airport, operated by AERIS, received Level 5 accreditation for the second consecutive year under the Airports Council International Customer Experience Accreditation program. Level 5 is the highest of five levels in the program.

The distinction does not simply rank airports based on how much passengers like them. Instead, ACI examines how well an airport has built the passenger experience into the way it operates, including how it listens to travelers, trains employees, measures service, uses technology and coordinates the different companies and government agencies working inside the terminal.

Juan Santamaría is one of only 12 airports worldwide currently holding Level 5 accreditation. Quito’s Mariscal Sucre International Airport in Ecuador is the other Level 5 airport in the Americas. “Renewing Level 5 represents for us an achievement as important as reaching it for the first time, because it demonstrates that we have managed to maintain a culture of service over time and that the passenger experience is part of the decisions we make to continue transforming the airport,” AERIS CEO Ricardo Hernández said.

AERIS has expanded its passenger service programs over the past year, including an Excellence Program aimed at improving customer service across the airport community. The airport also strengthened its Customer Experience Committee, which brings together airlines, airport operators, businesses and government agencies to identify problems and coordinate improvements.

About 500 employees from AERIS and other organizations working at Juan Santamaría participated in training, workshops and passenger service activities during 2025. Travelers have also begun seeing more technology designed to reduce waiting times and make moving through the terminal easier.

The airport is using LiDAR technology to anonymously monitor passenger flows around passport control and security in the international departures area. According to AERIS, Juan Santamaría is the first airport in Latin America to use the technology for this purpose. Other projects include automated eGates for immigration, self-service baggage drop systems and new scanning technology at security checkpoints. The airport began operating its first four eGates in the arrivals area on September 8.

Accessibility has also become part of the effort. Juan Santamaría joined the Hidden Disabilities Sunflower program, an international system that allows travelers with non-visible disabilities to discreetly signal that they may need extra time or assistance. The airport has also achieved Level 1 in ACI’s Accessibility Enhancement Accreditation program.

Recent passenger surveys indicate that the changes are being noticed. At the end of June 2026, Juan Santamaría scored 4.44 out of 5 for overall passenger satisfaction and 4.38 for overall experience under ACI’s Airport Service Quality program. Its satisfaction score was slightly above the worldwide average of 4.38 for airports handling a similar number of passengers.

The accreditation comes as Juan Santamaría continues a broader modernization program. The airport currently connects Costa Rica with 42 destinations and is served by 26 international airlines and two domestic carriers. For travelers, the Level 5 renewal does not mean every trip through Juan Santamaría will be trouble-free.

Lines, flight disruptions and busy travel periods remain part of airport travel. What the accreditation indicates is that passenger experience has become part of the airport’s formal management system rather than a collection of individual customer service projects. For Costa Rica, that carries added importance because Juan Santamaría is the first and last impression of the country for millions of international visitors each year.

World.title: Scientists Name First New Wild Cat Species in Over 100 Years
World.content:
A small spotted wild cat from the cloud forests of Bolivia has been formally described as a new species. Scientists say it is the first time in more than a century that a new living feline species has been formally named and described. The cat, now called Leopardus tilcayo, was described in a study published on Thursday in the journal Current Biology. Its name comes from tilcayo, the word local communities in Bolivia have long used for the animal.

It is smaller than a house cat and the species measures 46cm (18 inches) long and weighs about 1.4kg (3 pounds). Researchers describe light brown fur with irregularly shaped rosettes across its body. The tilcayo belongs to the tiger cats, small, wild cats in the Leopardus genus native to South and Central America. It lives in the Bolivian Yungas, the cloud forest where the Andes mountains meet the Amazon basin.

The discovery began with one cat at a wildlife sanctuary. In 2016, Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz, a biologist and National Geographic Explorer working in Bolivia, received a call from a local wildlife sanctuary that had just been given what they described as “a weird cat.” The animal came from a local man who found it as a kitten on a road near a forest and kept it at home for about a year before realizing it was wild.

The cat went to the Senda Verde Wildlife Sanctuary as Nogales-Ascarrunz first assumed it was a northern tiger cat, a species described back in 1775 from a single illustration of an animal seen in French Guiana and long thought to live across Central and South America.

National Geographic

Her doubts grew in 2019 as while she was preparing a booklet about Bolivia’s cat species, she realized the cat she’d photographed didn’t look like a guidebook reference photo from neighboring Brazil. That led to a large genetic study and the team analyzed DNA from 38 cats sampled across several South American countries, including eight museum specimens and found that tiger cats are really five genetically distinct species.

Co-lead author Jonas Lescroart, an evolutionary ecologist at the University of Antwerp in Belgium, said the team never expected the Bolivian cat to be a separate species, and no one had ever proposed it as a different animal, subspecies or otherwise. He described tiger cats as “cryptic species,” meaning it is difficult to distinguish them by appearance alone.

Scientists believe the tilcayo cat likely evolved from a common ancestor of “tiger cats” around 1.4 million years ago. The same study also identified a subspecies of another tiger cat species, named Leopardus tigrinus antisuyo, which lives in Peru.

Much about the new species remains unknown. Lescroart said the team’s information is limited to the two live individuals that we examined, and a small number of camera-trap records. Rodent remains in scat samples hint at its diet, and camera-trap evidence suggests the cats are more active at night.

The sanctuary cat, a 10-year-old male at the sanctuary is the only known tilcayo cat in captivity, but others are believed to have been photographed by camera traps placed in the cloud forests. The researchers say the finding raises urgent conservation questions. Tadeu de Oliveira, a co-author and ecologist at the State University of Maranhão in Brazil, said all five tiger cat species are in habitats that are vanishing fast.

Nogales-Ascarrunz said naming a new cat after more than 100 years shows how much remains to be learned about nearby biodiversity, and that it underlines the need to protect the Yungas forests, which are home to so many species—including some we are only beginning to understand.

World.title: Belize showcases new airlift, resorts and Eco-Tourism in New York
World.content:
Belize showcases new airlift, resorts and Eco-Tourism in New York

By Zoila Palma: Minister of Tourism, Youth, Sports and Diaspora Relations Anthony Mahler participated in a series of media and tourism events hosted by the Belize Tourism Board in New York on Thursday, September 17, 2026.

The events highlighted Belize’s expanded airlift options, new accommodation offerings and its growing reputation for eco-sustainable tourism.

The day began with a broadcast video interview between Minister Mahler and James Shillinglaw, Editor-in-Chief of Insider Travel Report, followed by a media breakfast attended by more than 20 prominent writers and editors from publications including Fodor’s Travel, Travel + Leisure, AFAR, Forbes, National Geographic, Condé Nast Traveler and Parade Magazine.

The event also provided Belizean hoteliers and tour operators with an opportunity to network with international travel media.

Minister Mahler later participated in a desk-side briefing with Amy Virshup, Executive Travel Editor at The New York Times, who expressed interest in Belize’s tourism developments, particularly expanded connectivity with BermudAir and plans for new marine sanctuaries.

Also attending the engagements was Eluide Miller, Deputy Mayor of Belize City and Administrator at NICH. During the afternoon, Minister Mahler and Michelle Bowers-Flowers, Director of Marketing and Communications, met with executives and digital marketing teams from Development Counsellors International, FINN Partners and TM Americas, who presented upcoming campaigns aimed at promoting travel to Belize during the upcoming Blue Season.

The day concluded with Minister Mahler’s participation in the United States Tour Operators Association (USTOA) New York City Mixer.

USTOA CEO Terry Dale welcomed associate members, including destination marketing organizations and airlines, as well as tour operators from the New York area.

World.title: Government of Belize advances Digital skills through Marketing and CRM Training in Corozal
World.content:
Government of Belize advances Digital skills through Marketing and CRM Training in Corozal

By Zoila Palma: The Government of Belize, through the Investment Policy and Compliance Unit (IPCU) of the Office of the Prime Minister, in collaboration with the Corozal Think Tank, has advanced efforts to strengthen digital skills among young Belizeans through a Digital Marketing and CRM Training programme.

Today, a graduation ceremony was held in Corozal following the completion of the programme earlier this year.

The initiative targeted young and early-career participants ages 15 and up, along with a small group of adult learners, providing them with digital competencies aligned with international certification standards.

Participants received training in industry-standard platforms including Canva, Shopify, Zoho CRM, Zapier, AdRoll and Taboola, while covering digital marketing strategy, content creation, social media marketing, e-commerce, customer relationship management, marketing automation, analytics and search engine optimization.

A total of 41 students from the Corozal District successfully completed the course, with most coming from Chunox St. Viator Vocational High School. Participants reported gaining practical skills in digital marketing, content production, social media management, e-commerce platforms, CRM systems and analytics.

The programme also incorporated soft skills such as communication, teamwork, time management, professional presentations and self-confidence, with participants reporting greater preparedness to engage with potential employers.

The graduation ceremony was attended by Minister of Human Development, Family Support and Gender Affairs Thea Garcia Ramirez, IPCU Director Lincoln Blake, Corozal ITVET Chairman Froylan Gilharry, Chunox St. Viator Vocational High School Principal Marconie Moh and Corozal Think Tank member Juan Carlos Menzies.

Christian Junior, head trainer from UK-based Rhics Ltd., which provided the training, participated virtually.

The programme forms part of efforts to equip Belizeans with skills relevant to the country’s growing digital services sector, including business process outsourcing, micro-businesses and public-sector digital transformation.

World.title: Belize makes historic debut at 2026 Americas Food & Beverage Show
World.content:
Belize makes historic debut at 2026 Americas Food & Beverage Show

By Zoila Palma: Belize has concluded its historic debut at the 2026 Americas Food & Beverage Show, marking the country’s first-ever participation with a dedicated Country Pavilion at the Miami Beach Convention Center.

Over three days, Belizean exporters engaged in business-to-business matchmaking, product showcases and networking with buyers, distributors and industry representatives from the Caribbean, United States, Latin America, Europe, the Middle East and Africa.

The participation generated interest in Belizean products and opened opportunities for exporters to access new international markets.

Belize also took the spotlight on the show’s official Beverage Stage, with Cuello’s Distilleries Limited showcasing its Belizean spirits through a live presentation and sampling session, followed by Caribbean International Brewery Company Limited, which highlighted its products and Belize’s growing beverage industry.

The seven exporters representing Belize were Cuello’s Distilleries Limited, Aqua Mar Belize Ltd, National Fishermen Producers Co-operative Society Ltd. (Natfish), Coco Fruta Ltd., ESADE Limited, Silk Grass Farms and Caribbean International Brewery Limited.

The Belize Country Pavilion was supported by BELTRAIDE representatives Monique Usher, Deputy Executive Director, and Zain Hernandez, Export Business Advisor.

BELTRAIDE said the event provided a valuable platform for Belizean businesses to build international connections and showcase the quality and diversity of locally produced goods.

World.title: PM Briceño: ‘Within five years, you’re going to see a major difference in this country; Five-year MCC clock starts
World.content:
PM Briceño: ‘Within five years, you’re going to see a major difference in this country; Five-year MCC clock starts

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Belize has officially moved from planning to implementation of its US$125 million Millennium Challenge Corporation Compact, beginning a five-year clock to complete major reforms and investments in education and energy.

Prime Minister John Briceño said Friday that work in both sectors will have to proceed simultaneously because Belize has only five years to deliver the projects.

“We only have five years, so we have to be simultaneously doing several things,” Briceño said.

On the education side, one of the immediate priorities will be the continued transformation of Belize’s Technical and Vocational Education and Training system, including establishment and operationalization of a National Training Agency.

The original compact requires the National Training Agency to operate as an autonomous institution responsible for planning and oversight of the TVET system, while sector skills councils are to connect training more closely to the needs of employers and the labour market.

The wider Education Project also includes teacher and school-leader training, national student assessments, strengthened teacher licensing, increased access to free secondary education and work-based opportunities such as apprenticeships.

MCA-Belize Chief Executive Officer Dr. Marcia Mahler Bouloy said the first year will involve continued work with ministries, educational institutions and other stakeholders, along with procuring consultants and carrying forward work already started during the preparation phase.

“What happens immediately is a continuation of our collaboration with the different ministries, agencies, university sectors that we have been working with,” Bouloy explained.

She said establishing the national training body and moving ahead with consultancies in the energy sector are among the activities that must be completed early if the compact is to remain on schedule.

Accountability and transparency mechanisms, she added, will continue throughout the five-year implementation period.

The energy component will meanwhile focus heavily on the new high-voltage submarine cable linking Ambergris Caye to the mainland transmission system, along with modernization of Belize’s electricity regulatory framework.

The compact was first signed on September 4, 2024. Under the agreement, its formal term lasts five years from its Entry into Force.

MCC is providing US$125 million, while the Government of Belize has increased its own contribution to approximately US$54.94 million.

Asked what Belizeans should expect by the end of those five years, Briceño pointed to both the shortage of skilled workers and the country’s energy challenges, saying he expects the investments to produce noticeable changes.

“Within five years, I have every confidence that you’re going to see a major difference in the development of this country,” the Prime Minister said.

World.title: Judge explains Juan Carlos Novelo acquittal in Leslie Verde murder: Key witness unreliable, circumstantial case fell short
World.content:
Judge explains Juan Carlos Novelo acquittal in Leslie Verde murder: Key witness unreliable, circumstantial case fell short

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Nearly two months after Juan Carlos Novelo was found not guilty of murdering his common-law wife, Leslie Margarita Verde, High Court Justice Candace Nanton has released a 29-page judgment explaining why the Crown’s circumstantial case failed to prove that Novelo was her killer.

Justice Nanton acquitted Novelo on July 20, 2026, following a judge-alone trial. At the time, she indicated that her detailed reasons would follow in writing. The decision sparked protests in Caye Caulker, where Verde’s relatives and supporters demanded an explanation for the verdict.

In her written ruling, Nanton made clear that there was no dispute that 32-year-old Verde had been unlawfully killed. Medical evidence from a doctor established that she died from asphyxia caused by neck compression and that the injuries were intentionally inflicted.

The crucial question, however, was whether the Crown had proven beyond reasonable doubt that Novelo was the person who inflicted those injuries.

The prosecution’s case relied heavily on Verde’s minor daughter, whose identity BBN is withholding. The child testified that she heard noises from her mother’s bedroom, peeped through an opening near the attic and saw Novelo beside her mother. She also claimed that she later saw him move her mother’s body behind the bedroom door.

But Justice Nanton found that the child’s evidence contained “material inconsistencies,” significant differences from earlier accounts and portions that were implausible when compared with the other evidence.

The judge noted that the inconsistencies went to the heart of the prosecution’s case rather than minor details. As a result, she said she could not safely rely on substantial portions of the child’s testimony — including the claims that she saw Novelo touching Verde and later moving her body.

That finding significantly weakened the Crown’s circumstantial case.

Surveillance evidence established that Verde returned home at approximately 4:29 a.m.; Novelo was at the residence and left around 5:28 a.m. He returned at approximately 8:16 a.m., went inside and shortly afterward left carrying beers. Verde was discovered dead closer to midday.

However, Dr. Blanco could not establish an exact time of death, meaning the remaining evidence did not prove that Verde necessarily died during a period when Novelo was the only person who could have killed her.

Justice Nanton said circumstantial evidence must form a coherent chain pointing to guilt as the only reasonable conclusion. Once critical portions of the minor’s testimony were rejected as unreliable, she found that the remaining evidence did not establish beyond reasonable doubt that Novelo caused Verde’s death.

Importantly, the judge stressed that the acquittal was not based on accepting Novelo’s version of events.

Novelo had given an unsworn statement maintaining that Verde was alive when he left their home and that during their eight-year relationship he had never harmed her. Justice Nanton said she did not need to rely on that account because the weakness was already present in the Crown’s case.

“The weakness identified is a failure of proof in the Crown’s case and does not arise from the Court accepting the Accused’s account,” the judgment stated.

Verde, a mother of three, was found unresponsive inside her Caye Caulker home on November 4, 2023. Police initially reported bruising around her neck and no signs of forced entry. Novelo was arrested and charged with murder days later.

Following his July acquittal, Verde’s family and other Caye Caulker residents staged a peaceful protest demanding answers, specifically calling for the written judgment explaining how the court arrived at the not-guilty verdict.

World.title: US$20M shifted from education to energy as MCC moves to fund new San Pedro submarine cable
World.content:
US$20M shifted from education to energy as MCC moves to fund new San Pedro submarine cable

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Twenty million U.S. dollars originally earmarked for education under Belize’s MCC Compact has been shifted to the energy sector, with Prime Minister John Briceño saying the Government will put up additional money to ensure that the education objectives are not sacrificed.

Officials explained the change Friday as the US$125 million Millennium Challenge Corporation Compact formally moved into its five-year implementation period.

When the compact was originally approved in 2024, US$73.8 million in MCC funds was budgeted for the Education Project and US$21.7 million for the Energy Project.

Following a U.S. Government foreign-assistance review, the compact was modified in July 2026 to move US$20 million from education into energy, primarily to accommodate major new electricity infrastructure, including a new 69-kilovolt submarine transmission cable to Ambergris Caye.

MCC’s current breakdown lists US$53.8 million for the Education Project and US$41.7 million for the Energy Project.

Briceño said Friday that the shift should not result in education programs being lost because the Government of Belize has stepped in to cover the funding gap.

“I don’t think there’s an impact because we are going to be filling the void or the shortage of the money,” the Prime Minister said.

Belize has now committed approximately US$54.94 million of its own money to the overall compact, up from the US$40.65 million contribution contemplated when the original agreement was signed.

MCC Acting Vice President Jason Small said Belize’s contribution is more than five times the minimum country contribution that MCC would ordinarily require, calling it a tangible demonstration of the Government’s commitment to completing the projects.

The urgency on the energy side centres heavily on Ambergris Caye.

Briceño told reporters that the existing submarine cable supplying San Pedro from the mainland had already reached the end of its expected lifespan in 2019.

“So there’s a sense of urgency to get that done,” Briceño said.

The Prime Minister said the project will involve more than the submarine cable itself, noting that new transmission infrastructure will also have to be developed from the Bomba area.

The modified compact officially provides for a new 69-kilovolt submarine transmission cable to Ambergris Caye, along with regulatory reforms aimed at modernizing the electricity sector and reducing wholesale electricity costs.

Briceño said the wider goal is to reduce Belize’s vulnerability to imported electricity and eventually place the country in a position where it can produce enough electricity domestically to meet its needs and potentially export power into the Central American market.

World.title: Repeat crack-pipe offender gets 3 months in jail after fourth conviction
World.content:
Repeat crack-pipe offender gets 3 months in jail after fourth conviction

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 46-year-old Belize City man has been sentenced to three months behind bars after pleading guilty to possession of a crack pipe, marking his fourth conviction for the same type of offence.

Marco Antonio Popper, a labourer of Belama Phase 1, appeared unrepresented before the Chief Magistrate in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Tuesday, September 15, where he pleaded guilty to possession of utensils used for smoking controlled drugs.

According to the court record, Popper had already been convicted on three previous occasions for possession of a crack pipe. In light of his previous convictions, the court imposed a custodial sentence of three months, effective September 15, 2026.

Police say that at around 1:30 a.m. Tuesday, officers and BDF soldiers conducting a foot patrol on Euphrates Avenue noticed Popper walking along the street.

An officer stopped Popper and informed him that he would be searched for illegal firearms and ammunition. When asked whether he had anything illegal to declare, Popper reportedly said no.

During the search, however, police allegedly discovered a silver-and-black metal pipe concealed in a compartment behind the zipper of his clothing. Police suspected the item was being used for smoking crack cocaine.

Popper was subsequently taken to the Precinct One Police Station, detained and charged.

He is now serving the three-month sentence at the Belize Central Prison.

World.title: Belize thanks Republic of Korea for US$3.4 million investment in stronger data for National Development
World.content:
Belize thanks Republic of Korea for US$3.4 million investment in stronger data for National Development

By Zoila Palma: The Government of Belize has expressed appreciation to the Republic of Korea for a US$3.4 million investment aimed at strengthening Belize’s statistical system and improving the use of reliable data for national development.

The partnership was reaffirmed during a meeting in Belmopan today between Minister of State in the Ministry of Economic Transformation Dr. Osmond Martinez, First Secretary and Consul at the Embassy of the Republic of Korea Lee Donghee, and UNDP Belize Deputy Resident Representative Michael Lund.

At the centre of the partnership is the Enabling Belize’s Statistical System Project, funded by the Republic of Korea through the Korea International Cooperation Agency (KOICA). The initiative is strengthening the Statistical Institute of Belize and the wider National Statistical System through investments in technology and equipment, technical skills, data collection and analysis, and improved capacity to measure poverty and other development challenges.

Minister Martinez thanked the Republic of Korea for its support, emphasizing the importance of reliable data in guiding government decisions.

“On behalf of the Government and people of Belize, I extend our sincere appreciation to the Republic of Korea for this important investment in our country. Better data helps Government understand where the greatest needs exist, make better decisions and direct resources where they can have the greatest impact on the lives of Belizeans.”

Lee Donghee reaffirmed the Republic of Korea’s commitment to Belize’s sustainable development, stating,

“The Republic of Korea is proud to partner with Belize in building stronger institutions and strengthening the use of data for national development. We are pleased that Korea’s support is contributing to capacity that will remain in Belize and continue serving the country well into the future.”

UNDP’s Michael Lund added, “This investment is about turning data into development. Through Korea’s partnership, Belize is building the skills, technology, and national systems needed to make better decisions today and in the future.”

World.title: US appeals court puts brakes on TCN deportations
World.content:
An image shared by US White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt depicting people boarding a deportation flight in January 2025. (Photo: @PressSec / via X)

WASHINGTON, United States (AFP) — A United States (US) federal appeals court on Friday broadly upheld a lower court ruling restricting a Trump administration policy of deporting undocumented migrants to countries that are not their own.

The three-judge panel of the US Court of Appeals for the First Circuit said people facing “third-country” deportations must be given effective notice ahead of time about where they are being sent to allow them to raise concerns about potential persecution.

Congress has made it US policy not to deport people to countries where their lives would be in danger or they could be subject to torture.

READ: No start date as yet to TCN agreement — Johnson Smith

“An individual’s right to contest removal to a country based on a fear of persecution in that country means little if one does not receive prior notice of the intended removal destination and a meaningful opportunity to contest that destination,” said Judge Seth Aframe, writing for the unanimous three-judge panel.

Department of Homeland Security (DHS) policy “would deny access to that protection to a substantial swath of noncitizens who are sent to third countries with no notice of their destination,” the judge said.

The Trump administration is expected to appeal the case to the conservative-dominated Supreme Court.

Donald Trump campaigned for president promising to expel millions of undocumented migrants from the United States and has taken a number of actions aimed at speeding up deportations since returning to the White House.

The Trump administration has defended third-country deportations as necessary since the home nations of some of those who are targeted for removal sometimes refuse to accept them.

World.title: Father clueless if daughter was intimate with Pastor Kevin Smith
World.content:
This combo photo shows deceased pastor Kevin Smith and Taneka Gardener who was killed at Smith's church in a 2021 incident

KINGSTON, Jamaica — The father of Taneka Gardner, the 39-year-old woman who had her throat slashed on October 17, 2021, at the Pathways International Restoration Ministries in Albion, St James, told a defence attorney on Thursday during cross-examination that he had no knowledge of his daughter being in a romantic relationship with the late pastor of the church, Dr Kevin Smith.

The murder trial of Andre Ruddock, the man accused of killing Gardner, got underway in the Home Circuit Court in Kingston on Thursday after a seven-member jury was empanelled on Wednesday.

Ruddock, under instructions from Smith, allegedly cut Gardner’s throat during what is widely believed to be a sacrificial killing.

Attorney-at-law Venice Brown, who along with Anthony Williams is representing Ruddock, appeared to have known something about a romantic relationship between Smith and Gardner, as the few questions she posed to the witness were mainly centred on that topic.

Brown asked the father if his daughter was involved romantically with Smith and he responded, “I don’t know about that one.

Brown right after suggested to the father that his daughter was in a romantic relationship with the pastor, however, trial Judge Leighton Pusey pointed out to her that the witness already indicated that he knew nothing about the alleged romance and prompted her to move on to the next question.

The next question to the father was if his daughter had any known medical conditions before she died.

“No, madam,” the father said to the attorney, who had no further questions.

During examination-in-chief, prosecutor LaToya Bernard asked the father a series of questions to establish for the seven jurors that he actually buried his daughter and that she was in fact dead.

The father shared that he received a call on October 18, the day after the incident, which prompted him to go to the church in Albion.

“I just went there because I heard what happened. I saw the police and the yellow tape. A lot of police and yellow tape, caution tape. I saw the tape blocking the entrance to the church. No madam, I didn’t go over to the church when I saw the caution tape,” he said.

He explained that he then proceeded to a location he referred to as Mango Walk, where his cousin resided. He explained that both of them went to the Freeport Police Station where he spoke to a detective inspector.

“I left for the Delapenha Funeral Home in Montego Bay, St James, to see the body because they said the body was there. They took out the body and showed it to me. It was Taneka Gardner, my daughter. I saw a slash on her throat. Workers from Delapenha were there with me. My cousin didn’t come inside.

“On November 19, 2021, I was called to come to St Catherine at Archer’s Funeral Home in Spanish Town. When I got there I was early so I waited until they opened. I went inside and a policeman spoke to me and took me to a room where the doctor was going to perform the autopsy. Taneka Gardner’s body was on a table and I was asked to identify her and I identified her as Taneka Gardner to the doctor as well as the police,” he said, explaining that he last spoke to his daughter about four days before she was killed.

After Gardner’s father left the witness stand, Corey James, the second witness, took up his position to give the jurors his chilling account of what occurred at the church on that fateful day in 2021.

“>He confirmed knowing Ruddock — the accused — very well as both of them had been attending the church together since 2014.

James, who is a livestock farmer, confirmed that Smith was the head of the church and that other members including himself and Ruddock were given various roles and functions.

He shared that while Ruddock was a security guard and Smith’s bodyguard, he on the other hand was given the role of getting Smith dressed and shaving his head.

“I helped Dr Smith get dressed before services,” he told the court.

James said that on the day of the incident, there was not supposed to be any service at the church because the day before, on Saturday, October 16, 2021, there was a “special ceremony”.

So, on the Sunday while he was cooking and resting, he had no intentions of going to church. However, his wife ran upstairs to him and told him something. He got out of bed and started to get ready to head down to the church. Asked by prosecutor Bernard why he, his wife and others got ready for church, James explained that Pastor Smith made a Facebook post where he informed his congregants of a flood and instructed them to come to him for safe haven.

“After she spoke with me we got ready, my wife, myself, our daughter and one of her friends, her friend’s mother and a nephew,” he said.

“Dr Smith made a post on Facebook. It was not his first time. He would post on his timeline on Facebook. Dr Smith made a post that a flood was coming. I am not sure what flood it was, but that was what he said, and we should come to the church for a safe haven. Yes, I did believe that a flood was coming, and I got ready and went to the church. When I reached the church it was between 1:00 pm and 3:00 pm. My family and friends travelled with me.

“When I got there, there were other individuals there. I was in yellow shorts, a blue hoodie, and I had a white sheet covering myself. Dr Smith said we should all cover ourselves with a white sheet. Everyone who travelled with me had a white sheet. When I got to the church, I saw others covered in white sheet. The covering up with the sheet was something new that started on the 16th, the day before at the special ceremony.

“I went on the boardwalk and was going inside the building. Dr Smith was at the top of the step at the main entrance of the building. Yes, I spoke with Dr Kevin Smith, and he spoke to me. I entered the building and sat down on the ground. He told us all to sit on the ground, cover ourselves with the sheets and not look in his face. Around 12 individuals [were in the building]. Mr Michael Brown, my wife’s cousin, was also at the church. Dr Smith started speaking. We started throwing food stuff outside. We threw away sanitary napkins, tissue and other stuff out the front of the building.

Because of COVID-19, Dr Smith was telling us the world was coming to an end,” James said, pointing out that the pastor was frequently telling them to take their money out of the bank.

He said Smith told them to throw out the food and other stuff because they were from Babylon.

While James and others threw out the items, he explained that a bottle fell from a table and broke on the ground inside the church.

He told the court that Smith informed them that those who were on the opposite side of the bottle would have to die in order for them to enter into the Kingdom.

“He said he got a revelation. I was on the opposite side, and Dr Smith said to me that in order for me to come over on the other side, my throat has to be cut. I was confused when he mentioned that to me. I spoke to Dr Smith, and he said I was a demon and that I should come out of the sanctuary. After I was told my throat would be cut, Kevaughn Plummer approached me with a knife, and he was trying to put the knife under my throat. I rest my finger under my neck to push away the knife. The knife was right under my chin. Dr Smith said I should get out.”

He said that when he turned around to walk outside, he felt someone stab him in the back, causing him to run out on the pavement.

“I felt like something was running down in my back. I wiped my back, and when I looked, I saw blood. Mr Smith was standing at the entrance of the door when I turned around. He said something to me. I spoke to Andre Ruddock and asked him if he could tie the white cloth around my back. He did not tie it, but Aldeane Campbell tied it for me. There were a lot of people outside the fence on the road, including my mom, sister, nephew and other people I would call friends. They wanted to come on the compound. The gate was closed, so they weren’t able to come over.”

The witness said he remained at the church because his wife and his daughter were still inside.

While on the outside of the church building, James said he could hear things being smashed and broken on the inside.

“It was still bright, so it was maybe around after 3:00 pm. Persons were shouting on the outside, ‘it’s Israel God, Israel King’. This was on the outside of the fence on the roadside. He shared that Smith took out a piece of paper with names on it. Among the names on the list were Taneka Gardner.

He appointed two archangels, Ruddock and another man and gave them two knives. He then instructed them to go to the church gate and not let anybody else in unless their names were called.

When Gardner was called, she entered and signed 999 beside her name on the paper. She was given instructions, including to kneel down.

“When Kevin Smith called Taneka Gardner’s name, Andrew Ruddock and Kayon Ramsey opened the gate and let her in. The people on the outside of the gate, I could see them over the picket fence. When Taneka Gardner was allowed to come on the inside, she was covered in the white garment. White cloth was tied around her head. I could see her face when she came in. Her head was covered as well. She had a suitcase in her hand, a mini suitcase. She came in with it and Kevin Smith asked her where she was going with that bag. One of the young men took it from her and went back to the gate with it.

“Kevin Smith said, ‘Taneka Gardner, your blood is not clean’. He was speaking very loudly. He continued to speak to her. He asked her, ‘do you believe that I am God? Do you believe I can heal you?’ She said Yes. He went further and he said, do you believe that if you die I can bring you back to life? She shouted on the top of her voice and said yes. Dr Smith gave a command. He said, ‘Archangel, cut her throat.’ He appointed Kayon Ramsey and Andre Ruddock as Archangel Gabriel and Michael.

“I was looking directly in the direction of Andre Ruddock. I watched Andre use his elbow to nudge Kayon Ramsey, but Kayon did not move. Andre Ruddock ran off from the gate and ran towards Taneka Gardner. Miss Taneka Gardner was kneeling down, and Andre Ruddock put the knife at her throat, and he was rubbing her throat with the knife. I just saw her foot kicking, and I could hear a gargling sound, like the blood was rushing down her windpipe as if she had fluid in her mouth, like when you put water in your mouth and gargle. He was rubbing the knife at her throat for about a minute before he brought her down to the ground. Mr Smith said to him to cut her head right off. While Andre Ruddock was cutting her throat, a cow was coming down from up the top,” he said, telling the court that it was at that time Smith switched focus from Gardner and told Ruddock and Ramsey to kill the cow.

The witness explained that Ruddock then got up from where Gardner was, while Ramsey chased down the cow.

“Taneka Gardner was just lying there. You could see the white sheet with what appeared to be blood and it was also on the sheet that Andre Ruddock had on,” he said.

World.title: 10 things only a Westwood High girl would know
World.content:
In this April 15, 2011 file photo, students of Westwood High School at an Earth Day expo put on by the Environmental Foundation of Jamaica and held at Devon House in St Andrew. (Photo: Bryan Cummings)

Westwood High School is known for producing talented, well-educated and poised young ladies. The institution, which has been in existence for more than a century, can credit much of this to its vibrant culture and traditions.

Observer Online spoke to a number of the Stewart Town, Trelawny-based school’s alumni to find out some of the things that every Westwood girl would know.

1. Jippi Jappa hat and wearing all white

Westwood High is one of the few schools in Jamaica where students wear hats as part of their uniform. The tradition, which has its roots in English school customs, has been passed down and retained by the institution over the years. The Jippi Jappa hat, also known as a Panama hat, is worn by the young ladies along with their uniforms. Students are not permitted to wear the hat past the principal’s building.

Students are also expected to have a set of white clothing outside of their regular uniform. This is worn on occasions when they are not required to be in uniform, except on Friday evenings and Saturdays.

2. The Jacaranda tree

The Jacaranda tree was one of the familiar landmarks on the Westwood campus and a popular meeting spot for students during break time. The ladies gathered beneath the tree to catch up with friends, relax and enjoy each other’s company. With its vibrant purple blooms and towering structure, the tree provided both a scenic and comfortable setting. Unfortunately, the tree has been cut down, but it remains a memorable part of the Westwood experience.

3. Observing silence

Silence is a familiar part of life at Westwood. Students are expected to observe silence during prep or study time, meal times and intervals. For many old girls, learning when to talk and when to remain quiet was simply part of the discipline and routine of school life.

4. Sarcasm and lapsing

Westwood ladies are known for their quick wit and, according to old girls, their ability to dish out a healthy dose of sarcasm. They also participate in what is known as “lapsing”. This is when a word is mispronounced and other students repeat the word or phrase, often drawing attention to the mistake. For Westwood girls, it is all part of the banter and camaraderie that develop among students.

5. Knife and fork

Table manners are a big part of the meal-time experience at Westwood. Students are expected to eat their meals using a knife and fork and to follow proper dining etiquette. This includes knowing how to conduct themselves at the table and, in some cases, asking permission before doing things such as chewing bones at the table. For many students, these lessons extended beyond the dining hall and became part of the poise and etiquette associated with being a Westwood girl.

6. Day girls and boarders

Westwood is one of the few schools in Jamaica that offers a boarding option for students. Those who live on the school compound are referred to as boarders, while students who travel to school are called ‘day girls’.

7. Walking to church

Boarders are expected to walk to church on Sundays. The girls are divided based on denomination and walk together to their respective churches. For many boarders, the walk to church is a familiar part of the Westwood boarding experience.

8. Out-of-bounds areas

The ladies of Westwood know that there are certain areas of the school that they are not allowed to enter. These include the teachers’ steps and staff rooms. Students are expected to know and respect these boundaries, with venturing into out-of-bounds areas likely to result in disciplinary action.

9. Students not allowed in stores without parental supervision

If a young lady wanted to enter a store while wearing her uniform, she had to be accompanied by a parent. If she entered a store without a parent and misbehaved, any report made to the school could result in her being reprimanded when she returned. The rule meant that students were expected to remember that their behaviour while wearing the Westwood uniform reflected on the school.

10. Silence as punishment

Silence was also used as a form of punishment at Westwood. Students who misbehave could be required to observe silence. The punishment was intended to give students time to settle down, reflect on their behaviour and regain their composure.

– Carlysia Ramdeen

World.title: Market Bag: Tomato now $500 as food prices continue to climb
World.content:
KINGSTON, Jamaica — Food prices continue to surge at the Coronation Market this week amid worsening drought conditions which have affected agricultural supplies across the country.

Among the more expensive items at the market are lettuce, selling for $1,500 per pound, and Scotch bonnet peppers at $700 per pound. Sweet peppers are going for $600 per pound, while carrots and tomatoes are selling for $500 per pound. Onions, sweet potatoes and Irish potatoes are each priced at approximately $400 per pound.

Speaking on the latest episode of Market Bag with host Carlysia Ramdeen, Andre Barnaby of the Kingston and St Andrew Municipal Corporation pointed to changing weather patterns as one of the major challenges affecting market supply and prices.

“I’d say the biggest challenge right now that we’re facing is climate change so the variation in the weather. So at times or different times of the year, we have large yields and like now for example, in the drought period, we have like way less in terms of supplies. So that affects the overall, that’s like the biggest challenge we face because it also affects price,” Barnaby said.

Catch the latest episode of Market Bag on all Jamaica Observer digital platforms.

World.title: Reggae Boyz squad named for opening Nations League games
World.content:
Jamaica’s Reggae Boyz Leon Bailey (left), Damion Lowe (second left) and Demarai Gray (partially hidden) celebrate with Jon Russell after he scored against Guatemala during the Concacaf World Cup Qualifier at the National Stadium on Tuesday, June 10, 2025. (Photo: Observer file)

Head Coach Rudolph Speid has named his Reggae Boyz squad for the first two games of their 2026-2027 Concacaf Nations League campaign.

Jamaica, drawn in Group B, will open the first round at the National Stadium against Guatemala on Friday, September 25, before welcoming Honduras four days later on Tuesday, September 29.

Speid has selected a 24-man squad for the assignment.

It will see the return to the Reggae Boyz squad for a number of players who last represented Jamaica in the failed World Cup 2026 qualifying campaign. Among them are goalkeeper and captain Andre Blake, wingers Leon Bailey and Tyreece Campbell, defender Richard King, midfielders Kasey Palmer and Karoy Anderson, and forward Renaldo Cephas.

The top two teams from the two Nations League preliminary groups will qualify for the finals where they will be drawn alongside the ranked teams- two-time defending champions Mexico, the USA, Canada and Panama in the quarterfinals.
