World.title: WATCH: Tensions flare at meeting over Charles’ Barking Lodge aquaculture project
World.content:
ST THOMAS, Jamaica — A sensitisation meeting over a controversial aquaculture project in Barking Lodge, St Thomas erupted in chaos Tuesday as tensions boiled over amid continued opposition to the development near a primary school in the community.

The meeting, held at the Barking Lodge Primary and Infant School, the institution located behind the proposed fish ponds, ended abruptly when Member of Parliament for St Thomas Eastern Rose Shaw and her team walked out.

Dr Michelle Charles, the former St Thomas Eastern Member of Parliament and director of St Thomas Farms Limited, the company behind the project, had organised the sensitisation meeting for the development which was suspended due to a lack of environmental permits.

At the meeting, an overview of the project was presented along with environmental and safety measures that will guide the development.

WATCH: Charles defends Barking Lodge aquaculture project, addresses safety concerns

Clive Williams, director of the National Fisheries Authority, said the organisation determined that the project was conducted according to agricultural standards and was indeed feasible.

“When we looked at the site, the water source that is available, the proximity to the community, we realised that the project is feasible… We don’t see any challenges of it having an adverse effect on the environment and the community,” Williams said.

Despite Williams’ assurances, tensions flared as critics of the project maintained their skepticism, while Shaw accused the chairman of the meeting of having a political agenda.

“I am utterly disgusted with what is taking place… a politician is cheering the meeting,” Shaw said.

The meeting subsequently erupted in a shouting match before ending prematurely, and even the police had to be called in to quell tensions.

Charles has described the initiative as having the potential to become one of the first major commercial aquaculture operations on Jamaica’s eastern side. She said responsible investment of this nature could contribute to job creation, skills training, infrastructure improvements and sustained economic growth in an area that has experienced limited commercial development since the decline of the sugar industry.

According to Charles, consultations were held with the school’s principal before construction of the ponds began, and student safety has remained a priority throughout the planning process.

World.title: ‘Mommy, them want me turn cruff”
World.content:
BICKERSTETH, St James — The lament of a 10-year-old student struck a chord with residents Thursday after thieves ransacked Bickersteth Primary and Infant School, making off with computers and tuck shop supplies in the fifth break-in there in just seven years.

“Mommy, them people yah want me turn cruff,” was how the boy reacted to news of the break-in, his mother told the Jamaica Observer.

The mother, who asked not be named, said her son, a grade five student, cried on the verandah of their house as he was told that school would be closed on Thursday and Friday because of the crime.

“I told him ‘Son, you nah turn cruff, we will stand with you’,” she related to the Observer.

Cruff is a Jamaican colloquial term for individuals who are deemed lazy, lack ambition, or have poor social etiquette.

The mother is among parents and residents who are now expressing anguish over the situation at the school.

“I usually send him out before me, but he has to stay home with his sister today,” the distraught mother said.

On Thursday morning, school administrators turned up to see windows and doors at the school pried open and items missing.

“They ripped the grill out the wall, broke the window and came in,” Principal Robert Gordon said. “Not even [Hurricane] Melissa did a job like that, the place was ransacked.”

Category 5 Melissa left widespread destruction across western and south-western parishes last October.

Principal Gordon said Thursday’s early morning break-in was the fifth in seven years.

“Last year, this time, they broke into the school twice, but that individual was held. We lost some equipment as well — computers and food items,” Gordon said.

He speculated that the robbery may be connected with others committed in western Jamaica in recent times.

“Based on what is happening now and the series of schools — Bogue Hill, Retrieve, Anchovy — it seems like they are just going through and hitting schools in a series,” Gordon said.

A man who gave his name as Anglin, described the break-in as disheartening.

“I have four daughters and all of them went through here. The last one was head girl at Anchovy, one got 11 subjects at Mount Alvernia, but this is the ground where it all started,” he said.

“This is heartbreaking, man,” he added.

On Thursday, following an emergency meeting of the school board, several members of staff were seen engaged in cleaning-up activities while listening to gospel music amid the sound of power tools as work was ongoing to replace a damaged window.

“We are trying to fix back as best as possible, even though it might be temporary, but we want to secure the area from the elements because rain may fall and the entire area is ripped out and we don’t want the office to be compromised any further,” Principal Gordon told the Observer.

“The gentleman that is working now is a community person; he’s from the area, his children came to school here. We called him, he dropped what he was doing, and he’s here and we are very appreciative of that,” Gordon said, adding that the school will be closed for the rest of the week while they work to sort things out. However, online classes will be held.

“One of the things we looked at is the impact it will have on the students seeing the school ripped apart and that could have a long-term impact on their mental psyche,” the principal explained.

“We said, ‘Okay, let’s sort of fix back the school in a way, because these children are very young, they are very impressionable, and we have to be mindful of what they see’,” he added.

“We have spoken to the teachers and we have asked them to send out work for the students to do virtually,” he revealed.

On Wednesday, Education Minister Senator Dr Dana Morris Dixon acknowledged that schools, particularly in western Jamaica, are being plagued by break-ins since the start of the academic year.

“The west has gone through a lot of trauma for us to be dealing with theft of computers for these schools and these children, it is really heartbreaking,” she lamented during the weekly post-Cabinet news briefing.

She said the series of robberies has resulted in her reaching out to the national security minister and police commissioner for assistance.

World.title: ‘It’s a fallacy’
World.content:
ROBINSON... we’re far from being in a good position in the economy

Opposition spokesman on finance Julian Robinson has dismissed as a “fallacy” the rosy picture of the Jamaican economy presented by Finance Minister Fayval Williams during Wednesday’s post-Cabinet media briefing.

Among other things, Williams noted that the rate of recovery from the fallout caused by Hurricane Melissa, which destroyed large swathes of south- and north-western parishes last October, was 18 months ahead of earlier projections by the Planning Institute of Jamaica (PIOJ).

However, Robinson is pointing to inflation running at nearly eight per cent and a $30-billion tax revenue shortfall as signs of a struggling economy.

In a video released by the Opposition People’s National Party (PNP) on Thursday, Robinson suggested that the finance minister was merely trying to put a positive spin on the situation. He reminded that in the last quarter the Government’s own projection for revenues was $28.7 billion lower than projected.

“It’s important to note that these projections were done in March 2026, which is after Hurricane Melissa, so they would have factored in Melissa and they would have made their projections,” he said.

Robinson pointed out that the revenue shortfall of nearly $30 billion forced the Government to go back to the market to borrow $30 billion but the Administration was unable to raise the full amount.

“To give this impression that the economy is doing great is really a fallacy,” he declared.

The Opposition spokesman also highlighted what he described as the cost of living pressures facing Jamaicans. He cited that at nearly eight per cent, inflation was “way above the Bank of Jamaica (BOJ) target range of four to six per cent”.

“I anticipate that when the BOJ’s monetary policy committee meets, they will be looking to raise interest rates to try and tame inflation,” he stated.

Were the central bank to take such a decision, Robinson conceded that this would put more pressure on businesses which will have to pay more on their loans, and on consumers, who will have to pay more on their mortgages and the various loans they are carrying.

“We’re far from being in a good position in the economy, we’re actually seeing the highest rates of car repossessions; we’re seeing bad loans at banks at elevated rates. So it indicates that there’s significant consumer pressure being faced, people are struggling to meet their basic obligations,” said Robinson.

Anticipating talk from some quarters that the cost of living pressure is being driven by factors outside Jamaica’s control, such as the higher cost for fuel and electricity as a result of the Middle East war, Robinson said while that is true, there are things within the control of the Government that would lessen the pressure on Jamaicans.

“The Government has the control to determine how much imported oil we use, it has been an absolute failure on the part of this Government to increase the amount of renewables that have been added to the grid,” Robinson argued.

“In the 10-and-a-half years that they have been in office, they have added no renewables to the grid,” he said, adding that what was in fact added since 2016 started under the previous PNP Administration with Phillip Paulwell as energy minister.

Pointing out that it took the Jamaica Labour Party Government eight years to issue a request for proposal for renewables, the Opposition spokesman said those companies that have been selected cannot sign private purchase agreements with Jamaica Public Service Company because the company’s contract is in limbo (its licence expires in July 2027).

He asserted that while we cannot control the price of oil, we can determine how much oil we import by building out more renewables. In this regard, he said the Government has failed; a failure with a direct impact on cost of living.

“Because, if we’re less dependent on oil, it improves our financial position and it means the impact is less on consumers,” he said.

Robinson also argued that the minister pointing out that the economy is recovering faster than projected masks certain uncomfortable realities.

“We’re underspending the capital budget. Our capital budget is required to build out schools, hospitals, roads, etc, we’re underspending that,” he reiterated. He argued that such spend is important to ensuring that there’s growth in the economy “because there’s a direct link between your capital budget and economic growth and for the last five years we have underspent it”.

Robinson pointed out that when the capital budget is underutilised, the money is shifted to recurrent expenditure such as wages and salaries. “This makes the fiscal situation look a little better but it does not account for the fact that we have been woefully underspending the capital budget,” he insisted.

He lamented that the vast majority of Jamaicans most affected by Hurricane Melissa — either at the individual or small business level — have received no assistance from Government. This, he said, has made it difficult for them to recover, resulting in lower tax revenues. He insisted that Government has taken too long to get help to those who are most in need.

In her take on the economy, Williams highlighted that in the quarter following the hurricane, the economy contracted 7.1 per cent, then 4.1 per cent in the next quarter and just 2.9 per cent in the quarter after that. She said the 2.9 per cent projection should be finalised by the Statistical Institute of Jamaica by the end of September.

The finance minister argued that the shrinking year-on-year numbers are themselves proof that the economy is recovering, adding further that “an economy in decline produces deepening figures, not improving ones”.

Williams urged Jamaicans to remember that immediately after the hurricane, PIOJ projected that the country would not get back to its pre-Melissa level of output until the last quarter of 2028. She noted that the PIOJ now expects that the economy will begin to see growth by the second quarter of 2027 — “six quarters earlier, a year-and-a-half earlier”. According to her, the PIOJ “has been able to revise their forecast because the out-turn keeps getting better”.

World.title: ‘There are no decent parties left’: Sham elections underscore Putin’s grip on Russia
World.content:
But other opponents of the Kremlin say Navalnaya’s strategy is giving credibility to sham elections that are only held to justify Russian President Vladimir Putin’s maximalist war against Ukraine and tighten his grip on Russian society.

“To whoever comes to us with a sword — do not expect mercy,” Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said in a campaign ad for Putin’s United Russia party, alongside NHL superstar Alex Ovechkin and the propagandist Margarita Simonyan, who runs the state broadcaster RT.

Putin’s veterans

The Kremlin’s response to the opposition suggests it is worried that people are growing tired of the war.

By removing anti-war candidates from the ballot and promoting pro-war voices, Moscow seeks to overstate public support for the invasion of Ukraine, says Ivan Preobrazhensky, a Russian political scientist based in Prague. “By electing them, people are effectively endorsing the policies of the ruling party and the government,” he told POLITICO, even though voters have no real alternative.

Yabloko received between 1% and 2% of votes in previous parliamentary elections and was seen as “politically dead” by the Kremlin, according to Maxim Reznik, a former party leader in St. Petersburg. By allowing it to run, Reznik said, the Kremlin “wanted to show that just 1.5% of Russians oppose war.”

But reports in Russian media suggested that Yabloko’s recent positioning as “the only peace party,” as well as its advocacy for an immediate ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, had boosted its electoral support. The Nezavisimaya Gazeta reported on a July poll from an unnamed agency giving Yabloko a rating of 9.4%. Faridaily, an outlet founded by independent journalist Farida Rustamova, reported that internal government polling put the party around 5.5%.

World.title: European leaders prepare public for ‘intensified threat’ from Putin
World.content:
The warnings underscore a growing sense of anxiety in Europe amid fast-proliferating incidents of airspace violations and sabotage attempts in recent months. NATO allies have repeatedly said they see the attacks as pressure from the Kremlin to reduce their support for Ukraine but have muted their response over fears of escalation.

French President Emmanuel Macron summoned party leaders and 2027 presidential candidates for an emergency meeting on Friday to talk about Ukraine, Iran and the growing energy crisis.

He called Tusk’s warnings “sound and well-documented” as he announced a new critical infrastructure protection plan, adding: “In recent weeks … the Russian hybrid threat against Europeans and France has intensified.”

Guillaume Lacroix, leader of the Radical Party of the Left, left the meeting saying: “At the age of 50, I have rarely felt such vertigo.”

“It is no coincidence that the Polish prime minister is speaking out so strongly,” Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said Friday. “We need to take that warning very seriously … we must consistently demonstrate that we do not accept this and that we will take action if necessary.”

On Thursday, Finnish President Alexander Stubb told his country it was “worth mentally preparing for something to happen” including sabotage and Russian drones.

World.title: Australia following Canada as EU associate member is ‘pure speculation,’ says Commission
World.content:
Asked whether the meeting could provide an opportunity to discuss the associate membership idea with Australia, Podestà dismissed the suggestion.

“We have a very strong and close relationship with our Australian partners,” she said. “All the rest is pure speculation, and we’re not going to enter into that.”

Von der Leyen pitched Canada as a potential first EU “associate member” during her State of the Union address on Wednesday. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has welcomed the ambition behind closer EU-Canada ties but has stopped short of endorsing the proposed status.

European Parliament President Roberta Metsola subsequently said countries such as Australia and New Zealand could potentially follow Canada.

But Commission spokesperson Olof Gill stressed that Brussels is currently focused solely on developing the idea with Ottawa.

“What we’re focused on here is putting flesh on the bone on this idea,” Gill said, adding that the Commission is working with member states and Canadian partners to establish what the concept could look like in practice. “All other discussions are subsequent to that.”

World.title: Germany gets its first F-35 as Europe’s fighter plans fall apart
World.content:
But without the FCAS, Berlin is left without an obvious European successor.

“We want and need to maintain nuclear sharing,” Pistorius said ahead of the handover. The F-35, he argued, is currently “the only aircraft in the world” capable of fulfilling that mission.

Under the NATO nuclear-sharing program, Germany and other select allies have aircraft that can carry U.S. nuclear bombs, although the decision to use them remains with Washington.

The first F-35s will remain in the United States for training, with German pilots and technicians preparing for operations before more jets are sent to Büchel in late 2027. Full operational capability is expected by 2030.

Berlin currently operates around 80 Tornados, and some missions will migrate to the Eurofighter Typhoon. But the collapse of FCAS has opened a longer-term gap in Germany's plans for its combat-air fleet.

During June's Berlin Air Show, Pistorius said Berlin is weighing whether to acquire additional F-35s as a “bridge” option after the FCAS failure, to join an existing international sixth-generation program or to develop a national effort headed by Airbus.

World.title: Macron to call emergency G7 meeting as energy prices spike and Russian hybrid attacks mount
World.content:
“The situation we face is serious. It is serious due to the international situation and the consequence of wars that we endure,” Macron said. “In this context we need to stay united.”

France’s dire fiscal outlook, which has prompted the government to pursue a €54 billion budget squeeze next year, will make it difficult for the state to massively subsidize increasingly expensive energy bills. Macron told reporters, however, that the government was working on targeted assistance proposals.

Macron also said he was seeking to firm up French access to oil and gas supplies during recent meetings with leaders from Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates. He added that he’d discuss France’s trade in petroleum products and liquefied natural gas with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney when the two meet on Sunday.

The president said France was stepping up efforts to protect critical infrastructure and defense production sites amid the uptick in cyberattacks and the intensified threat of so-called hybrid attacks from Russia, including recent ones on a Ukrainian passenger train and at Leipzig airport in Germany. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned Thursday that Russia was planning to target Ukraine’s European allies using drones or rockets.

Among those in attendance were center-right former Prime Minister Edouard Philippe, centrist Gabriel Attal, conservative candidate Bruno Retailleau, center-left Raphaël Glucksmann, Greens leader Marine Tondelier and Socialist Party chief Olivier Faure. Far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen, who has a commanding lead in the polls, was represented by her party’s president, Jordan Bardella, while far-left hopeful Jean-Luc Mélenchon was represented by a high-ranking lawmaker from his party, Manuel Bompard.

The politicians who spoke to reporters after the meeting acknowledged the gravity of what had been discussed. Guillaume Lacroix, the head of a small left-wing party, wrote online that the stakes of the three-hour briefing had made his head spin.

World.title: Ukraine’s NATO envoy calls for more air defense donations
World.content:
“We need to stop viewing assistance that enables Ukraine to defend itself as purely a matter of supporting Ukraine. It is also in NATO’s own interest … the more drones and missiles Ukraine can destroy in its own airspace, the fewer will cross the borders of neighboring NATO countries,” the envoy added.

Getmanchuk underlined that Western countries still have stocks of interceptor missiles to donate, including missiles close to the end of their service lives.

“There is hardly a better way to decommission them than by using them in the Ukrainian sky,” Getmanchuk said.

Kyiv is proposing a workaround: allies hand over interceptors from their existing stocks now, and Ukraine replaces them later with missiles it has already ordered.

“It’s a swap — not a donation. What we need is to get through this winter,” Getmanchuk said.

Ukraine is placing substantial orders, using both partner funding and the EU’s €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan. These contracts cover not only hundreds of Patriot interceptors — both PAC-2s and PAC-3s — but also European systems, including SAMP/T and Aster 30 missiles, IRIS-T and others.

World.title: EU to ban metal scrap exports to India, Egypt on environmental grounds
World.content:
The EU exported nearly 19 million tonnes of scrap metal in 2025, accounting for over half the bloc’s total recyclable raw materials exports.

Egypt and India respectively bought over 1.3 million and 850,000 tonnes of scrap metal.

Last-minute concerns over the EU’s trade deal with India led the European Commission to withdraw planned export duties on aluminum scrap earlier this month.

India is a major importer of aluminum scrap. The country last year exported over 350,000 tons of aluminum scrap alone.

The executive was due to present an instrument to slow exports of cheap aluminum scrap to buyers outside the single market, keeping prices down for aluminum producers and users within the bloc. The European aluminum sector has pushed for priority access to local scrap.

EU industry chief Stéphane Séjourné said, however, that the EU would scrap the measure after it became clear it would only cover around half of the bloc’s aluminum scrap exports and decided to pursue a solution “entirely independent” of trade policy instruments.

Egypt and India will still be able to export other scrap materials, including paper, wood, rubber, and textile waste.

The Commission will consult on the suggested country exemptions until October 16, before adopting the final list in November, as required under the regulation.

World.title: British MPs to tackle UK crisis — why it does so badly in Eurovision
World.content:
The British entry is currently selected internally by the BBC, one of the world’s largest public broadcasters, and chosen from the third biggest record industry on the planet, behind the U.S. and Japan. It also automatically qualifies for the contest’s final because the BBC is one of the largest contributors to the event’s organizer, the European Broadcasting Union.

Despite this, the U.K. has repeatedly finished in the bottom half of the leaderboard over the past 15 years, with only one exception: Sam Ryder, who claimed second place in 2022 with ‘Space Man.’

The committee is expected to hear from figures from the BBC and the music industry to establish whether the U.K.’s track record is “the result of bad song choice, weak performance … or something else,” Dinenage told the BBC.

The British broadcaster has yet to announce its entry for next year’s event, which will take place in May 2027 in Burgas, Bulgaria.

The contest has been overshadowed in recent years by boycotts from multiple nations over Israel’s participation, following the Oct. 7 2023 Hamas attack and subsequent Israeli military offensive in Gaza. Dutch broadcaster AVROTROS and Ireland’s RTÉ have already announced that they will not be taking part in next year’s contest.

World.title: Trump threatens to ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House
World.content:
President Donald Trump has said he is banning three major news organisations, CNN, MS NOW and Politico, from the White House with immediate effect, accusing them of publishing “fake news”, “fiction” and “lies”.

 

It is not yet clear what the ban will entail. Trump also warned that restrictions could be extended to other media outlets.

In a post on his Truth Social platform on Friday, the president said the three outlets “constantly write or report fiction and lies” about his administration, although he provided no specific examples.

President Trump writing on Truth Social via Truth Social

The move is the latest test of First Amendment protections guaranteeing freedom of the press in the United States.

It is also the latest move by Trump’s second administration to restrict press access. He has already tightened controls over which journalists can join the White House press pool, the small group of reporters who accompany the president into restricted spaces such as the Oval Office and aboard Air Force One.

CNN is part of the traditional five-network television pool that travels with and covers the president. It is not yet clear whether the new ban will affect that arrangement.

In 2025, Trump restricted Associated Press access to some presidential events after the news agency continued to use the name “Gulf of Mexico” rather than Trump’s preferred “Gulf of America”. AP subsequently launched legal action over the restrictions. The case remains ongoing.

During Trump’s first term, CNN reporter Kaitlan Collins was barred from a White House Rose Garden event after officials said questions she asked the president earlier that day were "inappropriate" for the venue.

While it is extremely rare for a US president to bar an entire news organisation from the White House, previous administrations have also imposed restrictions on individual outlets. President Richard Nixon restricted access for The Washington Post during the Watergate scandal in the 1970s.

World.title: As Russia strikes Kyiv and Kharkiv, Russian cooling tower hit by drone
World.content:
Russia has launched attacks on several areas of Ukraine, with two killed in Balakliia in Kharkiv and missiles launched at the capita, Kyiv.

 

In a post on Telegram, the head of Balakliia's military administration Vitalii Karabanov gave an update on the damage and loss of life: "Sadly, the consequences of this attack are terrible. Early reports indicate that two people have been killed in the strike. I extend my deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of those killed."

There have been further attacks on the Kyiv on Friday evening. Ukrainian media reports the city has been hit by ballistic missiles.

The Mayor of Kyiv, Vitali Klitschko, posted on Telegram at 19:32 local time (18:32 CEST) warning of the strikes, which read: "Air defense forces are working in the capital. Kyiv is under ballistic fire. Stay in shelters!"

Meanwhile, there have been repeated attacks on central Odesa, with strikes twice in quick succession. The second hit during the rescue operation. Local media reports 10 people have been injured in the attacks.

An office building on fire, in the aftermath of Russian strikes on central Odesa. Odesa Oblast Military Administration

In Russia, a drone hit a cooling tower of the Kursk Nuclear Power Plant early on Thursday. The International Atomic Energy Agency reported Friday that it was aware of the strike on the Kursk plant, adding that the power station remained operational at the time, but that there was no fire and operations had continued.

The IAEA reports that that a cooling tower of the Kursk Nuclear Power Plant in the Russian Federation was hit by a drone early on Thursday.

In the post, the Director General of the IAEA, Rafael Grossis warned against further attacks near nuclear infrastructure, and reiterated the need for "maximum military restraint to prevent the risk of a nuclear accident".

World.title: Irish Finance Minister says Hormuz closure, not Ukraine, causing energy crisis
World.content:
The closure of the Strait of Hormuz and Trump's war with Iran are causes behind the turmoil in the energy markets, not Ukraine's attacks on Russian diesel refineries. That is the message Irish Finance Minister and Deputy Prime Minister (Tánaiste), Simon Harris, shared with Euronews in an exclusive interview

 

Harris pushed back against recent remarks made by US President Donald Trump, who blamed Ukraine's strikes on Russian diesel refineries for creating a shortage. Oil prices are hovering around $108 per barrel.

"The reason there's a major energy crisis in the world right now is because the Strait of Hormuz is closed," Harris said on Euronews' interview programme 12 Minutes With. "I always make the point, and I would make it again today, that the greatest economic intervention we could see is de-escalation in the Middle East," he added.

He noted that this became evident during the summer, when there was a brief moment of respite in the conflict. "We saw a very rapid fall in the commodity markets and therefore a benefit at the pump."

Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil and gas facilities are squeezing Moscow’s oil output and having an impact globally, as Russia is one of the world’s largest oil producers, but experts agree the current energy crisis is primarily caused by the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz – the transit route for 20% of the world's oil and gas supplies.

The situation has escalated after Saudi Arabia shut its East-West pipeline, also known as Petroline, following drone attacks earlier this month from Iran-backed allied Houthis and Iraq.

"From an economic perspective, I'm very concerned [after] what we've seen on oil markets in recent days," Harris said. "I'm also very concerned about the fact that we aren't seeing de-escalation; we're actually seeing an escalation and indeed more fronts in terms of complications opening up regarding energy."

Windfall tax on the table

It is against the backdrop of mounting energy costs that finance ministers from eurozone countries gathered in Dublin on Friday, rushing to mitigate the rising prices and discussing measures to mitigate the impact on citizens.

One of the ideas circulating among EU ministers at the meeting is a windfall tax for firms profiting from energy price volatility, following calls from several member states to consider this measure.

"Some energy companies are making extraordinarily large profits on the back of this energy crisis," Harris said, noting that they are not doing so by "being innovative," but "because of the chaos that we're seeing in the energy markets as a result of the Strait of Hormuz being closed."

Without pre-empting possible outcomes of the talks, Harris said he would be having an initial conversation on such a tax with ministers in Dublin. Ireland currently holds the rotating EU Council presidency, allowing it to set the work programme and Council meeting agenda.

"It's likely that we will ask the European Commission to further examine this and that we would formally discuss it in Brussels at the next formal [Economic and Finance Council] meeting in October."

World 'cannot become numb to loss of life'

Harris stressed that, aside from the economic importance of ending the Middle East conflict, the world can not turn a blind eye to the human toll either.

"I think while I'm obviously speaking in the capacity of a finance minister, we should never become numb to the loss of life in war, whether that's the loss of life in Ukraine, whether it's the horrific genocide we've seen in Gaza, whether it's a situation in the Middle East more broadly," he said. "We need to see a de-escalation of conflict more broadly in the world."

On settler violence seen in the West Bank against Palestinians, the Tánaiste argued in favour of a tougher stance on Israeli settlements, which are illegal under international law.

"I'm massively pro-European, but I think when it comes to Gaza, it's been disappointing, to put it mildly, that more hasn't been done at that coordinated level," Harris said.

Several European countries, including Ireland and more recently the United Kingdom, have announced national bans on the import of all goods produced in illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank.

"Member states are listening to their public and are moving ahead, but we would always rather see action at an EU level because we think it's more impactful."

The EU’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, recently put forward an EU-wide ban on trade with illegal Israeli settlements as a "principled stance" for the bloc, comparing illegal settlements in the West Bank to Russia’s occupation of Crimea.

World.title: Three parties to attempt to form new cabinet following Romanian election
World.content:
Romania’s nominee for prime minister, Siegfried Muresan, has said he will attempt to form a government with a coalition involving three parties.

 

The country's president Nicusor Dan nominated Muresan after consultations with political parties. Muresan now has 10 days to present a cabinet to parliament and seek a vote of confidence.

Muresan, who is a member of the centre-right National Liberal Party (PNL) and the European Parliament, says he will try to form a government with the PNL, the Save Romania Union (USR) and the ethnic Hungarian UDMR party.

These three parties do not currently have a parliamentary majority, meaning Muresan will need support from other politicians for his proposed government to pass.

Romanian Prime Minister designate and European Parliament member Siegfried Muresan looks on during a press conference in Bucharest. 18 September 2026. AP Photo/Andreea Alexandru

He told reporters at a news conference that his coalition would pursue a “pro-European and forward-looking” programme.

Under Romania’s constitution, the president can dissolve parliament if it rejects two proposed governments within 60 days of the first rejection, which could trigger fresh elections.

Romanian President Nicusor Dan. 17 September 2026 AP Photo/Andreea Alexandru

The previous government, led by Ilie Bolojan, collapsed after a no-confidence vote following tensions over austerity measures and efforts to reduce Romania’s large budget deficit.

World.title: Sweeping raids leave Turkey’s LGBTQI+ community fearing what comes next
World.content:
Turkey has jailed dozens of people pending trial as a sweeping crackdown on LGBTQI+ groups widens, prompting international condemnation and protests outside Turkish embassies on Friday.

Advertising

By Thursday, courts in several provinces had jailed at least 82 people following raids on LGBTQI+ organisations, clubs, cafes and homes.

The cases include LGBTQI+ activists and members of rights groups as well as people accused of prostitution, drug offences and other crimes. Not everyone jailed is accused of gay rights advocacy.

The United Nations human rights office has called on Turkey to uphold human rights without discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity and to immediately release anyone arbitrarily detained.

Protests were held outside Turkish embassies in cities including Paris, Brussels, London, Oslo and Washington on Friday.

The crackdown began on Saturday, when police carried out coordinated raids targeting nine LGBTQI+ organisations. Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said legal action was being taken against 162 people, nine associations and 13 businesses in 15 provinces.

Turkey arrests dozens in ongoing crackdown on LGBTQI+ groups

Mass detentions

The raids prompted protests across Turkey, including outside Istanbul’s main courthouse on Tuesday. Police broke up the demonstration and detained more than 100 people, including journalists. They were later released.

“I am here because I want to say that LGBTQ+ friends are not alone in this country,” said Ayse, a protester who asked to be identified only by her first name.

“I want to support them and to stay in solidarity with them, which is not easy these days in Turkey, but they are not alone, and we are not alone, and we will be here until the end.”

Opposition DEM Party parliamentarian Ozgul Saki remained at the protest, protected from arrest by parliamentary immunity.

“This oppression against LGBTQ+ people is an attempt to compress society into a single type; to build an Islamist, Turkish, racist society,” Saki said. “Those who are here say, 'No! Society will live equally, freely and honourably with all its diversity,' and that's why they were all detained.”

The operations have been defended by Gurlek, from President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s conservative Justice and Development Party (AKP).

“No criminal organisation, abuse network or illegal activity which targets children, youths or families will be tolerated,” Gurlek posted on social media.

Among the organisations affected was Istanbul-based SPoD, which provides psychological support to LGBTQI+ people.

“As a community, we were expecting that such an operation would come one day. But we didn't imagine it as that violent, that much unlawful,” said a SPoD representative who asked to remain anonymous.

“They raided our office; I think four or five have been detained, and they are still in custody. What will happen to the LGBTQ+ community after this day? Like they can implement a kind of informal criminalisation upon our community, so my personal feeling is an immense feeling of uncertainty.”

Surge in anti-LGBTQ disinformation targets Pride in Europe

Obscenity allegations

Homosexuality has been legal since the foundation of the Turkish republic in 1923, but authorities are using an obscenity law as part of the crackdown.

“All of our board members are detained due to the allegations of obscenity,” said Yildiz Tar of Ankara-based KAOS GL, Turkey’s leading LGBTQI+ news portal.

“They look into our social media account, and our news articles are seen as obscene because, for example, there is one picture of two women kissing, and they see that it's obscene. So that is why they have been detained.”

The measures resemble actions taken against LGBTQI+ communities in Russia and Egypt, Tar said.

“It's very similar to Russia and Egypt, like the things they want to do is very similar to anti-gay propaganda laws, and there were huge operations, and people got detained,” Tar said.

“So it's very similar to both countries. And actually, like the Turkish government is very fond of Putin's way of dealing things.”

The crackdown has also drawn condemnation from the European Union and international human rights groups.

“It's an attempt to show LGBTQ+ people as immoral and against the family. But in fact, none of this does anything to protect the family at all,” said Emma Sinclair-Webb, who leads Human Rights Watch’s Turkey office.

“It's all about discrediting and stigmatizing people for their sexual orientation or gender identity.”

Turkey marks a decade since the coup that never was, but never really ended

Wider crackdown

The arrests form part of a broader crackdown on people regarded as opposing the government, Sinclair-Webb said.

“This operation should be set in the context of a very wide crackdown on anybody who is regarded as oppositional to the government, whether in terms of being politically or in terms of their lifestyle or their outlook… there is a general attempt by the government to impose as well as, you know, ideological conformity on people, lifestyle,” Sinclair-Webb said.

President Erdogan routinely refers to LGBTQI+ people as perverts and has stepped up his rhetoric ahead of much-rumoured early elections. Gurlek has called on prosecutors to increase investigations into the LGBTQI+ community, fuelling fears of further arrests.

The crackdown has also prompted condemnation across Turkish civil society, with trade unions, doctors’ associations and opposition parties voicing their opposition.

For Tar, that support offers some hope amid fears over what could follow for Turkey’s LGBTQI+ community.

“If this attack won't be stopped, it would mean a lot of maltreatment and torture; it can also cause hate crimes; it incites hatred inside the country too,” Tar said. “And it will mean that you cannot be openly queer; if they succeed in their operation, that is a really, really hellish scenario.”

World.title: A city at the crossroads of history: Unearthing Gaza's ancient heritage
World.content:
Before Gaza became synonymous with conflict, it was a place where merchants sold wine from local vineyards, pilgrims crossed continents, fishermen set out before dawn, and generations of families lived between sea and desert. RFI explores its deep history.

Advertising

Sitting on the coastal corridor linking Egypt, the Levant, the Arabian Peninsula and the Mediterranean, the port city has always been a strategic crossroads.

Like many places around the Mediterranean, Gaza's identity wasn't built by a single people or culture. It was shaped by generations of arrivals, departures and exchanges.

As the Mid-East Junction podcast returns from a six-year hiatus, we'll trace the city's history from the age of the Philistines until the creation of Israel in 1948.

In this first episode of season 3, a Gazan archaeologist, a historian, and a professor of contemporary Arab people shed light on Gaza’s little-known yet fascinating ancient history.

Mid-East Junction is produced by RFI's English-language service. This episode was mixed by Vincent Pora.

World.title: Deal with Denmark gives US 'permanent control' over Greenland security, Trump says
World.content:
The deal with Denmark, according to President Donald Trump, would give the US "permanent control" over Greenland's security. Denmark said the deal is "great for NATO and Europe."

President Donald Trump announced on Friday that the US had entered into an agreement with Denmark and Greenland that gives the US permanent control over Greenland's security.

"At my direction, ‌we worked with representatives of Denmark and Greenland to ‌guarantee ​that the United States will FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend ​the security of Greenland, and the United States of America," Trump said on Truth Social.

The US State Department said the deal bars US adversaries from establishing bases there.

"The agreement explicitly guarantees the United States the complete ability to do what it deems is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the American continent, including permanent access, basing, and overflight rights," a State Department official said. "This agreement guarantees that China and Russia cannot have a base in Greenland, they cannot send troops to Greenland, and the necessary mechanisms are in place to prevent investment in sensitive sectors."

In his post, Trump wrote that the US would "immediately" begin developing a larger military presence on the Danish territory.



Greenland's ice-covered minerals: No easy option To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What did Denmark and Greenland say?

According to a joint statement by the Danish and Greenlandic governments, the United States, Denmark, and Greenland have announced a breakthrough in their dispute over the Arctic island.

"I am pleased that there is a prospect of a good agreement for Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark and the United States," Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said in a statement.

She added that the deal was "great for NATO and Europe."

The agreement is expected to be signed next week on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.

Since returning to the White House last year, Trump has pressed Denmark to sell Greenland to the United States and even threatened to take it by force, insisting that the island is crucial for US security.

Denmark and Greenland have repeatedly stated that the island is not for sale and have condemned reports of the US gathering intelligence there.

World.title: Trump bars CNN, MS NOW and Politico from White House
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has accused CNN, MS NOW and Politico of spreading fake news. The outlets have vowed to take legal action against the ban.

US President Donald Trump announced on Friday that he is banning major US media outlets CNN, MS NOW and Politico from accessing the White House.

In a post on Truth Social, he accused them of spreading fake news.

Although Trump did not explain what exactly prompted the move, he said the media outlets were reporting "fiction and lies."

"Outlets shouldn't be able to constantly write or report fiction and lies when they're covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America."

He also indicated that other media outlets may also be ejected from the White House.

"Other fake news media outlets to follow," the US president posted, without mentioning any names. He also did not clarify what specific reporting he objected to.

A ban would prevent affected reporters from attending press conferences or events at the Oval Office.

Trumps say comedian Jimmy Kimmel should be fired To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

How did the media react?

CNN, the world's first 24-hour all-news television network, called Trump's media ban an "illegal assault" on the freedom of the press.

Politico, which is owned by the German media conglomerate Axel Springer, headquartered in Berlin and New York, vowed to "vigorously defend" rights after Trump's ban threat.

MS NOW (formerly MSNBC), a liberal cable news channel, has not yet responded to the ban.

Meanwhile, Bruce Brown, president of the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, said that banning the media outlets would be "flatly unconstitutional."

"The First Amendment is clear that once the White House invites in some journalists, it can't ban others because it doesn't like their reporting," Brown said.

"This is textbook viewpoint discrimination and will be quickly struck down by the courts if challenged," he added.

Trump's uneasy relationship with the media

Donald Trump has a long history of disputes with members of the press corps. During his second term, he became increasingly hostile toward the media.

The US president repeatedly urged broadcasters to cancel comedy or news programs that he disliked or that joked about or criticized him or his administration.

He even called on the Federal Communications Commission to revoke the licenses of stations he disliked.

Trump's administration imposed stricter controls on reporters during his second term. For example, they control which journalists can cover events as part of the "pool" admitted to confined spaces, such as the Oval Office and Air Force One.

Last year, the White House barred the Associated Press from some events because the news agency continued to refer to the "Gulf of Mexico" instead of the "Gulf of America," as Trump had ordered.

In another case, last year Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced new rules for reporters covering the Pentagon. The rules required reporters to sign a document acknowledging restrictions on gathering unauthorized information.

Most major news outlets refused to sign the document and left the Pentagon's press room.

World.title: Iran's 'new Hezbollah:' How powerful are the Houthis now?
World.content:
After Houthi victories in Yemen, the group's importance in the US-Iran war has grown. Previously Lebanon's Hezbollah was considered most significant in Iran's "axis of resistance." Now the Houthis are rising to the top.

After recent events in Yemen, a small crowd marched down an Iraqi street holding signs that were almost identical to those seen not too long ago further south.

The signs said, "death to America" and insulted Saudi Arabia and Israel, with slogans very similar to those used by the Houthi rebel group in Yemen. The men in the Iraqi video are members of one of Iraq's Shiite Muslim paramilitary groups.

Both the Iraqi paramilitaries and the Houthi group in Yemen are part of what is known as the "axis of resistance" in the Middle East, groups supported by Iran that often act at Iran's behest. Other members are Hezbollah in Lebanon and Hamas in Gaza.

After the US and Israel began attacking Iran in late February 2026, "axis of resistance" members responded by targeting sites associated with the US or Israel. But up until recently, the Houthi group had remained more or less on the sidelines.

However their latest military campaign, which has seen Houthi fighters take further control of the Yemeni coast and several islands in the Red Sea, "sets up conditions to establish… an axis of resistance-controlled body of water as part of [an] effort to assert control over regional oil exports," US-based research organization the Institute for the Study of War explained last week.

Iran and the US are already fighting for control over the Strait of Hormuz, another important waterway for oil exports and trade.

In Iran, hardline regime-supporting newspapers published laudatory articles about the Houthis' territorial gains.

The gains "greatly increased the weight of Sanaa [the Yemeni capital, under Houthi control] as a branch of resistance in the ongoing regional war," one of Iran's most conservative newspapers, Kayhan, wrote.

Supporters of the Iranian government have been holding nightly gatherings in major cities across the country since the US-Iran war began and this week, at the 200th such event, crowds chanted "you are my soul, O Yemen!"

The 'new Hezbollah?'

This was the kind of praise previously lavished on another "axis of resistance" group, Hezbollah. But Hezbollah's armed faction, degraded by recent Israeli attacks and the loss of their base in Syria, looks less intimidating these days.

And the Houthis now appear to be doing things that Hezbollah couldn't — for example, bringing down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet this week using a missile the group said it modified itself. Hezbollah has managed to shoot down large Israeli drones and has targeted fighter jets but never hit any.

Could the Houthis be taking Hezbollah's place as the potentially most important and possibly even more dangerous force in the "axis of resistance?"

The Houthis haven't had to fight Israel — they are too far away geographically.

"But I think they [the Houthis] have become more valuable than Hezbollah could ever be," says Farea al-Muslimi, a research fellow focused on Yemen at UK think tank Chatham House. "Of course, Hezbollah had decades of experience and was the one who built the Houthis' capacity over years. But the Houthis have now exceeded them."

The Houthis are "increasingly performing a similar strategic function for Iran [as Hezbollah] and in some respects a more useful one," confirms Andreas Krieg, a senior lecturer at the School of Security Studies at King's College London.

"Hezbollah gave Tehran deterrence against Israel from Lebanon. The Houthis give Iran leverage over Saudi Arabia, Israel and global shipping," he told DW. "So I think their strategic importance to Tehran has risen sharply as Hezbollah has come under much greater pressure."

Al-Muslimi notes that Houthi leaders, including current chief Abdul Malik al-Houthi, were devoted fans of Hezbollah leader Nassan Hasrallah, killed by Israel in 2024 and seen as a hero because of his organization's part in forcing Israel to withdraw from Lebanon in 2000.

"You can see how he even tries to imitate Nasrallah in his speeches," al-Muslimi, who co-founded the Sanaa Center for Strategic Studies, told DW. "And now Abdul Malik al-Houthi has more leverage than Nasrallah ever had."

Nasrallah was once seen as "the fixer" for the "axis of resistance," he notes, a leader who acted as a conduit between the different factions, giving orders to Iran-supported fighters in Lebanon, Yemen and Syria.

Al-Houthi is likely moving into that role now, al-Muslimi believes, pointing to the fact that one recent attack on Saudi pipelines actually came from Iraqi axis members.

Iranian proxy or ally?

Unlike with Hezbollah though, there's still disagreement over exactly how much control Iran has over them.

A review of press by the Iraq-based outlet Amwaj showed that while Iranian media celebrated Houthi gains as a victory for Iran's "axis of resistance," Houthi-run channels were more focused on their own fight against Saudi Arabia, which has set up a blockade on Houthi-controlled territories.

Krieg believes the biggest difference between the Houthis and Hezbollah is autonomy.

"The Houthis… have their own leadership, ideology, domestic constituency and territorial project," he pointed out. "Tehran can enable them, arm them and benefit from their actions, but it cannot necessarily switch them on and off at will."

The Houthis have not backed away from their hardline positions in the US-Israel-Iran war, which, one expert says, 'gives them a psychological advantage and makes them the heroes of the axis of resistance' Image: Khaled Abdullah/REUTERS

Other observers note that in the past, the Houthis moved ahead with certain military plans despite objections from Iran. Tehran has also denied having anything to do with this latest campaign.

But al-Muslimi isn't so sure. He says that over the past two years, the Houthis have come a lot closer to Iran. There are regular reports of Iran sending sophisticated weaponry to the Houthis. In July, sources inside Iran told Reuters news agency that Iranian leadership had discussed with the Houthis having them close off the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

"Even as Houthi leaders frame their actions in local terms, their alignment with Tehran appears to have tightened," Allison Minor, previously the US deputy special envoy for Yemen, said in Foreign Affairs magazine last week.

Can the Houthis be beaten?

The one thing everyone does agree on is that the Houthis will be hard to rein in. Past military campaigns by Saudi Arabia, the US and other countries have failed. Sanctions and economic pressure tend not to impact either because the Houthis don't operate within the international financial system.

The Houthis take a "zero sum approach," al-Muslimi explains. They collect taxes but don't pay salaries or provide public services; everything goes towards fighting. The group's founding father argued that contemporary Muslim societies were too "soft," and that poverty and hardship are a divine test.

The United Nations say that fighting in Yemen has displaced at least 125,000 people since the start of September 2026 Image: REUTERS

That's very different from Hezbollah: The Lebanese group also has a political branch at home, and offers social welfare services. It must also carefully balance relationships with other demographic groups in Lebanon.

The Houthis have none of those restraints.

"They don't care if the Israelis bomb the airport or the US bombs a hospital," al-Muslimi says. "It actually serves them very well because their ideology is all about martyrdom and sacrifice."

Which, he suggests, makes them potentially more dangerous than Hezbollah, especially for Yemeni civilians.

"They are a major international threat," he agrees, "but they're the biggest threat ever to the idea of a republic and citizenship in Yemen's history."

Edited by: Carla Bleiker

World.title: Ryanair boss apologizes for calling other airlines 'rapists'
World.content:
The airline CEO had used the term to describe other airlines with high fares. His comments were criticized by officials both in Ireland and the UK.

Ryanair CEO Michael O'Leary "sincerely and unreservedly" apologized on Friday for recent remarks in which he described other airlines as "rapists" because of their high fares.

O'Leary said 'careless' remarks caused 'considerable upset and offense'

"I have come to realize, however, that the word I used too carelessly has caused considerable upset and offense to a wide number of people, especially victims and survivors," O'Leary said in a video posted online.

It's a U-turn from earlier, when O'Leary refused to apologize for the comments. Dublin Rape Crisis Centre chief executive Rachel Morrogh said O'Leary trivialized rape with the remarks.

"Since I certainly did not trivialize the heinous crime of rape, I will certainly not be issuing any apology," O'Leary said last week.

O'Leary had originally made the remarks to journalists at Ryanair's company headquarters in Ireland.

Ryanair is known for its cheap, no-frills flights around Europe [FILE: September 14, 2019] Image: Nicolas Economou/NurPhoto/picture alliance

"You might find some people will choose not to fly with Ryanair — but you know they'll be overrun with the people abandoning Aer Lingus, Lufthansa, BA, and others desperate to get to Ryanair's low fares because they can't afford to fly with high-fare rapists around Europe," O'Leary said.

O'Leary's remarks met with backlash in Ireland, UK

O'Leary is one of Ireland's richest and most prominent businesspeople. His "rapist" remarks were met with criticism from leaders both in Ireland and the UK.

Ireland's Taoiseach Michael Martin said he was "disappointed" by O'Leary's comments and added the Ryanair chief "should just stand back and reflect and listen to the voice of women" regarding the issue.

Martin told RTE Radio One that rape is "an awful, awful violation of a person, which leaves a terrible trauma." However, the Irish leader of the centrist to center-right Fianna Fail party did not call on O'Leary to explicitly apologize.

Ireland's deputy prime minister, or Tanaiste, Simon Harris said O'Leary's comments were an "inappropriate use of language." However, Harris of the center-right Fine Gael party also did not explicitly call on O'Leary to apologize.

Laura Harmon, a senator belonging to Ireland's center-left opposition Labour Party, said O'Leary must apologize for the comments. "The casual use of the word 'rapist' to describe prices of his competitors is deeply shocking and could be traumatizing for any survivor of sexual abuse," Harmon said .

Fact check: Female politicians hurt by sexualized deepfakes To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The UK's Transport Minister Heidi Alexander of the British Labour Party, in comments to LBC radio, said "Mr. O'Leary is often quick to share his considered thoughts with me and with the wider world."

"I would say that women who have been raped and who have been subjected to such appalling violence, I'm not sure they're going to be rushing to book tickets with him, let's be honest," Alexander said.

O'Leary had earlier made controversial remarks regarding obese and Muslim passengers. He had also floated a fee for using a toilet mid-flight and expressed climate denial.

World.title: Strait of Hormuz attacks spill oil into Persian Gulf
World.content:
As war disrupts one of the world's busiest shipping lanes, satellite images reveal that oil is spreading toward protected coral reefs and mangrove forests.

A dark, muddied patch of blue, incongruent with the rest of the ocean; a winding thread of silvery white; a reflective metallic sheen — these are some of the telltale signs on a satellite image that oil may be leaking into the water.

Experts have identified these and many other visual signatures in the Strait of Hormuz, leading them to conclude that there's an environmental crisis playing out amid the US-Iran war, as tankers are struck by missiles, set on fire or sunk.

One recent example: In June, a Russian tanker carrying about 800,000 barrels of oil stranded off the coast of Oman, causing a major spill.

Earlier in the war, there were as many as 85 large oil-laden tankers stuck in the Strait — that number has since dropped to 13, according to Greenpeace. Each stranded tanker, plus every other vessel trying to move through the waterway, poses a distinct risk for attack and thus a spill. Since the start of the war, the environmental organization has used satellite imagery to track more than 100 spills.

There are likely several other spills that we don't know of, amid widespread GPS spoofing in the region that causes ships to broadcast false positions. Greenpeace released a report this week calling the situation an "ecological catastrophe" and pinpointing a number of oil slicks that are extending into protected and fragile ecosystems.

"People should be concerned," Nina Noelle, a Greenpeace expert on environmental disaster relief, told DW. The war has taken "a very, very heavy toll on the environment," she said, with the damage now reaching new scales.

Where is the oil spreading?

Greenpeace identified five major oil slicks earlier this week with a total visible area of 240 square kilometers (about 90 square miles) in the Strait of Hormuz. That's about four times the size of Manhattan.

These patches of oil floating on the ocean's surface are getting smaller — now about 80 square kilometers — according to more up-to-date satellite images, as weather conditions have likely made the slicks disperse. But that does not mean the ecological impact is any less severe, Noelle said. "Oil can also sink into the sediment and impact the ecosystems for years and years."

What's concerning is where the slicks were identified. One was found near Musandam National Park, a protected area in Oman that's home to coral reefs, sea life and important breeding grounds for sea birds. Another is close to Iran's Minab River Delta and its protected mudflats and mangrove forests. This kind of damage can take decades for ecosystems to recover from.

Tracking an unclear picture

It's hard to say exactly how far the oil has reached and how severe the damage is.

"What we have put out is the conservative estimate," Noelle said. "It might be worse. It's definitely not better."

Greenpeace and other environmental organizations are relying on satellite images provided by the Copernicus Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 satellites. They're part of the European Union's Earth observation program and are publicly available.

There are also private satellite providers such as Planet Labs that tend to have higher-resolution images. But they've limited access to satellite imagery during the war to prevent their data from being used for military targeting. And there are limits to on-the-ground reports too.

"We don't have a lot of information coming from the country itself, both in Iran as well as the Gulf states," Wim Zwijnenburg, an environmental researcher who uses open-source methods at the Dutch peace organization Pax, told DW. "There is quite restrictive policies of people posting imagery from what's happening on the shore."

The toll on wildlife and people

Oil pooling into the Gulf poses a number of threats — both to biodiversity and to humans.

Oil can be deadly for seabirds. It coats their feathers, reducing their natural waterproofing and buoyancy, making it harder to stay afloat, fly, and hunt for food. Even small amounts of oil can damage eggs too, causing them not to hatch or to be born with deformities.

Mangrove habitats, which provide safe harbor for coastal species, are also hit hard.

"Mangroves have aerial roots, and the oil is covering these roots like a film and actually hindering the mangroves in exchanging gases," Noelle said. "They're kind of suffocated by the oil. Most of the time, it leads to the trees dying."

The risks extend to people, as well. Coastal communities rely on fish that die off after being exposed to oil. And oil spills contaminate water used for Gulf states' drinking supply. Desalination — or converting seawater into drinkable water — is where 90% of drinking water in Kuwait comes from, along with about 86% in Oman and 70% in Saudi Arabia.

Vessels anchor near the Strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman Image: REUTERS

Cleanup is no easy fix.

"It's unlikely that it will be addressed quickly, because of the war," Zwijnenburg said. "War in general makes it very difficult to respond fast to these kind of emergencies. There are a range of limitations because of the military movement, because of mines — so it's very difficult to get vessels and cleanup operations to start."

Environmental groups have pointed to the war in Iran — and the rising scale of oil spills it has caused — as further evidence that the world needs to move away from its dependence on fossil fuels.

"The most sustainable long-term damage prevention for things like that would be to reduce and ultimately end our dependency on oil and gas," Noelle said. "Because, as long as our energy systems and transport routes are centered around fossil fuels, there will be a continued environmental risk."

Edited by: Sarah Steffen

World.title: Ebola: DR Congo outbreak not slowing, MSF warns
World.content:
Doctors Without Borders has warned against premature optimism amid the DRC's largest-ever Ebola outbreak. "The outbreak is not shrinking, it is moving," an MSF official said, entering new and more underprepared regions.

Medical charity Doctors Without Borders (MSF) said on Friday that "the race to contain the Ebola disease outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is far from over."

MSF issued the comments after DRC's government and the World Health Organization (WHO) had both spoken of signs of slowing transmission in some places earlier this week, prompting some relatively upbeat headlines and coverage.

The outbreak, which was first declared in mid-May but likely started spreading several months earlier, is the largest in DRC's national history and the fastest-spreading on record anywhere.

Did Ebola start spreading before officials even knew? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What did MSF say about the outbreak and its spread?

MSF — which has around 1,700 staff in the DRC, most of them Congolese — warned that while the observed spread was slowing in the initial epicenter of Ituri province, the number of new cases being recorded had not fallen on a national level.

"Assuming the outbreak is under control because some Ebola treatment centers are admitting fewer patients would be a mistake," MSF's emergency coordinator in DRC Anthony Kergosien said.

"The outbreak is not shrinking, it is moving: South Ubangi has become the seventh affected province, while North Kivu now accounts for nearly half of all newly confirmed cases, with test positivity rising sharply in recent days," Kergosien said.

He added that undetected chains of transmission had already taken hold in the worst-hit areas, and said "the spread of the outbreak into new areas with even weaker preparedness and response capacities poses a serious risk."

Incidental factors like the school year restarting this month provide new potential transmission risks Image: Dieudonne Dirole/AP Photo/picture alliance

Which factors helped DRC's worst Ebola outbreak spread so fast?

The deadly virus has killed more than 3,500 people from more than 7,200 confirmed cases since the outbreak was declared in May, according to WHO figures.

Based on the recorded data, the quality of which is gradually improving with the passage of time, the 2026 outbreak is the fastest-spreading in history.

It's also the largest in the DRC's history, second in overall size only to the West African outbreak of 2013-2016. The West African outbreak needed around two and a half years to reach a caseload of more than 28,000, not four months to pass 7,000.

Congo's Ebola crisis: Fear, mistrust and a growing outbreak To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Many of the cases have been concentrated in hard-to-reach areas in DRC's north and east long plagued by instability, poor health infrastructure and a series of armed groups.

Medical staff strikes have also contributed to problems fighting the spread, as have dearly-held funeral and burial traditions that pose the risk of post-mortem transmission as people bid their loved ones farewell.

The outbreak also involves a rare Ebolavirus strain, Bundibugyo, meaning that existing treatments and vaccines — several of which are prohibitively expensive by the standards of the region anyway — were untested and of uncertain value against it.

Edited by: Zac Crellin
