World.title: How an abandoned water park became a lightning rod for the Canberra community
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

If you grew up in Canberra, you might have fond memories of the capital's only outdoor water park, Big Splash.

It had been a public swimming pool in Macquarie in Canberra's north before it was bought by a family in the 90s and transformed into an attraction of slides.

That family sold up, and for the past couple of years the water park has been an increasingly dilapidated husk of its former self.

The state of the park, and several broken promises over its unrealised reopening, have caused frustration.

And anyone still hoping the water park will feature in their summer plans is likely to be left high and dry.

Big Splash water park's pool is disused and green. (ABC News)

Why isn't the government taking over?

The community has been frustrated by the lack of ACT government enforcement in relation to the site.

The government has been asked several times why it does not purchase, restore and publicly run the park.

It has never ruled that out, but said its strong preference was for the park to remain privately operated.

ACT government regulator Access Canberra has the capacity to issue a controlled activity order, which carries a penalty of up to $48,600, or to terminate the lease of the land completely.

So far, the government has refused to be drawn on exactly what it would take to enact those processes.

Who owns Big Splash water park?

The original Big Splash operators ran the park for decades before the lease was sold during the pandemic for a reported $7.5 million.

Like much of the capital, Big Splash is on a 99-year crown lease, which was last renewed 20 years ago.

The lease conditions for the 13,000-square-metre parcel of land stipulate that it must house either an aquatic facility, an indoor sports facility, or an unlicensed family restaurant.

The lessee, Translink Management Group, signed the contract in 2021, with the clauses unchanged.

Why hasn't Big Splash reopened?

After closing in 2024, the site was slated to reopen in November 2025, but the lessee did not deliver and blamed rising repair costs.

That same month, the ACT government confirmed the lessee had ambitions for the site to be rezoned for residential use, but that desire was shot down by the government, which said it had no plans for the area to be used for anything but its recreational purpose.

In April this year, Access Canberra decided against following through on a threat to terminate the lease, saying it was satisfied the owners had made moves to reopen the facility's 50-metre pool before next summer.

Have there been any offers to buy the park?

Big Splash water park is listed as for sale. (ABC News: Monte Bovill)

In June this year, the water park was put up for sale.

At the time, work to fix the main pool and ticketing facilities was set to continue, but recent images of the property tell a different story.

The ABC has been told no acceptable offer was received during the expressions of interest process and the property remains available for purchase.

Financiers have taken over decision-making

The 50-metre pool remains covered in vandalism. (ABC News: Monte Bovill)

Labor MLA for Ginninderra Tara Cheyne recently confirmed the person behind Translink Management Group was no longer calling the shots.

"I've met with these people now who have taken over and they are different to the person who effectively let Big Splash go into disrepair," Ms Cheyne said.

"They are the people who lent the money to him ... basically a small financing business running out of Sydney."

She described the group as "genuine".

Is a food van next for the site?

On Wednesday, the ACT government said it feared its latest deadline for the pool to reopen would not be met.

And ACT Planning Minister Chris Steel announced a "comprehensive options analysis", which would ask for public feedback.

But that solution was criticised by the ACT Greens, who insisted it was already clear the community wanted a water park.

Just a day later, on Thursday, the owners of Big Splash announced they would comply with their lease requirements by operating an unlicensed family restaurant at the site by November.

Big Splash Waterpark is not far from Belconnen's central shops. (Supplied: Colliers)

Head of Access Canberra Josh Rynehart confirmed a temporary way to do that could be to put a food van on the site.

What's next?

There are two possible outcomes as November approaches:

The first is that a food outlet pops up and authorities are temporarily satisfied. Though, many in the community will likely be unhappy, including the Save Big Splash group.

The second is that the deadline comes and goes with inaction, leading to renewed questions over enforcement.

There is a third, wildcard option, which could see the property sold. But that would not guarantee the buyer would be interested in restoring the water park.

The ABC has been told a builder has been engaged, with a deposit paid, in a bid to house a restaurant on the site by November.

World.title: New exhibition turning antiques into futuristic Lego world
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

It's the year 2130, humans have left Earth and Lego minifigures have moved into the belongings we've left behind.

At least that's how friends Jackson Harvey and Alex Towler imagined the future, while they spent years creating a whimsical, wonder-filled world for their exhibition RELICS: A New World Rises.

"The characters of Relics live in a world that's set in the not-too-distant future … where humans have left the planet for reasons that are left vague. But they have built new communities inside all the old objects and junk that we've left behind," Harvey explains.

A bustling Lego society housed inside a Volkswagen beetle boot. (ABC News: Simon Beardsell)

Across more than 15 large-scale installations at the Canberra Museum and Gallery, tiny communities have moved into the wreckage humanity left behind.

A fridge has become a cryogenic wellness resort, a grandfather clock has been reverse-engineered by a band of inventors into a time machine, a claw machine has become a futuristic space port.

"Lego has become [the] majority of our lives. It's lots of fun though — it changes the way we've looked at the world," Towler says.

Lego people mingle at a resort, in a world abandoned by humans. (ABC News: Simon Beardsell)

"We just like looking at cool stuff and figuring out what little plastic people will do with them," he says.

Vintage classics house intricate worlds

The pair created this new civilisation from old stuff.

"This exhibition was built on a majority of salvaged parts. It's mostly second-hand Lego," Towler says.

The pair blended relics with Lego to invoke nostalgia for viewers. (ABC News: Simon Beardsell)

Some of the objects were harder to find than others, the pair say. And all the detail that surrounds the larger objects help to build the story and the world.

"We've got a lot of really unique objects in the exhibition — some of them are really hard to find," Harvey says.

" My personal favourite is the 76-year-old jukebox, the antique Wurlitzer from the 40s. "

Immersive art

Harvey and Towler say there are many stories woven into the millions of small pieces and 2,500 minifigures making up the exhibition.

Harvey and Towler sourced an old jukebox for one installation. (ABC News: Simon Beardsell)

"Lego is only a small part of this exhibition," Towler says.

"There's a lot to see. There's the stories, there's the nostalgia of the objects, there's the scavenger hunt to help explore the detail. There's something for everybody in this exhibition."

They say the longer you look at it, the more you'll uncover.

"There's lots of little Easter eggs and hidden stories that you can only find if you look around a corner and down a hallway or behind a shelf," Harvey says.

They've built it. Now you can come

"This exhibition is at its core about not following instructions, doing something differently," Towler says.

Harvey and Towler want to encourage people to think outside 'normal' ways of doing things. (ABC News: Lish Fejer)

"Lego pieces aren't meant to fit in the front of a VW Beetle, but if you have a V-Dub and you have Lego and you squish them together, you can figure it out. That's the message."

The exhibition is designed to appeal equally to serious enthusiasts, families and anyone who's never clicked a little plastic brick in their life.

RELICS: A New World Rises is a ticketed exhibition on at the Canberra Museum and Gallery until January 31, 2027.

World.title: How knitting and crochet can be 'deceptively good' for the brain
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Will Seager taught himself to knit nine years ago. Now, it's something he does every day.

"I'm naturally a little bit of an anxious person so for me it's really nice to let go of any other worries or things that I need to be thinking about and focus entirely on my knitting," Mr Seager said.

Will Seager says knitting is both relaxing and challenging. (ABC News: Loretta Lohberger)

"I do it also because it's very intellectually stimulating for me … I like to choose patterns which are technically quite demanding and quite difficult."

Neuroscientist Sarah McKay said crafts like knitting and crochet were "deceptively good for the brain".

"It's like this ideal mix of repetition plus cognitive challenge," Dr McKay said.

Will Seager says he likes to continually challenge himself by seeking out more complex patterns. (ABC News: Loretta Lohberger)

"You have to remember where you're up to, you have to problem solve, you have to make decisions, you're constantly challenging yourself if you're doing more and more complicated patterns.

"But at the same time, it's challenging but it's low stakes … which I think might be one of the best kinds [of cognitive challenge] we can have," she said.

Dr McKay said craft activities could help with attention.

"What they're doing is they're almost training us to pay attention to something for quite a long time," she said.

Will Seager enjoys knitting socks. (ABC News: Loretta Lohberger)

Researchers have also studied how useful craft activities could be for mood regulation and stress reduction.

"We're mastering a skill, we're getting better at that and we're kind of just doing the task for the sake of doing the task … it's quite a simple form of mastery and there's something really soothing and good for our mood about that," Dr McKay said.

Mr Seager is constantly looking for new ways to challenge himself as a knitter.

"I like to choose patterns that enable me to learn new skills … Most recently I've got into a type of [ribbed] knitting called brioche knitting," he said.

" It took me a long time to get the hang of it … [but] after a little while you settle into the rhythm and your fingers and hands do the work without you having to think too much about it. "

Brioche knitting is a technique Will Seager has recently become interested in. (ABC News: Loretta Lohberger)

Mr Seager likes to knit alone so he can focus.

But, for others, craft is a way to connect with people.

Looking after each other through craft

Once a week in Hobart's northern suburbs, the Glenorchy Library Knitting Group meets. Its members mostly knit and crochet items to donate to local charities.

"Some of the ladies [who come], this is their only outing apart from the supermarket," Carolee Marino, who started the group in 2011, said.

"It's all about looking after each other … we all help each other."

Carolee Marino started the Glenorchy Library Knitting Group in 2011. (ABC News: Loretta Lohberger)

One of the group's newest members is Gill Shilling.

"It's awesome, I've met all these amazing ladies with interesting stories," Ms Shilling said.

"But the fact that we're actually making things to give to people in the community who are in need, that's really important to me."

Gill Shilling says she enjoys the social aspect of the group, as well as contributing to charity. (ABC News: Loretta Lohberger)

Another relatively new group member, Irina Bridges, learnt to knit after moving to Australia from Russia seven years ago.

She said she was looking to share her love of knitting with others.

"I dreamt to knit for my whole life, but I couldn't because when I was a kid in Soviet Union all stores were empty without yarn so I couldn't," Ms Bridges said.

"I enjoy our group and showing off what I [have] knitted."

Irina Bridges enjoys sharing her love of knitting with others. (ABC News: Loretta Lohberger)

Miriam Ritchie has been part of the group for about two years.

"This is it, this is my social, and I get pretty lonely so I can't wait to get here," she said.

Miriam Ritchie (right) looks forward to catching up with the other members of the Glenorchy Library Knitting Group. (ABC News: Loretta Lohberger)

Norma Kelaart joined the group after moving to Tasmania in 2024.

"I needed some company of other women to chat with and relax with and have a joke and a laugh," she said.

One part of a broader brain health plan

Dr McKay said there was not enough evidence to prove that activities like knitting and crochet helped prevent dementia — many of the studies were observational and self-reported, not randomised clinical trials that look specifically at dementia risk.

The magical healing power of crochet The steady click of needles and hooks on couches around Australia tells us that knitters have been onto the very real therapeutic benefits of crochet for a long time.

But she said the many clear benefits meant craft activities could be an important part of a broader lifestyle brain health program.

"Alongside exercise and diet and sleep and stress reduction … [and] taking care of your cardiovascular health, your metabolic health — all of the things that we know are good for our mental health in the short term and our brain health long term — this can sit really nicely and neatly in there," she said.

"We know that social connections are a really important part of long-term brain health, we know that having purpose and meaning in life are a really important part of brain health, so it can fulfil those requirements in a really lovely, non-digital way."

World.title: Huge flu spike puts pressure on struggling regional health service
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

A stretched regional health service facing significant patient demand amid a late flu season has advised doctors to consider discharging patients earlier and without physical consultant review.

An email to doctors sent from Albury Wodonga Health's chief medical officer Simon Craig on Thursday, which was verified by the ABC, warned that the service was facing "overwhelming" demands that were expected to continue for days.

Doctors have been asked to consider earlier discharge of patients where safe, early plans and rounds, and empowering registrars to discharge without physical consultant review where safe.

Albury Wodonga Health faces inpatient bed pressure. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

The doctors were also asked to consider Hospital In The Home and virtual care options.

"As we progress, we will be looking as an organisation into how we optimise flow and use of beds," Dr Craig stated in the email.

" Our resources are limited and we need to all collaborate in this. "

Demand on the cross-border health service has been at the forefront of community concern for years, while a proposed $558 million redevelopment of Albury's hospital has been criticised over whether it will meet the region's future needs.

Construction is underway at Albury hospital. (ABC News: Annie Brown)

Advocacy group Better Border Health (BBH) reported there was a 61-bed deficit at the health service on Thursday.

"This is not simply about getting through a difficult few days," BBH spokesperson Stan Stavros said.

"With daily bed shortages frequently reported at 40 to 70, we are starting each day behind.

"It should be the other way around; a hospital should have spare capacity to respond to surges in demand, not a persistent deficit."

A public sign by Better Border Health outlining daily hospital bed numbers. (Facebook: Better Border Health)

Late flu season surge

The health service warned residents on September 8 via social media that it was experiencing an increase in demand for inpatient beds due to a surge in respiratory illness, and a spokesperson said that it remained ongoing.

"This sustained demand is affecting patient flow across our hospitals and may mean longer waits for some patients requiring admission," the spokesperson said.

"Despite this, patients with critical or life-threatening conditions continue to be seen immediately and receive the urgent care they need.

"Our clinical and support teams are working hard to manage this demand, adapt our processes safely, and maintain capacity across our sites.

"Any operational adjustments we make during periods of high demand are made with patient safety as the first priority, and in line with standard clinical governance and protocols."

The flu vaccine for 2026 is still available. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

The surge in respiratory illness putting strain on Albury Wodonga Health has been reflected across Victoria as the Department of Health and Human Services reported a 400 per cent increase in flu cases since the end of July.

"We do expect to get seasonal spikes of flu each year and what is different this year is it is coming later in the season," Victoria's chief health officer, Caroline McElnay, said.

She said it was unclear what had triggered the virus to spike post-winter, but similar scenarios were playing out across New South Wales and New Zealand.

"It's not too late to get vaccinated if people haven't had that chance to get vaccinated," she said.

World.title: Fishy freight lands in Tasmania ahead of Bass Strait trial
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Placed in oxygenated bags then packed into insulated boxes, 15,000 juvenile kingfish have made the 3,000-kilometre journey from Fremantle to Hobart.

The arrival of the tiny fish, known as fingerlings, marks the next stage of aquaculture trial underway in Bass Strait, 12 kilometres off the coast of Burnie.

The packages travelled in two specialist air-freight shipments, packed in oxygenated bags sealed inside insulated polyboxes. (Blue Economy Cooperative Research Centre)

Blue Economy CRC says the cargo arrived safely. (Blue Economy Cooperative Research Centre)

Researcher and kingfish impact lead for the company running the trial, Blue Economy CRC (Cooperative Research Centre), Maxi Canepa, said the journey was "an interesting exercise".

"We didn't have mortalities. They are fantastic. They looked very healthy on arrival," he said.

"These fish grow really fast. That's why it's a very nice species for aquaculture."

The kingfish will grow to be around four kilograms when mature. (Blue Economy Cooperative Research Centre)

The fingerlings will grow on land at the Institute of Marine and Antarctic Studies (IMAS) in Taroona for three months until they weigh between 100 and 150 grams.

The not-so-tiny fish will then be transported to the trial site, where they will be acclimatised to the water and released into a sea pen where they are expected to grow to 4 kilograms before being harvested.

The kingfish will be held in tanks at the University of Tasmania's IMAS aquaculture research facility at Taroona for about three months. (Blue Economy Cooperative Research Centre)

Dr Canepa said it would be the first time kingfish are farmed offshore in Australia.

"It's a site that is going to offer some challenges but also opportunities," he said.

Blue Economy CRC says the fish pen infrastructure "stood up to the high-energy conditions of Bass Strait". (Blue Economy Cooperative Research Centre)

How will fish fare in 'wild' Bass Strait?

The three-year research trial, dubbed the Blue Economy Zone (BEZ), is the country's first aquaculture trial in Commonwealth waters, led by independent not-for-profit Blue Economy CRC.

The company is part of the federal government's CRC program, which supports industry-led collaborations between industry, researchers and the community.

The project aims to trial the viability of multi-species offshore aquaculture in Commonwealth waters.

In 2028 the site will be decommissioned; and any commercial operation will then be a question for aquaculture companies and will require government approvals.

Blue Economy CRC says the kingfish "are gradually acclimatised to the waters before being released into the research sea pen" in Bass Strait. (Supplied: Blue Economy CRC)

Three months after pens were established in 2025, 15,000 Atlantic salmon were introduced. Last week, the fish were harvested.

Blue Economy CRC chief executive Angela Williamson says the salmon "performed really well" in the notoriously rough waters of Bass Strait.

"They grew above the predicted modelled weight. Unlike within the state waters, they did not need to be bathed. We did experience regular mortalities across that time period," she said.

"All our information was put on our website on a dashboard. We know transparency is a really important component of this trial and (the public) understanding and trusting the process," she said.

Ms Williamson said infrastructure had also held up against the "wild and windy" conditions.

"We've had to really make sure that our mooring grid, our nets and our floating equipment meet those standards, not just of government, but also of keeping the fish safe, keeping people who are operating safe, and ensuring that marine debris is eliminated as much as possible."

According to the project's dashboard, the BEZ has recorded 13 pieces of marine debris and eight "wildlife interactions".

The kingfish will be transferred into large tanks aboard a vessel for the 12.5-kilometre journey into Bass Strait. (Blue Economy Cooperative Research Centre)

Opposition to trial in north-west

A public meeting hosted by Blue Economy CRC was held when the project at the start of the trial last year, with attendees opposed to the trial expressing concerns about environmental impacts.

Opponents attended a public forum on the fish farming trial in May, 2025. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

Tasmanian independent Braddon MP Craig Garland is staunchly opposed to the trial.

"We never wanted any salmon or any finfish aquaculture in our waterways," he said.

"One in five people are coming here for the tourism experience. They're not coming to see a flow-through hatch with algae growing downstream. They're not coming to see 20,000 ton of dead fish rotting and floating around the place."

Spike in dolphin deaths prompts questioning Tasmanian regulators question major salmon farm operator Huon Aquaculture about the effectiveness of its "predator" nets after a spate of dolphin deaths.

From January to April 2025, a bacterial disease known as Piscirickettsia salmonis caused the mass deaths of salmon in pens in south-east Tasmanian waters.

Data reported to the Environment Protection Authority (EPA) showed almost 15,000 tonnes of dead salmon during that period went to waste facilities.

Ms Williamson said there are a "variety of perspectives" on aquaculture across coastal communities.

"I think the debate about aquaculture more broadly across Australia is a strong debate," she said.

"At the end of the day, what we're looking to do is learn from all of those and provide for a regulatory environment, a policy environment that makes sense for Commonwealth waters, which are further offshore."

The company says the research is "about what greater sovereign seafood production could look like and the role our oceans can play in Australia's food and nutrition security". (Blue Economy Cooperative Research Centre)

Trial infrastructure to be decommissioned in 2028

How many salmon farms are there in Tasmania — and who owns them? Those black, circular things floating in the water off the Tasmanian coastline? They are salmon farms. Here is how many there are — and who owns them.

After the kingfish are harvested in May 2028, the site will be decommissioned and the research findings will inform future governance of aquaculture in government waters.

Harvested salmon, kingfish and seaweed products are allowed to be sold under the project's permit arrangement, with profits fed back into the CRC program to offset research costs.

"There'll be a wealth of information and knowledge available for industry and government to make decisions on what's next and whether that is unlocking Commonwealth waters right around Australia, what that looks like, how that will be done," Ms Williamson said.

World.title: Aboriginal leaders say 'I quit' leaving NT government in defence mode
World.content:
After resigning from her position as the boss of Aboriginal Housing Northern Territory this week, Leeanne Caton came out swinging.

Her target: the NT's Country Liberal Party (CLP) government, which was elected in a landslide in 2024 on a mandate to tackle crime and anti-social behaviour.

Since the CLP's election, it has overhauled laws on bail, youth criminal responsibility and child protection, and given police a range of new powers.

NT Police say the territory has been recording lower crime rates following the changes.

But Ms Caton said she believed this was all done without listening to Aboriginal leadership.

Leeanne Caton has resigned from her role as the chief executive of Aboriginal Housing NT. (ABC News: Felicity James)

"The reason why I'm leaving is basically every piece of legislation that gets put through has a negative impact directly on Aboriginal people," the Kalkadoon-Waanyi woman told ABC Radio Darwin.

"It's killing my spirit.

" I just can't stand to see what's happening to Aboriginal Territorians in this environment at the moment. "

The straw that broke the camel's back for Ms Caton was the handling of the future of a Darwin homeless shelter, which is being shifted to the regional town of Batchelor.

Darwin homeless shelter residents to be moved to Batchelor Up to 150 residents at a Darwin homeless shelter will be relocated 100 kilometres south to Batchelor after the site's owner and the NT and federal governments could not agree on a funding arrangement.

The departure of the peak body boss is the latest in a string of resignations by Aboriginal leaders and organisations in the Territory over fraying relationships with the NT government.

Among them, the NT Children's Commissioner Shahleena Musk, independent chair of the NT Children and Families Tripartite Forum Rob McPhee, Darwin Waterfront Corporation chairman Richard Fejo, members of the NT Justice Policy Partnership and independent Arnhem Land parliamentarian, Yiŋiya Guyula.

All have made public statements about their decisions to quit and, while each has been for a different reason, they have all shared ideological opposition to the NT government's laws or policies, with most citing an inability to have their voices heard.

'Still considered flora and fauna'

Now back in the Arnhem Land bush, Mr Guyula was asked for his reaction to Ms Caton's resignation and the current relationship between Aboriginal leaders and the CLP.

"They are creating a significant divide that is harming the NT," he said.

" They are tearing us all apart by treating our people as though we are not human, as though we are still considered flora and fauna. "

He described the CLP's move to relocate the homeless shelter as "about dividing people in an attempt to push our people out of Darwin".

Yiŋiya Guyula has criticised the NT government's treatment of Aboriginal people. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

"It just does more harm to everyone," he said.

Former NT Labor politician and long-term First Nations advocate Scott McConnell said he feared diminishing trust between Aboriginal groups and the government was damaging the jurisdiction's future prospects.

"The geography of the NT is vast [but] the community is very small," he said.

"Governments need to stop dividing us based on race and geography and remember we have one shared future.

"I am very concerned that prominent leaders I know, trust and respect are finding the current environment so difficult they are leaving the front line.

"We all need to continue to support these fighters."

Scott McConnell says the NT government needs to focus on uniting, not dividing, Territorians. (ABC News: Will Green)

CLP government denies division

The NT's Acting Chief Minister Gerard Maley has fiercely defended the government's relationship with Aboriginal people and communities following the resignations.

Mr Maley also said his government stood by its continued focus on stamping out crime.

"We are listening to Aboriginal people," he said in a press conference on Friday.

"We work with many, many Aboriginal organisations right across the NT.

Gerard Maley has defended the NT government's policies and the quality of its relationships with Aboriginal Territorians. (ABC News: Dane Hirst )

"And we need to work with them because we need to make sure the Aboriginal sector continues because there are a lot of Aboriginal people here.

"We want to make sure [their] safety is also our number one priority, and we're going to work with anyone we can to make sure that happens."

Mr Maley took issue with a question about why Aboriginal people were shut out of the conversation around the homeless shelter's move to Batchelor.

"We've been working with all sorts of organisations about that," he said.

In her parting shots at the NT government, Ms Caton vehemently disagreed: “It’s [been] disrespect and a lack of courtesy all round.”

Despite the vocal criticism and walk-outs, the government continues its mission towards a safer territory; no matter who argues against the way it’s going about it.

World.title: Bomb attack at Pakistan mosque kills at least 21 people
World.content:
A vehicle bomb has exploded at a mosque near police offices in north-western Pakistan as gunmen tried to storm the compound in an attack that killed at least 21 people and wounded 80 others, police and rescue officials say.

Among those killed and wounded were police officers attending prayers at the mosque.

The coordinated assault was the latest in a surge of militant violence near the border with Afghanistan, where Pakistani Taliban militants have increasingly targeted police and other security forces as the government intensifies operations against them.

The bombing occurred in Kohat, a district in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

An attacker apparently rammed an explosives-laden vehicle into the mosque, said Zulfiqar Hameed, the provincial police chief.

At least seven armed gunmen also attempted to enter the police compound and exchanged fire with officers.

Six of the gunmen were killed, according to police, who said one suicide bomber attacked the nearby office of an intelligence agency.

Dozens were wounded in the attack on the mosque. (AP: Muhammad Sajjad)

The police compound housed counter-terrorism police, who had carried out operations against militants across the province in recent years.

Most of those killed were police officers, hospital officials said. Bilal Faizi, a senior rescue official, said most of the dead and wounded had been attending prayers at the mosque.

Residents said the exchange of fire continued hours after the coordinated attack.

Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif condemned the attack and expressed sorrow over the casualties. He directed authorities to accelerate rescue operations.

The attack was the latest in a surge of militant violence near Pakistan's border with Afghanistan. (AP: Maaz Awan)

No group immediately claimed responsibility for the attack, but suspicion was likely to fall on the Pakistani Taliban, formally known as Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP.

The attack comes a day after a roadside bomb struck a security forces convoy in the north-western Hangu district and killed six soldiers.

Government troops also conducted raids in various areas Thursday, local time, and killed 10 militants believed to be members of the Pakistani Taliban, the military and police said.

Suicide bomber strikes in Pakistan A suicide bomber detonates a device at a rally moments after speakers had accused the government of failing to properly target militants.

The Pakistani Taliban has stepped up attacks on police and civilians in recent years. In 2023, a suicide bomber killed 101 people in an attack inside a mosque in Peshawar, the capital of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province.

The group is separate from but allied with Afghanistan's Taliban, which returned to power in 2021. Pakistan often accuses Kabul of sheltering the TTP and turning a blind eye to cross-border militant attacks. The government in Kabul has denied the allegations.

Tensions between Afghanistan and Pakistan have remained high since Pakistan targeted alleged TTP hideouts in Afghanistan in 2025. The strikes triggered border clashes, prompting Qatar and Türkiye to mediate a ceasefire. China later facilitated peace talks, but the two sides failed to reach an agreement.

Friday's bombing came a day after Türkiye's state-run Anadolu Agency reported Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin met with Mr Sharif, Pakistan army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir and intelligence chief Lieutenant General Asim Malik.

Mr Kalin said Türkiye would continue to make efforts to help resolve the tensions between Afghanistan and Pakistan through dialogue, the news agency reported.

The Turkish intelligence chief also met with the government in Afghanistan. Hamdullah Fitrat, deputy spokesperson for the Afghan Taliban, said Thursday that top officials in Kabul held talks with Mr Kalin and a senior Qatari security official. The talks addressed tensions between Afghanistan and Pakistan.

AP

World.title: 'Hell on earth' for owners of units of collapsed developer at heart of ICAC
World.content:
When Michael Jones bought his first home in 2017, his wife was pregnant with their first child.

The two-bedroom apartment at Toplace's Vicinity complex in Sydney was meant to be their "nest egg", a place to build memories for the young family.

Nine years and two more children later, his family has long outgrown the apartment.

But major structural defects in the complex have left them financially trapped.

Mr Jones says his dreams and aspirations have been put off. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

"We certainly didn't imagine that there would be three children stacked up in bunks in the same room," the 40-year-old said.

"It certainly puts off the dreams and aspirations that you would have when you're my age … I would have expected by now that I would have a house that fits the amount of people that we have."

Mr Jones is one of thousands of Toplace apartment owners left to pick up the pieces of the company's collapse amid a dramatic inquiry before the NSW Independent Corruption Against Corruption (ICAC).

At the heart of it all is Toplace founder, Jean Nassif, who has remained defiant as he continues to defend the crumbled property empire he built.

Huge losses and debts

At Vicinity, temporary steel props have been supporting parts of the building since 2022, after engineers raised concerns about key structural beams.

Owners have faced repair estimates running into the millions, with one structural issue alone estimated at $11 million.

Mr Jones projects he has spent an additional $150,000 on strata costs and repairs since 2017.

He said the apartments that once sold for as much as $800,000 may now be worth as little as $250,000 to $380,000.

Owners at the Vicinity apartment complex have been bearing the brunt, and costs, of structural defects. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

It has meant there is little escape for the owners.

Many are struggling to refinance, cannot sell without suffering huge losses, and are carrying debts on homes they cannot easily leave.

Some neighbours have taken on extra jobs.

"The irony of having the last name Jones and not even being able to 'keep up with the Joneses' is not lost on me," he said.

'No-one can make me shut up!'

During Mr Nassif's highly-anticipated appearance at the ICAC this week, where he appeared twice, his rage was palpable.

Appearing via video call from his bedroom in Beirut, he spent several hours protesting his innocence, ranting and lashing out.

At one point, Assistant Commissioner Fabian Gleeson SC intervened, prompting another tirade from Mr Nassif.

Mr Nassif spent several hours during his testimony over two days protesting his innocence and lashing out. (ABC News)

Mr Gleeson: "The purpose of this inquiry is to get to the truth of certain allegations. It's not for you to attack other people. "I'd like you to just pause, no, no. Please listen to me. I've listened to you." Mr Nassif: "No. No. No. No. No. No. No-one can make me shut up."

The 58-year-old, who is wanted by NSW Police on fraud charges, denied he was hiding from Australian authorities in Lebanon, claiming he has not returned because he has faced multiple death threats.

He told the inquiry he was not corrupt, and blamed former Liberal minister David Elliott and former state building commissioner David Chandler for the demise of Toplace.

Counsel assisting Peggy Dwyer SC put to Mr Nassif: "They [Mr Chandler and Mr Elliott] alleged that there were structural defects with Toplace projects, is that right?" "They alleged that. That's not true," Mr Nassif said.

Mr Nassif has been accused of trying to damage Mr Elliott's career and have Mr Chandler removed as the commissioner to stop him investigating Mr Nassif's developments.

Both Mr Elliott and Mr Chandler are not accused of any wrongdoing.

Mr Nassif has blamed Mr Elliott (left) and Mr Chandler for the demise of Toplace. (ABC News: Greg Bigelow, Abubakr Sajid)

'Death of their dream home'

Mr Chandler found multiple defects in several Toplace buildings and used his appearance earlier in the inquiry to point to the "real victims": the owners and occupiers.

The head of the residential strata body, Owners Corporation Network, Karen Stiles, told the ABC the damage could not be measured in dollars alone.

"It was hell on earth for the owners. Tenants too were subjected to disruptions, poor living conditions, noise, and stress," Ms Stiles said.

Ms Stiles recalled residents being forced out of their homes with little warning, sometimes unable to retrieve pets of belongings.

Ms Stiles says it has been "hell on earth" for owners. (ABC News: Amy Greenbank)

She said one elderly couple built a makeshift dam in their lounge room to keep floodwater out, while another woman had to be rescued after her apartment door jammed with subsidence.

"I could say that serious defects impacted owners physically, financially, and emotionally. But that's just words," she said.

" The full picture is miscarriages, broken marriages, serious health impacts. "

Ms Stiles added that many owners were left grieving the "death of their dream home".

"While ICAC investigates corruption, exposing small people playing silly games, let's give a thought to the thousands of victims of the cavalier chess moves played with their lives," she said.

'Unedifying' evidence at ICAC

Former ICAC assistant commissioner and chair of the Centre for Public Integrity, Anthony Whealy KC, said the inquiry has "shone a very unedifying light" on activities between the state's Liberal Party, lobbyists, and developers like Mr Nassif.

While Mr Whealy believes the commission has been well-represented by counsel assisting, he said proving that it goes beyond the ugly side of politics will be difficult.

The key figures in ICAC investigation Eight weeks of public hearings by the ICAC that could change the NSW Liberal Party forever begin on Monday.

"Their task now will be to pull all that evidence together and to put a compelling portrait to say, if this is to be their submission, this isn't just a matter of factional warfare or quarrelling," Mr Whealy said.

"They'll have to amount this argument that there are deliberate attempts on the part of all of the key personnel, together with Nassif, to actually corrupt the political process."

For owners like Mr Jones, he hopes the public inquiry offers accountability, but worries there may be little consequence for those responsible.

"My fear is that this is a toothless beast that will end up wagging the finger at a few people," Mr Jones said.

"It should be a 'Come to Jesus' moment where we see real change happen in a time where we need to go through a construction boom."

World.title: Trump says he is banning CNN and other news outlets from the White House
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaTrump's White House Trump says he is banning CNN and other news outlets from the White House Michael Koziol Updated September 19, 2026 — 6:38am ,first published 5:22am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Donald Trump said he was banning cable news channel CNN and two other prominent US media outlets from the White House because of what he referred to as their “constant ‘reporting’ fake news”. The US president made the declaration on his social media platform Truth Social on Friday afternoon (Saturday morning AEST). He said MS-NOW, formerly known as MSNBC, was also banned, along with politics-focused news outlet Politico – which has just launched an Australian division. US President Donald Trump in the Oval Office on Friday afternoon. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin “Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America,” Trump wrote. He said the ban would be effective immediately. “Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow.”



The announcement is an extraordinary escalation of Trump’s long-standing animosity towards the media and outlets that report factual stories he does not like. It was not immediately clear exactly what Trump’s directive meant, given there are various levels of access that outlets have to the White House and Trump. CNN’s Kaitlan Collins in the White House press briefing room on the night a shooter targeted the White House Correspondents’ Dinner. AP Reporters are issued passes for the White House grounds, but that does not guarantee access to the “pool” - a smaller, rotating group of journalists that are allowed inside the Oval Office. CNN reporter Kristen Holmes was still present and reporting from the White House on Friday afternoon.



Asked for clarification at a news conference in the Oval Office, Trump said: “I don’t want them in my office, I don’t want them here. The ban would go as far as you can.” Trump suggested there was no particular trigger for his decision to ban the three outlets now. “It’s really just cumulative stories over the last few years,” he said. “They purposefully write negative news, and they do that because they want to try and diminish the Republicans and a Republican administration.” Donald Trump takes questions from reporters in the Oval Office on Friday after announcing a ban on CNN, Politico and MS-NOW. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin The president went on to cite his election victory and wins in all seven swing states, and suggested the banned outlets did not extend him enough praise. “I won [in] a landslide and I don’t get fair press. I get it from Breitbart, I get it a little bit from Fox [News]. What I do ask is just a semblance of truth … everything’s been a victory. It has all been a victory.”



At one point, Trump was confused when a reporter attempted to ask him about the ban. “When you say ‘the ban’, which ban? Do you know how many bans I’m involved in?” he said. He later acknowledged: “Oh, the ban on the free press, right?” In his first term, Trump attempted to ban a CNN reporter, Jim Acosta, by revoking his White House pass. CNN succeeded in having it restored via a legal challenge. CNN’s Kristen Holmes at the White House in April. She was still reporting from the White House grounds on Friday afternoon after the “ban”. Getty Images But in Trump’s second term, the White House has taken more control of the daily press pool, giving space to smaller, “new media” outlets that are typically conservative or even far-right. The White House Correspondents’ Association has traditionally managed the pool. WHCA president Jacqui Heinrich, who is from Fox News, said the group stood in defence of its colleagues at CNN, MS-NOW and Politico, who were being “singled out for doing their jobs”.



“The Constitution protects the freedom of the press from government interference,” Heinrich said. “That protection does not depend on whether the president likes a news organisation’s coverage, agrees with its reporting, or approves of the questions its journalists ask. “This is about more than the rights of journalists. It is about the right of the American people to receive a full and independent account of the activities, policies and decisions of whoever occupies the nation’s highest office.” The White House press pool in the Oval Office on Friday. Bloomberg Founded in 1980, CNN provides close coverage of US politics, with several prominent reporters ordinarily based at the White House. Owned by Warner Bros Discovery, it is set to be sold to David Ellison’s Paramount Skydance as part of a $US110 billion ($154b) merger, though Paramount recently said selling the channel was an option to resolve market concentration issues in the deal. Trump has frequently targeted CNN for its coverage of his war against Iran and other matters. He has directed many attacks at high-profile anchor Kaitlan Collins, whom he called “very dumb and unhappy” last week. He regularly accuses her of failing to smile sufficiently.



Politico’s inclusion on the banned list was surprising given it is not a regular Trump target. In his Truth Social post, he dredged up an old complaint about the outlet receiving $US8 million from the Biden administration, suggesting it was “corruption”. In fact, the money was for subscriptions to Politico’s premium products. Related Article US politics ‘Be quiet’: Trump berates reporter who asked about his relationship with female staffer CNN said it stood behind its White House team and its fair and accurate reporting. “We have right under the US Constitution to do that reporting without hindrance or interference from the government,” the network said. “Should the ban which President Trump threatened go ahead, it would be an illegal assault on that fundamental and constitutionally protected right.” There is currently no White House press secretary after Karoline Leavitt departed the role last month. She has not been replaced. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: How this team of experts guides 80-metre turbine blades down our roads with just millimetres to spare
World.content:
It is just after midnight on a winter morning when we gather at the Port of Newcastle.

In the background coal ships slink by, in the foreground an almost inconceivably vast wind turbine blade lies along the spine of a truck bed like some sort of alien life form strapped to a gurney in a sci-fi film.

It’s so big that it’s hard to fit it all into the frame of your eye from any reasonable perspective. At its tip it tapers to the length of schoolkid’s ruler. Towards that tapered end it has a jagged edge like a cartoon dragon’s teeth, a shape designed to reduce noise as it slices through the air. Peering up at its midsection, you could be looking at a warship’s prow from the ocean’s surface.

A team of transport specialists are making last-minute preparations to move this beast through the sleeping streets of suburban Newcastle and the coal villages of the Hunter Valley, along the Golden Highway to a hillside outside Wellington on the NSW Central Slopes, where it is to be raised upon a tower as part of a Squadron Energy wind farm that will soon be generating enough electricity for about 220,000 homes.

It seems absurd that this thing can be moved at all, let alone along busy roads, but the man in charge of this circus, Steve Spiller, seems impossibly calm. Jovial, even.

The police and pilots gather before the start of the turbine blade’s trip from Newcastle port to the Uungula wind farm near Wellington in NSW Photo: Janie Barrett

Form and function

Wind turbine blades, explains engineer Dr Rosemary Barnes, are the largest single-component objects that humans regularly either build or seek to move. Artefacts of the modern world tend to shrink as technology advances, but wind turbines, shaped by both economic and physical forces, keep growing.

Longer turbine blades scoop up more wind and generate more electricity with each rotation, says Barnes, who has spent a career designing, building and repairing turbines and blades around the world and now runs a renewable energy consultancy. A dozen huge turbines need fewer gearboxes, less cable and wiring, less maintenance, less concrete and steel to generate as much electricity as dozens of small ones.

As the turbines grow in length, so do the forces exerted upon them. In extreme conditions, a large blade might bend 10 to 15 metres from a straight line. Imagine, says Barnes, a diving board wilting under the weight of a herd of elephants.

“They have to survive that transfer of force hundreds of millions of times over a life of about 30 years. Every time the blade is in the three o’clock position, gravity is bending it one way, and then when it goes into the nine o’clock position, it’s bending the exact opposite way, and it keeps repeating like that as it spins. It’s just like if you bend a paperclip back and forth repeatedly, you know that small load is not going to break it, but you do it enough times, and you get fatigue loading, it is going to break.”

All this means that not only must a blade be handmade from tough, light composite materials, they are stronger when they are crafted in a single piece, rather than disassembled for transport, which brings us back to Spiller and his crew in Newcastle.

The monster they are about to move is 82 metres long and weighs just over 20 tonnes.

The port

The crew is doing last-minute checks on vehicles and equipment. Craig Carpenter is inspecting the Kenworth truck and the purpose-built trailer he is about to drive. The trailer has a long spine that can be extended to suit its load, and six sets of axles at the rear.

The steerer, Freddie Scheepers, checks the truck prior to the start of the turbine blade’s trip from Newcastle port to the Uungula wind farm near Wellington in NSW. Photo: Janie Barrett

Tonight Carpenter’s load from front grille to blade tip will be 92 metres long. Carpenter picked up the nickname Blade Runner One for his smooth driving while moving blades in Western Australia last year, but just as crucial is Freddie Scheepers, who is “steerer” and will pursue Carpenter in a van close behind the truck.

Scheepers must not only keep his own vehicle on the road, but when necessary will use a remote control to steer the rear axles of the trailer. He keeps in constant contact with Carpenter so at any given moment the two know exactly where the blade tip is in relation to the road and the rest of the rig.

“Those two are very, very close, and they’ve got a really good bond. They know what the other bloke is going to do before he does it.” Steve Spiller, project manager

When the front of the rig moves upwards and is forcing the tip towards the ground, Scheepers will also be able to raise and lower the blade itself, the last metres of which rest in a hydraulic jack that sits over the axle sets.

“Those two are very, very close, and they’ve got a really good bond,” says Spiller, watching Carpenter and Scheepers make final preparations. “They know what the other bloke is going to do before he does it.”

Mayfield Macca’s

The convoy pulls out at about 1am. There are two police cars, as required by law when moving a load of this size in NSW. There are four pilot vehicles which help manage traffic around the truck and trailer. Scheepers’ steering van hunts along behind the blade like a sheepdog, and we follow in a four-wheel drive with Spiller, the project manager.

The turbine blade starts its journey from Newcastle port to the Uungula wind farm near Wellington in NSW. Photo: Janie Barrett

Also in tow is a Transport NSW vehicle with a couple of observers, there to see if anything can be learnt or improved for future runs. After this, there are still another 195 blades to go, let alone the turbine hubs, tower sections and generators.

“When you pull back the curtain, this is what building a wind farm looks like – thousands of individual movements, decisions and people are needed to get every component to site,” Squadron Energy’s chief executive Rob Wheals later observes.

Steve Spiller, Ares Group project manager, accompanies the turbine blade on its journey from Newcastle to the Uungula wind farm near Wellington in NSW. Photo: Janie Barrett

“At 80 metres long and shaped like a banana, each blade is one of the most challenging pieces of infrastructure to ever move.”

From Spiller’s radio we can hear occasional chatter from the pilot vehicles, but he leaves the “Bladerunners” to their own quiet comms channel so they can concentrate. Before we’ve even left the port precinct the blade tip sweeps out over a cyclone fence, clearing it by what seems like centimetres.

Spiller doesn’t flinch. Every move is rehearsed, every distance measured.

The turbine blade crosses the highway from the wrong side on its journey from the Port of Newcastle to the wind farm. Photo: Janie Barrett

At a McDonald’s on a roundabout on Industrial Drive in the neighbouring suburb of Mayfield, the cop cars and pilot vehicles splay out to halt traffic coming from three directions, and Scheepers climbs out of his van to flick a switch on the rig to remote control. He adjusts the height of the suspension, and then he steers the rear of the rig around the turn.

The turbine blade crosses the highway from the wrong side at the intersection of Industrial Drive and Maitland Road, Mayfield. Photo: Janie Barrett

Speed picks up, at least until the caravan reaches the Hunter Expressway. To make it onto that section, the pilots block traffic on the expressway in both directions while the Bladerunners navigate the rig 80 metres down an off-ramp into what would otherwise be oncoming traffic, then drive a kilometre down the wrong side of the road before crossing back. Spiller seems pleased by how smoothly this dance of traffic and truck is performed.

The remote used for steering the rear of the truck that carried the enormous turbine blade. Photo: Janie Barrett

As we head northwest towards the Golden Highway, Spiller relaxes enough to tell his story. He became an expert in moving big stuff almost by accident. At 19, he took a job with a logistics firm and began moving shipping containers. Half a decade later he was moving wind turbine parts, and the work took him around the world with the global giant GE. He has moved bits and pieces of wind farms by sea and land and even air, at one point chartering the world’s biggest aircraft, an Antonov, to move a wind turbine hub and six generators from Leipzig to Adelaide.

In Germany, near the Polish border, he recalls coaxing blades through tiny villages on a truck that could raise them to near vertical from the base to navigate tight spaces.

Freddie Scheepers changes the steering of the rear of the truck from manual to automatic via an external switch on the truck. Photo: Janie Barrett

In Australia, it’s easier because we have so much space. “I moved 300 blades through Toowoomba without complaint,” he boasts. Today he works for the Ares Group, which was contracted by GE, who built the blade at a factory in China, to shepherd it safely off the ship in Newcastle and on to the Squadron Energy site outside Wellington.

Despite the late hour you can tell the convoy is having an impact along the way. In one hamlet we pass within metres of the old coal miners’ cottages. A man in a dressing gown watches on in the pre-dawn from his veranda. His expression is impossible to read in the revolving lights.

Craig Carpenter, the truck driver who drove the turbine blade from Newcastle to the Uungula wind farm. Photo: Janie Barrett

From the sections of widened road you can see along the way the years of preparation that went into this operation. EnergyCo, the NSW government authority responsible for delivering the state’s five renewable energy zones, has spent $130 million preparing this route.



Inland

There are rules about moving oversized loads in the dark on the Golden Highway, so the convoy pulls over before dawn. A quiet pall descends across the still convoy, except for cheerful noises from Carpenter’s cabin. He hums and sings to himself and taps out a rhythm before drifting into silence.

In bright early light, against the country homes in Denman, the enormity of the blade begins to become clearer. It is longer than whole blocks of the little town. Along the Golden Highway, the convoy at times creeps up to something approaching normal traffic speed, and time passes quickly until we reach the site of the wind farm, headquartered on a sheep and cattle operation on rolling green hills east of Wellington.

As the truck prepares to tackle the narrow dirt roads built for the project we are taken into a sprawling site office for a safety induction. Whiteboards on the walls show the progress in the construction of each of the 69 turbines that will soon be operational here. There are posters boosting the “core values” of Squadron Energy, which is owned by Tattarang, the investment company that is in turn owned by Andrew Forrest and Nicola Forrest. The values include “Humility” and “Frugality”.

It is midafternoon on a hilltop I had last seen two years earlier when Energy Minister Chris Bowen and Forrest attended a sod-turning ceremony. Bladerunner One finally steps out of his cabin and offers up a great two-armed stretch to the sky. By now Spiller has left the site on his way back to his head office in Melbourne. Workers on-site scramble over the blade, breaking it free of its harnesses and lowering it into a cradle by a half-built tower. By the time it is operational it will stand 148 metres from base to blade tip.

There’s no getting around the impact the project is having on a beautiful landscape. Construction pads are scraped into the ground by each tower and the new roads hum with the sort of traffic flow you’d expect in a prosperous town.

The turbine blade arrives ar the Uungula wind farm near Wellington in NSW Photo: Janie Barrett

Later I ask farmer John Holland, owner of Uungula, for which the wind farm is named, what he makes of it all. He speaks with a careful, precise manner, aware of the controversy that wind projects attract. Squadron, he says, will clean up after the construction is complete, leaving him with new roads, giving even better access to the property’s ridge lines.

He says he has no fear about the impact of the turbines on his stock. Visiting other wind farms, he has seen sheep “camping” under the towers for shade. He reckons the turbines look majestic, but admits that when he saw renders of what they would look like spread across the land he loves he found it “a little confronting.”

He thinks renewable energy is a part of the solution for Australia’s growing energy demand, but not the only one. Like many farmers, he opposes grid-scale solar plants taking up agricultural land. But he has practical considerations too. The rent Squadron will pay for each turbine will let the family retire a fair chunk of debt, though he won’t say how much. Nor will he say how many turbines his farm will host. “That’s a bit like asking how much money I’ve got in the bank. It’s a bit rude.”

But he is happy to say the income has helped settle the questions of succession that can cause such grief to farming families, and to update equipment and improve fences and dams.

“It’s the confidence to be able to run the property the way it should be run.”

I ask him what Uungula means.

“It’s an Aboriginal word,” he says. “It means wind in the hills.”

Workers unload the turbine blade after its long journey. Photo: Janie Barrett

Get to the heart of what’s happening with climate change and the environment.

World.title: Celebrity accountant Anthony Bell to offload Rose Bay pad after $26m buy
World.content:
Exclusive PropertyNewsTitle Deeds Celebrity accountant Anthony Bell to offload Rose Bay pad after $26m buy Kristy Johnson September 19, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Accountant to the stars Anthony Bell has put his Rose Bay apartment on the market in an expression of interest campaign. Bell, whose clients have included Karl Stefanovic and Michael Clarke, said that while he initially intended to make the Rose Bay unit his principal place of residence, he enjoyed renting at Barangaroo’s Crown Residences so much that he decided to buy there. Money manager Anthony Bell has decided to offload his harbourside Rose Bay apartment in Sydney that he renovated. Records show Bell, chief executive officer and principal of accounting and advisory firm Bell Partners, bought the five-bedroom, four-bathroom Rose Bay apartment for $9,657,000 in 2024 from architect Andre Heyko-Porebski and his wife, Louise. Bell intended to make the unit his principal place of residence.



While renovating the interiors, Bell rented at Crown Residences in Barangaroo, a complex now home to a smorgasbord of corporate heavyweights and rich-listers such as Alex Birkenstock, heir of German cult sandal brand Birkenstock, Luna Park co-owner Bill Gravanis, and Lawrence Myers, chief executive officer of James Packer’s family office Consolidated Press Holdings. Anthony Bell and Annika Martyn For a short time, there was also a tenant at the Rose Bay pad. Bell said that he enjoyed Crown’s proximity to his office at King Street Wharf, a short walk away, so much that he decided to purchase there. Records show Bell bought a four-bedroom apartment at Crown for $26,588,000 in December 2024 that settled in July the following year.



Also in 2024, Bell sold his Dover Heights home for $20.78 million after he bought it for $11.5 million in 2017 from his mate, Channel Seven star Larry Emdur and his wife, Sylvie. Related Article Exclusive

Title Deeds Fruit and veg supplier drops about $9.5m in 24 hours on Crown unit Bell also owns two Queensland properties – a Surfers Paradise home bought with wife Annika Martyn, the founder of wellness brand GG Vitality, for $5.3 million in 2024, and a Noosaville abode purchased with then-wife, former model and TV presenter Kelly Landry, for $10,301,000 in 2017. Bell now has sole ownership of the Noosaville residence. The Rose Bay harbourside pad features a neutral palette with refined marble finishes, a custom bar, private gym/Pilates studio, jacuzzi and a north-east facing terrace. Bill Malouf and David Malouf of Highland Double Bay are the listing agents.



Fashion designer lists Byron Shire home Wayne Cooper, the fashion designer behind the eponymous brand that was stocked in Myer for many years, has put his Byron Shire home on the market with a price guide of $4 million to $4.5 million. Fashion designer Wayne Cooper is selling his Myocum abode in the Byron Shire. Records show Cooper and his ex-wife, model Sarah Marsh, purchased the five-bedroom, five-bathroom, resort-style acreage with a pool in Myocum for $5.09 million in 2022. But when the marriage fell apart, it was listed the following year with a $4.5 million guide. Photos on the walls in the listing show Cooper and his wife, Elizabeth Adams.



When it didn’t sell, it was put to auction, attended by Cooper as one of the bidders and Marsh as an observer. After about two bids, Cooper secured sole ownership of the luxury property for $3,871,000. Wayne and his ex-wife Sarah Marsh Scott Barbour The three-level abode has wraparound balconies, covered entertaining areas, a tennis court that awaits a refresh, and views across the coast to Julian Rocks and Mount Warning. Eagle-eyed buyers may notice photos of Cooper and his current wife, Elizabeth Adams, a former UBS banker whom he wed in 2023, in photos on the walls of the listing. Ku Darroch of Byron Bay Property Sales, who is selling the residence alongside Riley Buckland, said the property was a rare estate that immediately left an impression.



“The combination of its elevated coastal outlook, generous scale, privacy and established grounds is exceptional. There is a wonderful sense of space and freedom here, less than 20 minutes from Byron Bay’s fabulous beaches,” he said. Related Article Exclusive

Cammeray listing The Cammeray home of architect, developer and former restaurateur Dominic Choy and his wife, Irina, is for sale, with local sources indicating the price guide is in the high $20 million range.
