World.title: That NFL match actually cost double previous estimates. But the jubilation made it worth it
World.content:
NationalVictoriaOpinion That NFL match actually cost double previous estimates. But the jubilation made it worth it Stephen Brook September 19, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Winter in Melbourne was awful. The weather unremitting: cost of living, deadly potholes, local shops firebombed, local gyms firebombed, teenagers stabbing each other. But unexpectedly, a burst of joy. The three-hour, 10.35am Friday NFL match at the Melbourne Cricket Ground between the Los Angeles Rams and San Francisco 49ers last week had it all. Grand spectacle, folly (courtesy of the LA Rams attempts to defy jet lag) and something we have been missing for a while – jubilance. I didn’t attend the match nor understand what was going on. And for me, the real pleasure was not the onfield clash of titans but in the stuff that surrounded it. Fans show their support at the NFL game at the MCG. Ruby Alexander I owe thanks to a bunch of US sports writers (plus at least $30 million of taxpayer money) to blast away my jadedness about Melbourne and appreciate its pleasures anew.



I know that genuflecting to foreign arrivals is uncool, verging on pathetic. We Australian journalists have been doing this shamelessly ever since 1961 Hollywood star Vivien Leigh, fresh off the plane at Sydney Airport, was asked by the press corp what she thought about Australia. Before she had even left the terminal. Her famously arch response was: “I don’t know. You are standing in the way.” Last week it was San Francisco 49ers chief executive Al Guido smoothly telling me how “starstruck” he was arriving at the MCG. Yes, this made me happy. And I wouldn’t be the only one who looked upon their city anew after a crack squad of US football reporters arrived a week early alongside the 49ers and got among it, listing the CBD cafes they loved, posting snaps of their big brekkies. David Lombardi, of The San Francisco Standard, even taught a few Melburnians a thing or two as he looked out at the MCG from Princes Bridge, noting the City of Melbourne motto was “We gather strength as we go”. Who knew that? We all do now.



Even the highest powers were not immune. “Prayer the winning strategy as NFL makes its Australian debut,” proclaimed the newsletter of the Catholic Archdiocese of Melbourne. “Ahead of their Friday morning clash, a group of players from the San Francisco 49ers joined Melbourne’s Archbishop Peter A Comensoli for a pre-game celebration of the Eucharist. The Mass was organised through the team’s coaching staff and allowed players like star running back Christian McCaffrey, a Catholic, to partake in a different kind of preparation before the big game,” the newsletter reported. And you thought queues of 200 people outside the NFL pop-up shop on Bourke Street was the real story. NFL fans queuing up for official merchandise on Bourke Street on September 10. Eddie Jim All appropriate deference to Him, but the real star of the show was Grant Cohn, who covers the 49ers on SI.com. He posted on every aspect of his Melbourne visit. His lunchtime sausage roll and an iced coffee at 7-11. How to eat Vegemite on toast (a little bit of spread and a lot of butter). His honest assessment? “Pungent, definitely not Nutella.”



Fans include Victoria’s newish Major Events Minister Anthony Carbines, who took over from Steve Dimopoulos. And the AFL, which promptly hired him. There are lessons here for local journalists, about energy, intensity, but also in the foregrounding of daily pleasures that we treat nonchalantly. For Craig Hutchison and Eddie McGuire, ceaseless impresarios of sport and major events through their various media companies, the NFL match was nothing less than an exclamation point marking the end point of Victoria’s listless COVID-19 years. “It was a demonstration of love of sport, our passion for big events and why our city stands above all others in the world per capita in the want, willingness and enthusiasm to do that at 10.35am on a Friday morning (for) a sport that is not played here,” Hutchison enthused on his SEN podcast The Sounding Board. McGuire, unofficial ambassador for exuberance on Triple M’s Mick in the Morning radio program, said he was proud of the city.



“This is the end of the COVID era … this is the end of all the dramas, we can lift our head and be proud of Melbourne again. Back in town in a big way. “Let the politicians fight it out I don’t care about any of the stuff like that … fill a pothole in, throw a machete in a bin, we don’t care. It was tough on the Broadmeadows line in the 1970s.” Another perspective Opinion

Victoria After 37 years, I finally visited Melbourne. Here’s my verdict Paul Marshall Travel writer This was a lot, even for FM breakfast shows that are noted for exuberance – and we should note that one of McGuire’s very many hats is as a board member of Visit Victoria, which funded a large chunk of the NFL visit. Which brings us very neatly to the question of cost. The normally forthright Hutchison was uncharacteristically coy when asked directly how much the game had cost the state. “More than $15 million and a lot less than it was worth.”



While the “ballpark” figure of about $15 million per game was broadly quoted in the media, what was largely ignored was the other cost – staging the event. Simply put, that doubles the cost to at least $30 million. Extra transport, security, fan zones, the exclusion perimeter around the MCG, replacing the turf at the MCG, the MCG underground carpark becoming a vast player dressing room with players’ cabinets. And don’t think that all that media attention from NFL journalists just happened without some input from Visit Victoria. Then there was grand dinner at Government House for more than 230 guests featuring a trio of chefs – Andrew McConnell, Karen Martini and Dan Hunter, organised by The Big Group and Food + Drink Victoria. But the industry is very confident of a handsome return on investment. Hoteliers were ecstatic. Crown’s hotels had its second-biggest Thursday ever, while the Accor group, which has 53 hotels across Melbourne, including the Sofitel, Pullman and Novotel, was 25 per cent up on standard occupancy compared with the same time last year. What a waste of money better spent of schools, hospitals and potholes, I hear you say. Yes, critics might well complain such major events are a sugar hit, but there is no doubting the importance of the visitor economy for us, worth a record $48.6 billion (in the year to March 2026), creating 320,100 filled jobs, the government says.



Tourism is the state’s second most valuable export sector – bringing in overseas dollars – after education, which is undergoing a reset as the federal government bans family visas and visa hopping for international students. So the visitor economy is a long-term sustainable one. NAB put out a press release predicting that about $300 million would flow through Melbourne businesses thanks to the NFL. Which was quickly adopted as gospel. But it didn’t say what would be ordinarily spent over that period anyway. The real economic impact assessment will come later, if it is ever released. Carbines would not talk costs, either the NFL fees or staging costs, but said government investment in major events cemented the city as “Australia’s sporting, creative and cultural capital” that would “showcase Melbourne to millions around the world”. “A packed major events calendar … generated $3.64 billion in economic impact in 2025,” he said.



Major events must be bought at sensible price and have an ongoing benefit, as one-off events are a waste of money, says former premier Jeff Kennett, who took the grand prix off Adelaide in the 1990s in what was regarded a signature move indicating Victoria’s revival, giving the state a sign of hope amid painful restructure and large job losses. “Other states are envious of what we deliver. We must be forever on our toes,” Kennett says. In reference to the state’s poor balance sheet, he doesn’t suggest crimping on major events. “Here are a few other things we are wasting money on,” he says, nominating government waste, the Suburban Rail Loop, Big Build corruption, and interest payments on government debt, which could rise steeply if the state suffered a credit downgrade. Major events and sport such as the AFL were a “regular contributor to people’s happiness” he concludes. And NFL will be back again as part of its three-match commitment over four years (with an option for a fourth). But is there any Visit Victoria money left to spend on anything else?



Visit Victoria, which is on the cusp of releasing its latest annual report, must demonstrate a 10 to one economic benefit, which is in its constitution. The proof will be in whether the state can continue to attract other major events. The undoubted jewel in the crown of global musicals, Paddington, is rumoured to be going to Sydney. Can Visit Victoria win it for Melbourne? Watch and see. The strategy of bread and circuses, panem et circenses, literally as old as the Roman Empire, means subsidising the cost of grain and staging mass public spectacles to keep the masses happy, and – crucially – distracted from their rotten status in life. But it worked, here and in the US, where the game averaged 18.5 million viewers, ranking it among the top three most streamed games for its time slot. Related Article Analysis

NFL 2026 Singing, cheering and an American takeover: Why the NFL’s MCG experiment was a smash hit



David Lombardi, of The San Francisco Standard, says the popularity of his videos from Australia were an “explosion even bigger than Super Bowl coverage”. “Melbourne, you made this exponentially more massive than Americans expected. The 49ers certainly benefited from their time in the sporting capital of the world.” The fact is, we need this. As one damning assessment I came across put it:“Melbourne has to buy its visitors, Sydney, London and New York do not.” Now the days are warmer. I no longer wake at 3am. The ACO is playing Mozart’s Last Symphonies at Hamer Hall next week. The grand final is a week away. A ringtail possum is camping out in my barbecue, nesting in some local shrubbery. My niece has named it Nicholas Jr after her dad. Even Southern Cross Station seems cleaner. Meanwhile, Grant Cohn is still going. Back home, he has watched Two Hands and is trying to source a copy of The Castle.



And he announced a return visit to Australia in April when he will go wine tasting with his dad and cover the AFL. But in Adelaide, for Gather Round. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Flu season passes peak - but watch out for a second wave
World.content:
Many doctors are breathing a sigh of relief as the flu season passes its peak - but there is a warning of a sting in its tail.

Hospitalisations from flu-like illnesses have dropped sharply in latest figures - to about 10 in 100,000.

Children under-five have fallen for the first time since 2 August.

College of General Practitioners clinicical lead Luke Bradford said GPs had also noticed a big drop-off in the community.

After a mountain of cases this year, there was now a level of herd immunity from both vaccinations and people who had the virus, he said.

"That's why the peak drops off each year - it gets to the point where the virus can't pass on to the next person at the same rate, because they are immune to it."

Auckland GP and Immunisation Advisory Centre senior Māori medical advisor Mamaeroa David said it was great to see the drop, as warmer weather hit, but another spike may yet come.

A resurgence or a long tail of winter illnesses was not unusual, she said.

"Often every year, we relax, but I feel like we've got another cold spell to come and that's when we get another round of sickness come through," she said

Influenza A had driven the big surge in winter illnesses this year, with the super infectious K strain, and influenza B could still take off.

Weekly hospitalisation rates with SARI. Supplied/PHFScience.nz

Even though hospitalisations had dropped in the latest figures, they were still very similar to the peak of last year's outbreak, another illustration of how big this season was.

Both doctors said anyone who had not been vaccinated for flu should still take the chance to get one.

The vaccine was now free for under-fives, for 65 and over, and for many others vulnerable to serious infections.

World.title: A Niue-based trust has been named a finalist in the prestigious Earthshot Prize
World.content:
The Niue Ocean Wide Trust has been announced as one of the finalists in the Earthshot Prize.

The trust sells Ocean Conservation Commitments to individuals, companies and governments, building a 32 million dollar endowment to fund permanent protection of the Pacific Ocean for future generations.

Coral Pasisi, Vice Chair of Niue Ocean Wide Trust and co-architect of Ocean Conservation Commitments Earthshot Prize

Coral Pasisi, Vice Chair of Niue Ocean Wide Trust and co-architect of Ocean Conservation Commitments, said

Niueans do not see the ocean as separate from us; it is part of our identity, our knowledge and our responsibility to future generations.

"We did not want protection to remain a promise dependent on the next grant. We wanted finance that matched the length of that responsibility.

Earthshot recognition can help us complete the Trust, deepen the work already under way and share what we are learning with other island nations on their own terms," she said.

The Earthshot Prize was launched six years ago by Prince William and is seen as the world's most prestigious environmental prize.

The BBC reports Earthshot remains one of the key priorities of Prince William's public work.

"Around the world, people are proving every day that we can restore nature and tackle climate challenges. Our 2026 finalists are an incredible example of that," he said.

Britain's Prince William, Prince of Wales Jordan Pettitt / POOL / AFP

The five winners will be announced in November in Mumbai, and will each receive more than NZ$2-point-3 dollars.

World.title: 'We're one people' - a young Tongan man's te reo Māori journey
World.content:
Over the years, 21-year-old Siaosi (George) Lavelua (Kolomotu'a, Makave) has often made the trip north to the Waitangi Treaty Grounds with freshly made 'otai in tow.

His whānau business, Lav's 'otai - dealing in the much loved Polynesian drink that typically mixes coconut and fruit - is the longest-serving 'otai operation in Tāmaki Makaurau.

It has become a familiar fixture at Waitangi celebrations, Auckland night markets and various community events across the region.

"It's something I've grown up around my whole life. Wherever there's a big event, we're usually there serving 'otai and meeting people," Lavelua said.

Over the years, events such as Waitangi have become extra special for Lavelua - a Tongan who has dedicated over five years of his life learning te reo Māori.

"When I was able to go up there (Waitangi) and then converse with a bunch of different people in te reo Māori, just seeing the connections and friends and people that you can make just through speaking te reo, it definitely, yeah, made me very appreciative to be able to learn the language," Lavelua said.

Lavelua grew up in central Auckland, speaking Tongan at home with his parents.

Siaosi (George) Lavelua serving 'otai for his parents business, @lavsotai Geoffery Matautia

His reo journey began as a year 9 at Auckland Grammar School, and was initially an opportunity for him to spend class time with other tauira Māori and Pasifika.

"For the first three years of my schooling, in every other class except Te reo Māori, I was the only, like one or two Pacific or Māori people in my classes," Lavelua said.

"I just wanted to be with other people from the Pacific, and so then I took te reo Māori."

Lavelua loved it so much that he stuck it out until year 13, and quickly realised the merging similarities between the Tongan language and the Māori language.

"As I started to learn the language, I noticed that there were so many similarities in terms of, like, old Tongan," he said.

"There was quite a lot of words or the same sentence structure that mirrored exactly what I was learning, what I speak at home. And so it just made my journey a whole lot easier."

While it wasn't an 'easy journey, Lavelua said it was well-worth the investment.

Crossover

Online, he has began sharing content speaking te reo Māori.

People often comment on how impressive his trilingualism is, something Lavelua said reinforced his own appreciation for the Tongan language.

"Since I grew up speaking Tongan, it was always sort of something on like a back burner, it wasn't necessarily something that I thought too much about," Lavelua said.

That changed as he watched how people responded to his reo, including Māori who frequently tell him of their desire to learn and speak their own language one day.

"It's really a deeper love for my own language and my own culture. And just seeing how blessed I was to retain that."

"Growing up, I've always had such a deep respect for the Māori culture and Māori people," he said.

"I think it's a beautiful thing what Māori had done here in New Zealand, and Aotearoa, being able to retain the culture and traditions and languages, even all the way up to religion, and that's something that we certainly didn't really have in other parts of the Pacific, being very Christianised and things."

The values between cultures cross over, too, Lavelua said.

When asked which te ao Māori principles resonate, he landed on whanaungatanga.

"Hospitality and that sort of relationship they have with other people…it's about the home, it's the relationships of those around us, the community, the environment," he said.

And Lavelua said that point is one of the real lessons he came to learn while learning te reo Māori.

"There are some people who very distinctly categorise Māori and Pasifika as two separate categories, or two separate people," he said.

Siaosi (George) Lavelua's whānau @lavsotai Siaosi (George) Lavelua

"But then definitely through learning te reo and learning a lot more about the culture, you really see that overlap and like that true understanding that you actually are one people at the end of the day."

One of the biggest surprises on his journey so far has been understanding the historical relationships between Pacific and Māori.

Lavelua began reading Pacific history, and came across accounts of Pacific sovereigns - he points to King Tāwhiao, alongside Tongan and Hawaiian royalty - who would write to one another as colonisation took hold.

"They all had actually been writing letters between each other to sort of help each other maintain their own sovereignty," he said.

" Seeing that back in the day, specifically with these leaders that we had in our communities, it was definitely heartwarming to see and really opened my mind on just how interconnected the Pacific really is, and how interconnected the Pacific should be."

Journey

Now based in Brisbane, working across marketing and hospitality, Lavelua said distance from Aotearoa has sharpened the meaning of events such as Te Wiki o Te Reo Māori, and what they mean to him.

It's a good reminder, he said, to celebrate the week, identity, and community.

He also has advice for other Pasifika and non-Māori who are thinking of undertaking their reo journey.

"Just give it a crack, just give it a go. I don't think that anybody can ever be perfect in a language. I definitely wasn't perfect when learning te reo Māori, I'm still not perfect at this point, but that's definitely something that holds a lot of people back.

His favourite whakataukī encompasses this message well.

World.title: Tonga claims Oceania netball championship title
World.content:
Tonga's national women's netball team has claimed a double win at home in the Oceania Women's Netball Championship in Nuku'alofa.

The Tala has not only secured an invite to the 2027 Netball World Cup but it's also taken the Oceania title, after beating Samoa 71-63 on Friday evening.

Tonga finished the week-long competition undefeated.

Coach, Jaqua Pori Makea-Simpson said the team is over the moon.

"Feels good waking up today," she said. "An epic performance to close out an undefeated week."

Tonga led that game 31-24 at halftime.

Tonga secured its world cup spot by beating Fiji 72-60 in a close match on Thursday, that win coming on the back of victories over Papua New Guinea, 71-47 and the Cook Islands 81-55.

The Tongan Tala was also the only Pacific team at the recent Commonwealth Games, by virtue of its top 10 placing in the World Netball rankings.

Meanwhile, Samoa also celebrated getting the second world cup invite available to Oceania at the event.

World Netball's head of events Kate Agnew said the invite means the teams have qualified in terms of results, but documentation still needs to be completed to make it official.

The Samoan Netball team has qualified for the Netball World Cup Oceania Netball

Despite losing to Tonga on Friday, Samoa recorded wins over PNG, 72-56, a close 56-50 win over Fiji and a 72-50 defeat of the Cook Islands.

Tifaimoana Samoa head coach Natalie Mathews said although the team lost the final match to Tonga she was proud of the team's performance.

"Proud of our seniors for leading from the front and our debutants will be better for the experience on the biggest stage there is, " she said.

Fiji ended up as the third-best team in the Oceania competition, their young side managing to beat both Cook Islands and PNG.

Cook Islands [green] and Samoa at the Oceania Women's Netball Championship in Nuku'alofa. Oceania Netball

The Fijian Pearls beat the Cook Islanders 65-63 and PNG 61-40.

Cook Islands managed a win over PNG 64-54, with PNG returning home from the event without a win.

World.title: Country Life: The farm photographer who captured a changing New Zealand
World.content:
Ron Vine's crisp, observant and sometimes intimate black and white photos capture New Zealand farming at a turning point.

Now a collection of more than 1400 images he took between 1934 and 1947 has received UNESCO recognition, sitting alongside the papers of Katherine Mansfield and the photography of Marti Friedlander.

Vine travelled to remote parts of the country as the Great Depression was easing, towing his mobile dark room behind him to record how farmers and communities were transitioning into more modern methods.

His photojournalism helped influence the take-up of new agricultural trends and developments, according to archivists.

The farm photographer who captured a changing New Zealand Country Life Download MP3 8m

Follow Country Life on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, iHeart or wherever you get your podcasts.

The collection has been recognised by Aotearoa New Zealand's UNESCO Memory of the World Trust and achieved inscription on the Memory of the World Register.

It is now housed at the Walsh Memorial Library in the Museum of Transport and Technology (MOTAT) in Auckland.

Vine's attention to detail is a feature of the collection, MOTAT pictorial librarian Malcom Duffy told Country Life.

Mr E.D. McLennan and farm workers in a paspalum field, 1940 Ron Vine, Walsh Memorial Library, The Museum of Transport and Technology (MOTAT)

"They were very beautiful and it took a bit of research to understand the context and the place of this photography in the New Zealand context, but they were still remarkable, very, very crisp and clear photography, done in natural light, of course, because he was out in the field."

And there was a real sense of intimacy between Vine and his subjects.

"Especially when it came to the farmers, the farm workers - there was a real sense of the pride in their work that came through."

Vine began his agricultural journalism career riding a motorbike.

Ron Vine sitting on a motorcycle sidecar combination Ron Vine, Walsh Memorial Library, The Museum of Transport and Technology (MOTAT)

"He literally just hit the road in his motorcycle sidecar. He went out there, he introduced himself to farmers, was happy to talk about their problems, possible solutions and this was a network he built up over the next four or five years. So we do know that he got sick of travelling on the motorcycle side car after roughly 12 months."

Vine then moved on to a more sophisticated way of getting around.

"That's where his story really starts to pick up as both an agricultural journalist and a man very invested in technology because he proceeded to then take a Model T Ford and break it down and made a whole caravan from packing cases - the Model T Ford chassis - and that's how he continued his journeys for the next few years, towed by a little Austin 7 and he built his own dark room in that caravan as well, which was made by hand, with almost no training or experience, and he created his own photographic enlarger using a headlamp from a car."

His number 8 wire solutions included a developing tank designed to be placed in creeks and streams to wash film and prints when he was out and about.

Ron Vine's car on road to Maungapiko, 1936 Ron Vine, Walsh Memorial Library, The Museum of Transport and Technology (MOTAT)

Vine's photos are significant as a record of New Zealand agriculture in transition.

In the 1930s and '40s, land was being cleared and turned into pasture.

"The landscapes and areas he documented, a lot of them had been deforested and then had just developed naturally into scrubland, a lot of fern, a lot of mānuka, and so when he arrives in the 1930s, the government is actually starting to release these lands.

"They still don't have the significant visual elements we always identify with farming - there's no full irrigation ditching, the races aren't really visible yet, the fences, the sheds, the shelter belts, they're not fully there.

"Often they're very wide open vistas and to me it's a very interesting aspect because we often see either the wilds of New Zealand or we see farms that are very well established."

A man standing near fallen trees and scorched earth. Ron Vine, Walsh Memorial Library, The Museum of Transport and Technology (MOTAT)

Seedling pine trees planted on sand dunes. Ron Vine, Walsh Memorial Library, The Museum of Transport and Technology (MOTAT)

Experts say the collection is also significant for its images of Sir Āpirana Ngata's Māori land development scheme and Māori communities.

"I think it's really important to Ron because he was raised amongst the native school communities, and he grew up in Māori communities which were often farming not the best lands, not totally productive, and so for him to be there as the Māori land development scheme was gathering strength, I think his connection with Māori communities around the Ruatoki and Urewera area, that enabled him to get that sort of relationship where he could be very documentarian in his photography.

"It was very warts and all, but it's also possibly the best record of Āpirana Ngata's Māori land development scheme in the country.

Duffy said mutual respect comes through in the photos of Māori.

Mr P. Osborne and students standing outside Horohoro Native School, 1939 Ron Vine, Walsh Memorial Library, The Museum of Transport and Technology (MOTAT)

A group of children standing near the Kaikohe Native School bus charabanc., 1940 Ron VIne, Walsh Memorial Library, The Museum of Transport and Technology (MOTAT)

"Also his respect for the hard work that's gone into the land. So much of it was done without any sort of mechanisation. It was all done by hand or with horses. And it's a real testament to the hard work that was put in."

Farmers, labourers, livestock breeders and heads of local agricultural associations were typically subjects for Vine's camera and many would become friends and subjects of future reporting for publications like The New Zealand Farmer.

"There's a real dichotomy in those images too, because he was also photographing communities that were actually quite wealthy at times ... but then we go to those rural communities and we see people who are often living and working within raupō huts or very primitive structures, so we've got that real contrast between urban and rural life of New Zealand in the 30s."

Vine wanted people to prosper and believed in the value of institutional and generational knowledge, without being judgmental, Duffy said.

Opouriao Dairy Factory in Rūātoki, 1932 Ron Vine, Walsh Memorial Library, The Museum of Transport and Technology (MOTAT)

Two men and a dog on the porch of a house at Glinks Gully Ron Vine, Walsh Memorial Library, The Museum of Transport and Technology (MOTAT)

"I think his approach often was looking back at what had worked and what hadn't.

"We know that that's very important in the agricultural sector - if the farmers aren't aware of the sort of problems and outputs of their land and their stock over the previous decades, it's hard to find a way forward that's going to be productive."

Duffy said people can view the collection at MOTAT in Auckland and librarians would be happy to guide them through it.

"If there's a particular family or geographic location that people are interested in, we can always assist them with that."

Men packing lemons inside the Kerikeri Citrus Factory. Ron Vine, Walsh Memorial Library, The Museum of Transport and Technology (MOTAT)

World.title: Country Life: 25 years of Banks Peninsula conservation
World.content:
Surveying 1600 hectares of rolling hills could be done on foot - but it's much easier from the air.

"This is our most recent drone purchase," James Wright of the Banks Peninsula Conservation Trust told Country Life.

"We use it on farms for capturing, basically, native biodiversity from above."

Banks Peninsula Conservation Trust uses this drone for land surveys. RNZ/Anisha Satya

25 years of farmland conservation Country Life Download MP3 18m

Follow Country Life on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, iHeart or wherever you get your podcasts.

He's flying over Tim Coop's property in Port Levy - a massive sheep and beef operation, and also home to remnant indigenous flora.

Sheep and beef farmer Tim Coop. RNZ/Anisha Satya

"These totora are kind of the last few giants on the bench there, something we're looking to protect as much as possible." Coop said, leaning over the remote in Wright's hands to watch its camera feed.

Wright mans the drone while colleague Josh Foster follows it with binoculars, keeping an eye out for birds that might chase or run into it.

Wright and Foster are part of BCPT's farm biodiversity team. They help farmers and landowners on the peninsula learn about what's in their backyards.

BPCT biodiversity team members Josh Foster (left) and James Wright. RNZ/Anisha Satya

On-foot surveys and eDNA tests added to the information provided by drone photography, Wright said.

"I'll capture the imagery, send it to [Josh], he looks through it, figuring out what sort of biodiversity we've got on the property, put that all together in a nice package and send that back to the farmer."

Coop, the fourth generation to farm his land, said he was in the "early stages" of understanding his farm's mix of flora.

"The way that you know what you've got is by doing surveys and tests. It's quite cool.

"You don't realise how much it regenerates, until you start looking down on it."

That sentiment is shared by Sarah Anderson, kaituitui (co-ordinator) of Te Ahu Patiki charitable trust, who care for the farmland-turned a public park and native restoration project.

Te Ahu Patiki charitable trust kaituitui Sarah Anderson. RNZ/Anisha Satya

"Pictures tell stories and they reach a much wider audience," she said. "That's incredibly valuable.

"The whole range starts [on] the highest peak on the peninsula and goes all the way over to what's previously been called Mount Bradley."

BPCT surveyed the 500-hectare area just two weeks before heavy flooding in mid-February, which left "fingernail scratches" through some parts of the park.

Anderson said it provided a rare change to document how native plants grow back from barren 'ground zero' strips.

"We will be able to bring these guys back every couple of years and map the changes… which I think will be fascinating for lots of people."

The Te Ahu Patiki mountains, viewed from Orton Bradley Park. RNZ/Anisha Satya

The farm biodiversity programme began in 2023, but the trust itself celebrates a quarter century of conservation work this year. It was formed in 2001 by a group of farmers.

Foster said the trust's collaborative approach to on-farm conservation made for good long-term progress on the land.

"We can talk to farmers more on their level, and not show up and say, 'We are the experts, listen to me'.

"My expertise is only valuable in the context of the expertise of people who actually live and know that land.

Coop said: "There's such a respectful relationship. If you're going to move forward, that's incredibly important.

World.title: Tauranga eyes options to sell stake in airport
World.content:
Tauranga City Council will consider its first steps towards potentially selling off shares in Tauranga Airport this week.

On Tuesday the council would vote on whether to establish a working programme to evaluate future options to run the airport - including a Council-Controlled Trading Organisation (CCTO) - which could allow fundraising through the sale of an interest in the facility.

The airport was currently operated as a standalone council activity and did not receive ratepayer funding, but the council noted its role in supporting regional connectivity, tourism, trade and investment.

The working programme would evaluate five potential options, among them: establishing a trust, creating a Council-Controlled Organisation (CCO) or establishing a CCTO to run the airport.

Council documents said moving to a CCO could enable the airport to be run at arm's length from council and allow for improved focus and accountability.

However, the CCO could not be established with a specific goal of profiting from the management of the airport.

The establishment of a CCTO would be explicitly commercial and better suited to optimising revenue generated by the airport.

The CCTO could also be established with the express provision of providing an ability for the council to raise funds through the sale of a minority interest in the organisation.

Council officers noted that considerations could be included to ensure that any proceeds from such a sale would be used to assist with council activities.

If approved, the working programme would be overseen by an Airport Working Group comprising two elected members and one mana whenua representative.

The group would provide guidance throughout the options development process, including stakeholder engagement, due diligence and assessment of the potential governance models.

Council head of commercial Alastair McNeil said Tuesday's decision would be confined to establishing a process of how best to re-evaluate council's future ownership of the airport.

"Council is not being asked to make any decisions on the future ownership or governance of the airport at this stage. The proposal is simply to undertake further analysis of the available options and bring the findings back to Council for consideration," McNeil said.

World.title: ACT faithful line up for selfies as Paul Henry roadshow rolls through New Plymouth
World.content:
Paul Henry brought a bit of showbiz razzle-dazzle to the campaign trail on Friday night as his Unlocked roadshow rolled through New Plymouth.

The former journalist and television presenter mixed politics and banter with a few anecdotes from his long career in front of a friendly crowd of more than 250 people at a packed-out Devon Hotel conference centre.

No sign here of the type of interjections which saw a private security guard remove a podcaster from a similar event in Dunedin.

Instead dozens of party faithful lined up politely for selfies with the man of the hour at the end of the show.

Nicky Howarth was one of those who posed for a picture.

"I just decided why not, he's a bit of a celebrity, isn't he. So, I can actually share that on Facebook, which is what I was thinking of doing, you know, just sharing on Facebook to say that we'd been and to encourage people to vote."

She liked ACT's plans to scrap the Waitangi Tribunal and Climate Change Commission, but wasn't so sure about its support of data centres and genetic engineering technology.

Dozens of people lined up for selfies with Paul Henry after his election campaign event in New Plymouth. More than 250 people packed out the Devon Hotel's conference room. After outlining ACT policies, Henry took questions from the floor. Robin Martin / RNZ

A woman, who preferred not give her name, had also got a snap with Henry - who was ranked number four on ACT's party list.

"Well, I've actually already had a photo with him. I've always loved him, always loved his shows and stuff.

"He's awesome. I was always going to vote ACT, but when Paul Henry's standing I was like perfect, cherry on the top."

She reckoned ACT had strong values, and were not afraid to challenge the status quo."

Henry shared with his audience that there'd been some trepidation at ACT headquarters about the roadshow's name - Paul Henry Unlocked.

"One of the chiefs said it sounds like he's been released from prison? And another chief said, 'You haven't been to prison, have you?'"

Cue a Henry anecdote about being jailed in Iraq while working as a foreign correspondent.

"I was beaten up quite badly with a group of other journalists and some other combatants and other annoyances to Saddam Hussein.

"All of us were locked up in the desert. It was horrible. I was the only one that got out. After about four days I was let out... that is just how bloody annoying I can be."

His audience chuckling, Henry then rolled through ACT policy - cutting red tape, equality under the law, no new taxes, lowering of corporate tax, a tougher benefit regime for those out of work, targeted immigration settings and the general encouragement of excellence - before taking questions from the floor.

He was quizzed about cutting immigration when some New Zealanders didn't want to work, the breaking up of the electricity gentailers, supposed handouts to iwi, the emergence of data centres and how to get young people into homes.

Whereupon he reached into the ACT policy grab-bag for responses which for the most part mollified his audience.

Henry finished the evening with another anecdote about one of the times he'd met Queen Elizabeth II while working as a royal correspondent. It involved a swan-shaped hors d'oeuvre, pâté and a mistimed expletive... and then it was time to queue for selfies.

Paul Henry. Robin Martin / RNZ

Those choosing to head home were mostly happy with what they'd heard.

Glen Stevens was in property development.

"I've liked him for a while, he's got some guts and stands up for what he believes in and doesn't sit on the fence, which I like."

He was attracted to ACT's promise to cut red tape.

Denise Wood enjoyed what she'd heard.

"I though it was fantastic. I've changed my views on politics. What Paul said made sense and he answered [questions] honestly."

She supported ACT policy to broaden assisted dying laws.

Mike Morrissey enjoyed his night out but wasn't happy with ACT's strategy of targeting the party vote, arguing it could contribute to a parliamentary overhang.

World.title: 'Never too old': 83-year-old footballer still getting a kick
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Robert Johnstone has just two rules when he crosses the white line to enter the football field.

"The first rule is don't fall over, because you're out of the game and you look a fool," the 83-year-old says.

"The second rule is get a kick."

Mr Johnstone, affectionately known by his teammates as "Robbie J", lives in South Australia's Riverland, but has also lived in Victoria, New South Wales and Queensland.

Robert Johnstone says he is always trying to improve and is constantly working on his skills. (ABC Riverland: Jackson Byrne)

He was a latecomer to Aussie Rules football and only picked up the game in his 70s.

And despite his age, he's not ready to give up the sport he's fallen in love with.

"I'd never tried a group sport. I'd been a loner. I did a lot of fun-run walking and stuff," Mr Johnstone says.

"Now I can't walk past a footy without wanting to kick it.

" It's just magic to be out there with like-minded spirits. "

Still quick off the mark

Mr Johnstone plays for his local team, the Riverland Superdogs, who compete in South Australia's AFL Masters league.

The league only allows players age 35 and up, and has competitions across Australia.

The Riverland Superdogs played in the curtain raiser before the 2024 SANFL Russell Ebert Tribute Match. (Supplied: Robert Johnstone)

Mr Johnstone has the title of oldest player in the competition.

"There's an element of danger to it, and I've still got that little bit of ego; I want to be out there," he says.

" You've just got to accept the fact that everyone's quicker than me, but I do have some little wins. "

Riverland Superdogs president Rob Romeo has played alongside Mr Johnstone for almost 10 years.

He says even in his old age "Robbie J" has grown, becoming a better, more refined player.

He might not be a spring chicken, but Robert Johnstone can still kick the ball "almost 30 metres". (ABC Riverland: Jackson Byrne)

"He's usually the first one at trainings," Mr Romeo says.

"Things have slowed down slightly over the years, but there was a time when he would put us to shame.

"He's like a little kid, just trying to get a little bit better at kicking, and we'd just say, 'Don't put too much pressure on yourself. Just come out and enjoy yourself.'"

'No-one keeping score'

While there is no finals series or a premier in the AFL Masters, the competitive spirit and camaraderie has brought players back season after season.

Mr Romeo says the Superdogs don't care how good prospective players ae, as long as they are willing to give it a go.

He encourages anyone over 35 looking for community involvement and exercise to consider it.

"As a kid, you go to footy because your mates go, and this is no different," he says.

Robert Johnstone says finding the AFL Masters competition is one of the best things that's ever happened to him. (ABC Riverland: Jackson Byrne)

"It opens up your friendship web, whether you come from broken relationships or whatever else that may have happened in your life.

"The exercise also helps with mental health."

Inclusivity the key to success

Former AFL Masters and West Adelaide chief executive Conny Wilson also resides in the Riverland.

She has seen "Robbie J" up close on a number of occasions, and says he embodies inclusivity, which AFL Masters is all about.

"As an aging society, these are great opportunities for people to either reconnect with past teammates or for people looking for friendships to come out and try," Ms Wilson says.

"It's also been exceptionally well received by women, who growing up didn't have the opportunity to play football."

Mr Johnstone's passion for the game also extends to his adopted state, seen in his distinctive mullet, transforming from grey to SA's iconic red, blue and yellow for the annual AFL Masters state carnival, which he will play again this year in the over-65s.

Rob Johnstone's hair is ready for the masters state carnival in Newcastle at the end of September. (Supplied: Robert Johnstone)

While the octogenarian doesn't expect to dominate his competition at the carnival, he is confident he can once again make his mark.

" I rarely get pinged for holding the ball, that's a badge of honour. "

World.title: How Jack Gunston became an unlikely key to Hawthorn's flag hopes
World.content:
There are a lot of things that get better with age. Fine wine, cheese and even a good pair of jeans can improve as the clock winds along.

Football players aren't meant to be in this class. They start to break down as they get old. The mind is often willing, but the flesh is weak. The physical game takes its toll, with years of hits adding up.

Players like Jack Gunston, however, are determined to prove this wrong. Turning 35 next month, Gunston has preserved himself but actively gotten better. His last two years have been his most fruitful in front of the big sticks, and his value to Hawthorn never more important.

Gunston failed to top 60 season goals in the first 15 years of his AFL career. Since turning 33, he has done it twice.

Gunston's longevity has already seen him kick more than 35 per cent of his goals since turning 30, the sixth-highest rate among AFL-era players with over 500 goals. By the end of his career he may be on the podium.

Gunston sits at the vanguard of a revival of a slice of old-school footy. The era of the stay-at-home lead-up forward was recently thought to have gone the way of the dodo, but its revival has been largely implemented by a rising young crop, alongside Gunston that is. That's thanks to a somewhat hidden rule change.

In his fourth stint, at a third club, Gunston is set to lead a Hawthorn forward line into a shot at its first grand final in 11 years. In its way stands his old club.

Gunston's fourth coming

It's a well-worn cliche that nobody knows what a player will become when their name is first read out on draft night. While pundits will be quick to offer a comparison to a current player, each develops on their own, at their own pace.

Gunston was tabbed by Adelaide on potential, more than what he had shown to date in junior football. One of the youngest in the 2009 draft class, Gunston was green, slight and seen as a work in progress.

But as would eventually be the story for the rest of his career, Gunston quickly exceeded expectations at West Lakes. While the skinny frame and blond tips make him seem like a completely different player, Gunston's first goal — beating his defender for pace on the end of a full field rebound — bore a striking resemblance to his final evolution.

Gunston has been blessed to never carry his burdens alone. His whole career has been spent forming multi-pronged partnerships with multiple All-Australian quality forwards.

Most famous was his key role as one of five career All Australians in Hawthorn's legendary 2010s dynasty forward line, but before that he cut his teeth with Taylor Walker and Patrick Dangerfield. Most recently, he has partnered dangerous smalls, including current foils Nick Watson and Dylan Moore.

Gunston's stint in Adelaide wasn't long, but was fruitful. As the young Victorian was trialled all over the ground and worked on building fitness, there were more than just hints at the electric nature of his career to come.

Most know what happened next at the Hawks: three premierships and plenty of acclaim.

But the good times didn't last forever, and that boom period was followed by a fallow one. Injuries, and a short-lived move to Brisbane, left Gunston's career at the precipice.

His move back to the Hawks, and a shift in the way footy is played, has more than revived his career.

The connection is made

Over the past two years, Gunston has effectively become a player reborn.

Instead of the high-roaming beast pushing away from his match-up, the veteran now stays anchored closer to goal. Gunston often sits in space light years from the play, wastelands usually ignored by forwards in years past.

Gunston has forged a fast connection with the Hawks' contingent of skilful young midfielders such as Jai Newcombe, Connor Macdonald and Josh Ward. In some ways it resembles past great Jason Dunstall's bond with Platten and Jarman.

Hawthorn's set-up usually preserves this open space for Gunston to operate in. With this amount of grass, the 300 gamer gets the chance to deploy all the time-honoured tricks in his arsenal.

Gunston feigns, feints and baulks his opponent into submission. He'll lead to one side before darting back. Without support, direct defenders can be trapped in the blender of his athleticism. The connection between Gunston and his teammates is such that they know where he is going before his last decisive move.

Gunston is also unafraid to use the pockets. The instinct for most defenders is to hedge towards goal, and to cede the territory towards the boundary line. Over the past two years Gunston has made opposition sides pay for doing so.

Gunston has converted more goals from near the boundary, at a better clip, than anyone in the league in the past two years.

Gunston isn't alone in the depth in which he is deployed. A handful of players and teams across the league are experimenting more with "vertical spacing", or making the once-compressed ground long again.

Intriguingly, many of the other stay-at-home forwards are on the younger side of the league's key position forwards. Part of this influence may be down to the introduction of anti-density rules in junior footy, and the flow-on effects when those players have entered the league.

Marks inside 50 have steadily increased since the introduction of the rule in junior footy that requires a certain number of forwards to stay within the forward half and 50 at resets. This may have influenced younger players to be more patient with movement patterns, and shown coaches the value of space in the modern game.

The Brisbane test

Hawthorn faces a fearsome opponent on the way to the grand final: Gunston's old team, Brisbane.

The move of Gunston to Brisbane was designed to help the Lions get over the top. The veteran was meant to help mentor younger Lions forwards in the dark arts of finding space. In reality, early-season injuries, the tragic death of his father, and natural development meant Brisbane found different pathways to premiership glory.

Now it's Hawthorn that is the upcoming challenger.

Six weeks ago the reigning premiers saw off Hawthorn easily. Gunston held up his end of the bargain, kicking three of the Hawks' eight goals, but they were convincingly beaten all over the park. Despite dominating clearances, they completely lost the transition game and were torn to shreds by the furious Lions attack.

In order for Gunston to have a chance to be a difference maker, the Hawks have to be patient in the middle of the ground, and get the ball forward enough to have a chance.

World.title: History beckons for Fremantle as greatest-ever fightback propels it into grand final
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

When Hayden Young went back and kicked a remarkable goal from the boundary after the three-quarter time siren, he couldn't have known it would spark his side's greatest comeback.

Never, in 753 AFL games across more than 30 years, had the Dockers recovered from more than 18 points down at the final change to win.

But against Sydney, after what can only be described as an underwhelming three quarters of football, Fremantle created yet more history in a season that keeps on giving to turn a 21-point deficit into a 12-point win.

The Dockers had never won while trailing by 18 points or more at three-quarter time. (AAP Image: Dan Himbrechts)

Shai Bolton produced a stunning long set shot, before Patrick Voss fended Dane Rampe into next week and curled home a brilliant goal to cut the margin to nine points.

Isaiah Dudley, in just his second AFL season, then booted the goal that sent Fremantle to just its second Grand Final.

"We were down for so much, we were playing so poorly for it felt like large parts of it, but we hung in there," Dockers captain Alex Pearce told Fox Footy.

"I don't want to say it's a sense of relief; it's a sense of joy and pride for my teammates in how we were able to play our best footy in that last quarter when the pressure was at its highest."

Flicking the switch

Fremantle fans would have been forgiven for giving up on the Premiership dream midway through the third quarter.

Sydney, undermanned as they were, had an answer for every challenge the Dockers threw their way.

Fremantle had more of the ball but struggled on the short SCG, kicking over the head of their forwards time and again.

Josh Treacy struggled to have an impact as the Dockers missed targets inside 50 on numerous occasions. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

Voss, Jye Amiss and Josh Treacy combined for just eight disposals in the first half, which was emblematic of the Dockers' struggles.

Sydney's pressure was intense, as it appeared the Dockers would crack as they did against Hawthorn two weeks ago.

But after the final change, they showed the resolve that had made them the best second-half side for the season.

"We put a bit of pressure on them [Sydney], and they probably didn't play with the same dare," Dockers coach Justin Longmuir told Fox Footy.

"It was a game of adjustments. I didn't think our intensity was off early; I think our method was off early."

Swans fairytale ends

With all the personnel missing, it seemed inevitable that at some stage the Swans would run out of legs.

And in the face of the Dockers' onslaught, they wilted.

Errol Gulden was immense with 36 disposals and eight tackles, while Brodie Grundy toiled in the ruck in a salivating contest against Luke Jackson.

Luke Jackson won his battle against Brodie Grundy, kicking two crucial goals. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

But ultimately, the Dockers had too much talent across the ground, and somehow found another gear to run over the top of the Swans.

It brings to an end a season that will forever be remembered for the events in mid-August which saw the Swans suspend five first-choice players.

The Swans produced a stunning win over Brisbane in their qualifying final in which they also lost captain Callum Mills to a serious knee injury, but couldn't repeat the dose.

"We were in a really good position for three-and-a-bit quarters, and to their credit, at this time of the year you can't give a team any momentum, and they took it," Swans coach Dean Cox said.

"They've been the best team all year, and it showed you've got to play a full 120 minutes against those teams to get the result you're after."

Sydney will be pondering what could have been, while Fremantle has an eye on history.

World.title: Wallaroos edge towards their version of the 'Matildas effect'
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Earlier this year, when speaking about the Wallaroos contesting the 2029 World Cup on home soil, Rugby Australia (RA) president Kristy Giteau revealed her dream.

"I envision packed stadiums, girls screaming after a game to get an autograph by one of our Wallaroos players," she said in June.

Giteau and her RA colleagues are hoping the Wallaroos will create a similar buzz to that generated by the Matildas at the 2023 FIFA Women's World Cup, which was co-hosted by Australia and New Zealand.

Many have described this as the "Matildas effect", with the inspiring run to the semifinals triggering a massive spike in female participation numbers and driving record TV audiences.

RA knows the Wallaroos — ranked ninth in the world — must improve on the field to achieve a similar impact, although this relies heavily on the ongoing process of shifting the program to full-time status.

The players and coaches are doing their part, as illustrated in last weekend's encouraging performance against world champions England.

Despite the 48-15 defeat in Salford, the Wallaroos produced an effort suggesting they can be competitive at the World Cup in three years' time.

They led 10-5 at half-time, which was uncharted territory for the England squad.

The Red Roses hadn't trailed at the half-time break since 2020.

This wasn't a fluke, as the Wallaroos played with aggression in both attack and defence, forcing the Red Roses to make uncharacteristic mistakes.

Wallaroos captain Siokapesi Palu Sekona illustrated her side's physical approach against the Red Roses. (Getty images/Rugby Australia: Lewis Storey)

But it wasn't just the Wallaroos' physicality in the first half that was impressive.

The build-up to prop Faliki Pohiva's 31st-minute try showed they'd identified weaknesses in England's defensive formation and line-out.

Test rugby, though, is an 80-minute game and the Red Roses steamrolled the Wallaroos in the second half, scoring seven tries to one.

This was largely due to the fact they're on a full-time program and their superior strength and conditioning shone through against the semi-professional Wallaroos.

Honourable defeats won't count at the World Cup, but given where the Wallaroos are at this stage of their journey, they deservedly took positives from the result against England.

"It was a pretty good outcome for us, that first 40 minutes," Wallaroos scrum half Samantha Wood said.

"I think the confidence was gaining throughout the half, when we defended our line successfully a few times, and then being able to score one try … it gave us a lot of confidence."

'Intent and purpose'

The Wallaroos want to build upon the confidence Wood spoke about as they prepare to face world number four France in Aix-en-Provence on Sunday morning, AEST.

The coaching staff have drilled into the squad the need to maintain an aggressive approach for more than one half of rugby.

Wallaroos fade after strong start vs England The Wallaroos give world champions England a scare in Salford, but the Australians cannot take advantage of a half-time lead as the Roses secure a thumping victory.

"A lot of the momentum that we did build was off the back of our intent and purpose around contact and collision [on] both sides of the ball," Wallaroos assistant coach Mike Ruthven said.

"A lot of our focus [against France] will be making sure we're really consistent in that contact and collision space.

"You take a huge amount of confidence out of that [England Test] but it's our capacity to be able to sustain that and be really consistent over 80 minutes that is ultimately what we're chasing."

Implementing an effective game plan is just one of the Wallaroos' goals during their three-Test European sojourn as part of the WXV Global Series, which also includes a clash with Scotland in Edinburgh on September 27.

With an eye on the World Cup, blooding players to build depth is among their priorities.

Winger Amelia Whitaker started against England in her first Test, while reserve forward Jemma Bemrose was also given a debut.

Piper Flynn has the chance to make her Test debut against France. (Getty Images/Rugby Australia: Lewis Storey)

Another winger, Piper Flynn, has the chance to earn her a Test cap after she was named on the bench to play France.

RA director of women's high performance Tim Walsh, who's essentially caretaker head coach until Sione Fukofuka assumes the role next year, made it clear to 23-year-old Flynn she's not on tour to make up the numbers.

"He's given me a lot of confidence in myself," Flynn said.

"As he said to me, and I'm sure to a lot of the other girls, we've been picked here for a reason."

That reason is to build towards the World Cup.

As RA dreams of enjoying its version of the Matildas effect in 2029, Flynn doesn't want to miss out on the action.

"It's a really exciting target to work towards," Flynn said.

"It gives us all a little bit of fire in our belly to try and build up and grow stronger, and grow our game to push towards winning a home World Cup."

World.title: Canberra ends Wests' NRLW fairytale in finals shut out
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Zahara Temara's big-game experience has driven Canberra to their first NRLW finals win, helping break the heart of Wests Tigers with a low-scoring 6-0 shut out at Campbelltown Stadium.

With both sides playing their maiden finals match after four years in the competition, it was Temara who shone brightest on Friday night.

The former Queensland State of Origin star laid on a bullet cut-out pass for Isabella Waterman for Canberra's first-half try.

With the Raiders holding a slender four-point lead for much of the second half, the Canberra No.7 then broke the line wide open and drew a penalty to go 6-0 up.

Beyond that, the Canberra halfback's management of the game proved the difference, forcing two dropouts and kicking the Tigers into submission.

Temara won a premiership with the Sydney Roosters in the 2021 season and could now come up against her old club next Saturday in a grand-final qualifier.

The Raiders will play the Tricolours if the all-star Brisbane roster beats Newcastle this weekend, otherwise they will face Gold Coast if the Knights win through.

Canberra controlled the majority of Friday night's game, with prop Chloe Saunders laying an immense platform with 173 metres and 73 of them post contact.

Do you have a story idea about women in sport? Email us abcsport5050@your.abc.net.au

In truth the Tigers did well to hold on as well as they did, forced to make 85 more tackles with the Raiders camped on their line for the majority of the first half.

But they were unable to land a blow at any point in the second half, with a 10-5 penalty count against them stifling the chance for many opportunities.

And when Tigers fullback Caitlin Turnbull put on a last-minute kick and chase to try and pull off a miracle, it was again Temara who was there to clean it up.

The defeat ends what has been a fairytale season for the Tigers, who won only five games combined in their first NRLW three seasons and collected the past two wooden spoons.

The joint venture had been in contention for a top-two spot before a brutal end to the season, as they reached the first top-flight men's or women's finals series in 15 years.

But their momentum was halted when they were flogged 58-0 by the Titans a fortnight ago, before last week's 22-10 loss to Canberra.

The Raiders, meanwhile, have beaten the Broncos and pushed both Gold Coast and the Roosters, making them a genuine threat over the next fortnight.

AAP

World.title: North Melbourne's 32-game winning streak over after shock loss to Hawthorn
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

North Melbourne's record 32-matchwinning streak is over after Hawthorn pulled off a massive AFLW upset.

The Hawks' 4.8 (32) to 3.7 (25) win on Friday night in Cairns is their greatest win since they joined the women's league in 2022.

The Kangaroos' sequence of straight wins is the longest in AFL, VFL and AFLW history. They had not been beaten since 2023, going undefeated in their 2024 and 2025 premiership runs.

Hawthorn's Jacqueline Dupuy said the feeling was "unreal".

"In my head, I was just panicking, thinking, 'How long have we got?' I reckon I looked at the bench three or four times in the last 90 seconds, just praying for the siren," Dupuy told ABC Sport.

"It was pretty unreal when it finally went. And to be able to look around at these girls I love so much and just see the sheer joy and feel that myself was amazing."

Hawthorn's win was made even more impressive given the absence of captain Emily Bates, who went down with an ACL rupture last weekend.

The triumph came off the back of relentless pressure.

North led by 10 points at the main break in blustery and humid Cairns conditions, but Hawthorn's Mikayla Williamson kicked the only goal of the third term, pulling the match to within three points.

Four straight behinds gave Hawthorn the lead in the last term for the first time since the first quarter. Cairns native Jacqueline Dupuy then kicked a goal to give Hawthorn a seven-point buffer at nine minutes.

Jacqueline Dupuy of the Hawks said the win was unreal. (Getty: Emily Barker)

But North was not done, with Blaithin Bogue kicking a goal against the run of play.

Inside the last two minutes, Hawks ruck Lucy Wales snapped the sealing goal.

"It's just a credit to the kind of player Lucy is. She's clutch. She is one of the most consistent players for us and I just feel like it was very fitting that she was able to kick that winning goal," Dupuy said.

North's last loss was the 2023 grand final against Brisbane. The Kangaroos then started the 2024 season with a win and a draw, before starting their historic streak.

Friday night's tally was also their lowest score since 2023.

It is a great start to the weekend for the Hawks, ahead of Saturday's AFL preliminary final against Brisbane, when they will also start as underdogs against the two-time defending premiers.

The AFLW victory puts the team just outside the top four.

"It's always tough to go to sleep after a game, and certainly feeling pretty jacked right now," Dupuy said.

"But I'm sure we'll get a rest and go up again in six days, which would be exciting to head down to Geelong."

With AAP

World.title: 'Devastated' Swans' tumultuous season ended by stirring Freo fightback
World.content:
Fremantle has pulled off a sensational last-quarter comeback to surge into the AFL grand final with a tense 12-point win over Sydney.

Trailing by 27 points late in the third quarter, the Dockers kicked the last six goals of their preliminary final to win 12.11 (83) to 10.11 (71) at the SCG.

Fremantle advances to the second grand final in club history, where they will meet either Hawthorn or Brisbane.

Justin Longmuir's men were staring down the barrel of an early exit before Hayden Young converted a difficult set shot after the three-quarter time siren, and were full of running in a gripping finish.

Young (28 disposals), Andrew Brayshaw (29), Caleb Serong (28) and Shai Bolton (two goals) were instrumental in the victory.

But it wasn't assured until the dying stages, when Isaiah Dudley ran into an open goal with less than two minutes on the clock.

"Words can't describe how proud I am of everyone for stepping up," Fremantle captain Alex Pearce told Channel 7.

"There were just so many moments where guys stood up under the fiercest of pressure.

" We played our best footy in the last quarter when everything was against us. "

Luke Jackson finished with two goals in an entertaining ruck battle with Brodie Grundy.

Dudley's second major was the Dockers' fifth of a dominant final quarter, in which Patrick Voss's huge fend-off and checkside goal on the run was a highlight.

"[Our forwards] were beaten early, and it was hurting us a little bit," Pearce said.

"Our ball use into the forward line was diabolical at times. We were just kicking it to the red jumper.

"But wow, our forwards stood up [in the final quarter]. They stood up like big men."

Sydney's brave effort came without injured captain Callum Mills and the five stars banned in the fallout from the Pullman Hotel scandal.

Errol Gulden (36 disposals) was brilliant in setting up their lead, with Logan McDonald (three goals) dangerous in attack.

"It's gut-wrenching, devastating, but I'm overwhelmed with pride in what we've been able to do over the last couple weeks," Swans stand-in captain Dane Rampe said.

"We didn't get that result tonight, but I felt over the last couple of weeks we took a couple of steps in the right direction towards [getting] back respect and trust of not only our fans and our club, but the AFL community in general."

Swans coach appeared emotional during his post-match press conference, but spoke of his pride in the group.

"I'm extremely proud. To put on a performance like that, I'm just extremely proud of everyone uniting and galvanising to get our season to the last game, and we fell short," Cox said.

"It is raw, but that is footy, footy is a hard game. I learnt a hell of a lot. I've got a chance to really reflect on the season we've had.

"We want to be playing these games of footy every year, that's what we strive for. I love prelim finals.

"We've got to learn, and I do as well, and we'll spend the off-season doing that. They've been really supportive and wanted to action everything we wanted to put in place. They've just been really hungry to improve.

"It's hard to say it's a missed opportunity when you play a really good footy team."

AAP

World.title: Blistering Head ton leads Australia to victory in second ODI in Zimbabwe
World.content:
Travis Head has returned to his blistering best after a lean spell with a 75-ball century to help power Australia to a convincing 84-run victory over Zimbabwe in Harare and wrap up their ODI series triumph.

Stand-in captain Mitch Marsh, who cracked a fine half-century himself, saluted "a complete performance" as the world champs found a new gear following their opening win on Tuesday and moved into a 2-0 series lead with a match still to come.

Head hadn't mustered more than 26 in any of his last eight knocks in all cricket, including Tests and IPL fare, but the left-hander was back at his intimidating best on Friday as he crushed 112 off 84 balls to spearhead Australia's formidable 6-356 after being asked to bat.

In reply, the hosts never looked like challenging as the return of Josh Hazlewood (2-48), and a couple of wickets apiece for the spin trio of Adam Zampa, Cooper Connolly and part-timer Matt Renshaw, ensured Zimbabwe could muster only 272 off their 48.3 overs.

Connolly, able to bowl his left-arm spin again after five months when he was unable to do so because of back trouble, delivered another fine all-round performance.

The left-hander built on the magnificent start provided by Head and captain Mitch Marsh, who put on a thunderous opening stand of 130 off 19 overs, as he followed up with 78 off 69 balls. Rising star Ollie Peake then chipped in with 41no off 18 balls, with three sixes, to give the innings a rousing finale.

Connolly also took a catch and the final two wickets of Zimbabwe's innings off successive balls to finish with 2-25.

It also proved a landmark day for Australia's premier white-ball spinner Zampa (2-62) as he picked up his 200th ODI wicket.

The only downside for Australia, who are using this trip to Africa as a reconnaissance mission before next year's defence of their ODI World Cup, was an injury to paceman Billy Stanlake, who went down with a side strain in his fifth over.

The final match of the series will be played at Harare on Sunday before the tour rolls on to South Africa for three ODIs and three Tests.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.
